title: A StayGold-based calcium ion indicator
abstract: Abstract Genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca 2+ ) indicators (GECIs) enable visualization of Ca 2+ dynamics in living systems but often suffer from limited photostability during prolonged imaging. The recent discovery of StayGold, a green fluorescent protein (FP) with exceptional brightness and photostability, opened the possibility of addressing this longstanding challenge. Here, we sought to establish whether a monomeric variant of StayGold (mStayGold) could be converted into a single FP-based GECI. Through extensive protein engineering, we generated a functional mStayGold-based GECI, HiCaRI (Highly intensiometric Ca 2+ Responsive Indicator) by fusing Calmodulin (CaM) and the ckkap binding peptide from K-GECO1 into mStayGold(J). HiCaRI exhibits a large Ca 2+ -dependent inverse fluorescence response (Δ F / F min = −15) while retaining high brightness and improved photostability relative to previously reported GFP-based GECIs. Although the current variant represents a first-generation prototype with shortcomings in terms of Ca 2+ affinity and photostability (relative to StayGold and mStayGold(J)), this work demonstrates the feasibility of constructing single FP-based GECIs from a highly photostable fluorescent protein.

title: Engineering the NAT–ULT module increases seed number per pod in soybean
abstract: Abstract Seed number per pod is a major soybean yield-component trait, yet experimentally validated causal modules remain poorly defined. Here, we identify and functionally validate a soybean NAT–ULT regulatory module controlling ovule and seed number per pod. Through a visual screen of a fast-neutron-irradiated Glycine max cv. Williams 82 population, we isolated MO27, which increased four-seeded pod frequency from approximately 2–4% in wild type to 27–30%, without major changes in plant architecture, total pod number, or seed morphology. Comparative genome hybridization mapped the phenotype to a 46.7-kb chromosome 2 deletion containing GmNAT1 and chromosome 6 deletions encompassing GmULT-B1 and GmULT-B3 . Ovule-clearing analysis showed that increased seed number originated before fertilization through elevated formation of four-ovule ovaries. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis of GmNAT1 , GmULT-B1 , and GmULT-B3 increased four-seeded pod frequency without detectable penalties in 100-seed weight, total pod number, or plant height. Tomato SlULT triple mutants also increased floral organ and locule number, supporting conserved ULT-like function in reproductive organ patterning. RNA-seq interaction analysis revealed a chromosome 6-dominant transcriptional state, accompanied by selective non-additive reprogramming of hormone/ovule-number and cell-wall-remodeling modules. Integrated genetic and transcriptomic analyses support a hierarchical model in which NAT–ULT perturbation may enhance meristematic competence and remodel reproductive developmental programs, while additional fast-neutron-background-associated transcriptional changes may further modulate the phenotype. These findings define NAT–ULT as a molecular target for engineering soybean seed number per pod.

title: Cytokinin regulates the gravitropic setpoint angle of seminal roots in barley and wheat
abstract: Abstract Plant root growth angle determines the spatial distribution of roots in soil and thereby influences access to water and nutrients when these resources are heterogeneously distributed. In barley, multiple seminal roots emerge at distinct gravitropic setpoint angles (GSAs) and they reliably re-establish their characteristic growth angles following reorientation, indicating robust intrinsic control. However, the molecular basis underlying GSA variation among roots within a single root system remains unknown. Here, we combined individual root type-specific transcriptomics with laser-capture microdissection to profile gravity-responsive zones (root cap, meristem, and elongation zone). We identified two CYTOKININ OXIDASE/DEHYDROGENASE ( CKX ) genes whose expression in the root cap was associated with root-specific GSA. Functional analysis showed that ckx mutants, which show higher cytokinin levels, exhibit significantly steeper seminal root GSAs, implicating cytokinin catabolism in root angle regulation. Consistent with this, exogenous cytokinin treatment induced a dose-dependent steepening in root angle in barley. Analyses of gravitropic curvature after gravistimulation further showed that ckx mutants exhibit altered gravitropic responses, indicating that CKX -mediated regulation of the root angle depends on gravity-responsive pathways. Notably, GSA-associated CKX expression patterns and cytokinin-dependent root angle responses were also observed in wheat, suggesting a conservation of this mechanism across cereals. Together, these findings identify cytokinin as a key regulator of root specific setpoint angles within a root system architecture, with potential implications for optimizing crop resource acquisition and yield.

title: A claim-centred atlas distinguishes biological corroboration from analytical depth in plant stress transcriptomes
abstract: Abstract Plant stress transcriptomes are reanalysed far more often than independently replicated, obscuring whether apparent consensus reflects biological corroboration or repeated analysis of the same experiments. Here we present PLEASE (PLant Evidence Atlas for StrEss), a claim-centred atlas that treats the independent experiment, rather than the analysis, as the unit of evidence. PLEASE resolves 88,789 analytical records into 62 dependency-resolved study families. A calibrated core of abiotic and biotic stress programmes persists after dependency collapse. Yet support erodes sharply as claims become more specific. Across stress, organ and cell-lineage contexts, independent-match coverage falls from 1.00 to 0.26 while directional agreement remains near 0.68. Three quarters of sampled contexts contain only one study family. Thus, missing comparable experiments, not pervasive disagreement, is the main barrier to context-specific corroboration. PLEASE separates analytical depth from biological corroboration and pinpoints where independent experiments are most needed.

title: Agronomic characterisation of a common buckwheat germplasm collection unlocks resources for genomics-assisted ideotype breeding
abstract: Abstract The mechanisation of agriculture has achieved major increases in labour productivity but has also led to an erosion of agrobiodiversity. Neglected and underutilized crops such as common buckwheat ( Fagopyrum esculentum Moench) offer the potential to diversify food production systems but require major genetic improvement to compete with established crops. Although target traits for breeding such as more homogeneous ripening, reduced height, larger seeds and higher and more stable yields are well known, large-scale and field-based phenotyping data of diverse common buckwheat accessions across multiple environments are still scarce. Here, we tested the agronomic performance of a common buckwheat germplasm collection consisting of 170 accessions of diverse origin. The collection was tested at seven year-sites, and 19 agronomic traits related to phenology, growth habit and yield were assessed. Most traits showed high repeatability (0.31 < R 2 < 0.98) and heritability (0.45 < H 2 < 0.97), indicating genetic control of these traits. Coefficients of variation ranged between 6.19% and 46.15%, showing the high phenotypic diversity within the collection. By combining multiple traits, distinct ideotypes for different roles in the crop rotation were investigated, and accessions with promising agronomic profiles identified. Genome-wide association studies revealed marker-trait associations for 18 traits, allowing the identification of putative candidate genes influencing these traits such as a putative GRF-INTERACTING FACTOR associated with flowering time and biomass production. Our results show that the collection offers vast phenotypic diversity that can be exploited for the development of improved varieties tailored to meet specific agronomic purposes. The efficient utilization of these genetic resources should be supported by the application of genomics-based breeding approaches. The development of genetic markers and search for putative candidate genes mark important steps towards the establishment of efficient breeding schemes. Thus, these genomic resources provide a foundation for accelerating the genetic improvement of common buckwheat and developing agronomically competitive varieties.

title: Unstructured regions differentially modulate the activation of RBOHD and RBOHH
abstract: Abstract Reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced by plant NADPH oxidases (RBOHs) must be precisely controlled to generate appropriate signaling outputs in profoundly diverse physiological contexts. RBOHs are activated by Ca²⁺ and phosphorylation, yet how structural variation in their regulatory regions shapes these responses and contributes to functional specialization remains unclear. To identify regions underlying functional diversification among RBOHs, we performed phylogenetic and sequence-comparison analyses across land plants. The most variable regions are two N-terminal unstructured regions (URs), UR1 and UR2, which flank the EF-hand Ca²⁺-binding domain (EFD). We investigated whether these unstructured regions contribute differently to the regulation of Arabidopsis RBOHD and RBOHH, which function predominantly in immune signaling and pollen tube growth, respectively. Our functional assays in HEK293T cells suggest that UR1 plays opposing roles in RBOHD and RBOHH, restraining Ca²⁺-dependent activation in RBOHD while facilitating it in RBOHH. Our analyses indicate differences in the regulatory contribution of UR2 between RBOHD and RBOHH. In RBOHD, our results suggest that UR2 phosphorylation promotes formation of an α-helical conformation and its interaction with the catalytic domain, contributing to enzymatic activation, whereas our analyses do not support a comparable regulatory mechanism in RBOHH. Domain-swapping experiments between RBOHD and RBOHH suggest that the EFD coevolved with UR2 in RBOHD to enhance phosphorylation-dependent activation, whereas in RBOHH it coevolved with UR1 to favor Ca²⁺-dependent activation. Together, our findings support a model in which diversification of unstructured regulatory regions adapts the conserved RBOH enzymatic core to distinct physiological contexts, including immune signaling and polarized growth.

title: High-throughput variant libraries and machine learning enable robust target-site selection for toehold-switch design in Detectrons
abstract: Programmable RNA sensors enable sequence-specific detection of RNA inputs for diagnostics, genetic circuit control, and multiplexed molecular readouts. Although readily programmable, their performance varies substantially with the target site selected within a transcript, making target-site selection a major challenge. Here, we report DeSTAR (Detectron Sensor TARget-site ranker), a machine-learning-assisted target-site ranking model for programmable RNA sensors. To train this model, we generated transcript-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution tiling sensor libraries across six diverse RNA targets, enabling generalization to be tested across transcripts rather than within a single RNA. In leave-one-transcript-out evaluation, DeSTAR's top-ranked sites were enriched for high-performing sensors in held-out transcripts, driven predominantly by interpretable sequence grammar in the sensor stem rather than transcript-specific patterns. Prospectively, on an unseen SARS-CoV-2 transcript, the model's top-ranked sites yielded working sensors roughly five-fold more often than random selection. These results support DeSTAR as a generalizable strategy for target-site selection in RNA sensors across transcripts.

title: Modular Cell-Free Extract Mixing Enables Soluble, Active Biomanufacturing of Difficult-to-Express and Aggregation-Prone Proteins
abstract: Abstract Cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) is a powerful platform for rapid protein prototyping and biomanufacturing, but expression of complex proteins remains limited by labor-intensive extract preparation as well as the inability of conventional Escherichia coli extracts to efficiently support disulfide bond formation and prevent protein aggregation. We previously developed a Cell-Free Autoinduction (CFAI) workflow that simplifies extract preparation, however, CFAI-derived extracts retain the folding limitations of standard E. coli systems for producing traditionally difficult proteins. Here, we address these challenges by utilizing extracts enriched with molecular chaperones or Erv1p-based oxidative folding catalysts and combining them through a modular extract mixing strategy to enable independent tuning of the cell-free folding environment. This workflow supplies folding factors through enriched extracts, avoiding recurring purchases of purified supplements and enabling a modeled reagent-cost advantage. To evaluate real-world applications and utility of lysate mixing for protein production, we demonstrate a 10-fold increase in solubility of the aggregation-prone bacterial toxin Colicin M, achieving >95% soluble protein while retaining antimicrobial activity. We further used a Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to optimize combinations of chaperone-enriched and Erv1p-based oxidative folding extracts containing either protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) or DsbC. The optimized compositions produced >95% soluble truncated human tissue plasminogen activator (vtPA), comprising the kringle 2 and protease domains, while preserving enzymatic activity. Together, these results demonstrate that CFAI-derived modular extract mixing provides a tunable, high-throughput strategy with low modeled materials costs for tailoring cell-free biochemical environments for difficult-to-express proteins, expanding CFPS utility for protein engineering and biomanufacturing. title: Non-canonical cleavage expands prime editing in 5’ direction
abstract: Abstract Cleavage-dependent CRISPR-Cas gene editing relies on RNA-guided DNA cleavage that drives cellular machinery to incorporate intended edits. Beyond canonical cleavage, CRISPR nucleases can also execute non-canonical cleavage on the displaced DNA strand. Here, we report a modified design principle for prime editing that leverages the non-canonical cleavage activity, enabling editing in the 5’ direction of a classic nick site. We elucidate the non-canonical-cleavage-driven reverse transcription pathway that initiates upstream of the classic nick site. We identify competition between the canonical and non-canonical routes, which can be modulated by rationally designing RNA templates carrying the intended edits. We demonstrate that cellular physiology enhances editing efficiency from individual reverse-transcription product yet exerts limited influence on pathway competitions. Our findings revise the design principle of prime editing and establish a new dimension for engineering CRISPR-Cas systems by harnessing its intrinsic, non-host-specific, non-canonical cleavage activity.

title: Antiviral Sulfonated Polymersomes Inhibit Corona-, Influenza-, and Alphavirus
abstract: Abstract A broad-spectrum antiviral is required to enable rapid intervention against current, newly emerging and mutating viruses. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A virus (IAV), Sindbis virus (SINV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV) all engage negatively charged moieties on host cells, such as heparan sulfate (HS) and sialic acid, to facilitate attachment for entry and infection. We designed HS-mimetic nanoparticles in the form of polymer vesicles (polymersomes) by blending membrane-forming and sulfonated copolymers. These biocompatible polymersomes successfully inhibited host cell infection of HS-dependent SARS-CoV-2 and HS-independent IAV in vitro with sub-nanomolar potency. Multivalent interaction of several virus ligands with a single polymersome as quantified by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy likely contributes to their potency. The sulfonated polymersomes also functioned in vivo as demonstrated by a reduction in the spread of SINV, an alphavirus model for CHIKV, in zebrafish embryos, which led to a significantly increased survival. Hence, our polymersomes could form the basis for an urgently required multifunctional broad-spectrum antiviral nanomedicine.

title: Rational Design of 5’ UTRs for Optimized mRNA Expression and Cost-Effective, Rapid Analysis of Capped mRNA
abstract: Abstract In vitro-transcribed (IVT) messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics require rigorous quality control of 5’ capping efficiency and 3’ poly(A) tail length, both of which constitute critical quality attributes (CQAs). Current analytical workflows for these CQAs rely on hybridization with nucleic acid probes and biotin-based affinity purification, which constrain throughput and increase per-assay cost. Here, we report a rationally designed 5’ untranslated region (5’ UTR) that sustains high translational efficiency while enabling probe-free, one-step purification for rapid quantification of capping efficiency and poly(A) tail length distribution. This approach exploits a strategically engineered 5’ UTR incorporating a purine-only RNase A-resistant fragment terminating at a single pyrimidine cleavage site, together with a translation-enhancing element comprising an N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) deposition motif and an 18S rRNA complementarity sequence. This dual-function design accommodates GA-rich sequence segments without compromising mRNA translational output. Compared with conventional probe- and biotin-dependent workflows, the present method substantially reduces cost and processing time and is compatible with simultaneous detection of homopolymeric poly(A) tail. This integrated platform provides a simplified, probe-free and construct-universal mRNA analytical platform.

title: Design and characterization of peptide-responsive biosensors
abstract: Gram-positive bacteria use secreted peptides and peptide-responsive transcription factors for quorum sensing. Here, we demonstrate that intracellular expression of these peptide effectors with their cognate transcription factors leads to regulation of gene expression in both in vitro and in vivo systems. Because both effector and regulatory parts can be readily expressed, complex circuits, including auto-activation schemes, can be developed, with switch-like behaviors. Moreover, the peptide effectors can be fused to proteins, enabling a direct intracellular readout of translation and potentially allowing any protein to encode regulatory interactions in cells. Our results support a foundation for regulatory circuits that extend beyond canonical components such as LacI and TetR.

title: Fibrosis burden and spatial pattern affect left atrial appendage stasis in multi-beat multi-physics simulations
abstract: Abstract Purpose Atrial fibrosis is associated with thromboembolic risk in atrial fibrillation, but it remains unclear how fibrosis-related contractile impairment alters blood transport in the left atrium (LA) and left atrial appendage (LAA). Prior multi-physics simulations coupling electromechanical (EM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models showed that fibrosis impairs LA function and flow, but were limited to booster-only contraction and could not separate the effects of fibrosis burden from its spatial distribution. Here, we examined how fibrosis burden and spatial pattern independently relate to long-term LA and LAA hemodynamics in full-cycle, multi-beat simulations on a common LA anatomy. Methods Three fibrosis patterns derived from late gadolinium enhancement MRI were applied globally to a common LA anatomy at matched burdens of 15.6% and 31.2%, yielding six global-fibrosis cases and a non-fibrotic reference. Two patterns were also confined to the LAA at local burdens of 10%, 25%, and 50%, yielding six LAA-fibrosis cases. A 3D EM model of the LA anatomy coupled to a 0D circulatory model resolved the reservoir, conduit, and booster phases, and the EM-derived wall motion drove subsequent multi-beat CFD simulations. Region-specific emptying fraction (EF), non-dimensional kinetic energy (KE), and the 90th percentile of blood residence time (T R ) were evaluated in the LA and LAA. Results Left ventricular stroke volume remained nearly constant across cases, whereas increasing global fibrosis burden progressively reduced LA and LAA EF (LA: 36% to 30–31%; LAA: 44% to 28–38%), lowered both active and passive LA EF, and monotonically increased LA T R across all patterns. Non-dimensional LA KE showed an approximately quadratic association with LA EF across patterns, whereas LAA KE was more scattered but still increased with LAA EF. In contrast, the 90th percentile of LAA T R did not increase monotonically with decreasing LAA EF for one pattern. When fibrosis was confined to the LAA, non-dimensional LAA KE collapsed onto a single relationship with LAA EF for both patterns, whereas LAA T R followed distinct, non-monotonic trends. Conclusions Fibrosis burden, through its association with functional impairment, predominantly governed whole-LA hemodynamics, whereas LAA stasis additionally depended on the spatial distribution of fibrosis. In the LAA-fibrosis cases, LAA EF was a robust descriptor of chamber-averaged KE regardless of fibrosis pattern, but did not fully explain LAA residence time. These findings support evaluating imaging-derived fibrosis pattern, in addition to fibrosis burden and functional metrics, as a potential determinant of LAA transport and stasis. Its incremental value for thrombogenic-risk assessment requires prospective clinical validation.

title: Evaluation of Iodine-Based Contrast Agents for Ex Vivo Micro-CT Imaging of Porcine Hearts: An Application to Cardiac Conduction System Imaging
abstract: Abstract Objective Visualization and segmentation of the cardiac conduction system (CCS) enable advanced mathematical modeling and improve the diagnosis of heart rhythm disorders. Background This study investigates iodine in ethanol (I 2 E) and Lugol’s solution (I 2 KI) for optimizing high-resolution micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) imaging of the CCS in porcine hearts. The study evaluates their efficacy in enhancing tissue contrast, shrinkage, and downstream processing. Methods Dissected porcine hearts were stained with I 2 E and I 2 KI for contrast enhancement and scanned with micro-CT system. Volumetric shrinkage of tissues during staining was evaluated. Additionally, qualitative visualization of CCS-related anatomical landmarks, such as the sinoatrial node (SAN), atrioventricular node (AVN), and Purkinje fibers, was performed, along with assessment of artifact occurrence and sample integrity. The regions corresponding to CCS were segmented from micro-CT image data and were then validated against histology. Results Although both contrast agents yielded comparable Signal-to-Background ratios (p = 0.8871), I 2 E demonstrated significantly superior imaging quality with a higher Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (p ≤ 0.05) and lower overall noise (p ≤ 0.05) than I 2 KI. Furthermore, while I 2 KI offered faster staining, it caused leaching, artifacts, and structural disintegration that compromised downstream applications. In contrast, I 2 E preserved sample integrity and minimized artifacts, facilitating seamless post-processing and histological sectioning. Conclusions These results suggest that I 2 E could be a viable alternative to I 2 KI for CCS micro-CT imaging when sample preservation and downstream analyses are essential.

title: HECT-type ligases facilitate autoubiquitination and degradation of other ubiquitin ligases to activate plant immunity
abstract: Abstract The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) serves as the primary proteolytic machinery in eukaryotes, governing intracellular protein turnover to maintain proteome homeostasis. In plants, the HECT-type UPL3/4 ubiquitin ligases play vital roles in developmental and immune signaling. After ubiquitination by pathway-specific E3 ligases, substrates are physically relayed to proteasome-associated UPL3/4 ligases for further modification, which is necessary for their proteasome-mediated degradation. In this study, we investigated if the cellular influence of UPL3/4 extends beyond their direct role in substrate degradation. We discovered that UPL3/4 govern the ubiquitination not only of a broad array of immune-related substrates, but also of many UPS components, including E3 ligases. UPL3 physically interacts with PUB22, a pathway-specific U-box E3 ligase that negatively regulates immunity. PUB22 is controlled by a phospho-switch that converts it from an instable autoubiquitinated state to a stable phosphorylated E3 ligase that marks substrates for degradation. Remarkably, UPL3 only interacted with unphosphorylated PUB22 and facilitated its autoubiquitination-mediated degradation, thereby promoting the accumulation of PUB22 substrates. Moreover, the compromised immune phenotypes of upl3 upl4 mutant plants were largely dependent on PUB22 and its close paralogues. Thus, UPL3/4 control the stability of immune-related substrates not only through direct ubiquitination, but also indirectly by promoting autoubiquitination of PUB22 ligase and its paralogues. Controlling the stability of autoubiquitinating E3 ligases may be a universal mechanism whereby HECT-type ligases and the proteasomes they associated with, orchestrate cellular proteostasis in eukaryotes. Significance Statement The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) governs intracellular protein turnover to maintain proteome homeostasis in eukaryotes. Proteasome-associate HECT-type ubiquitin ligases play an important role in processing and degrading substrates delivered to the proteasome by pathway-specific E3 ligases. Here, we discover that in plants, HECT-type ligases not only promote the degradation of substrates, they also modify the E3 ligases that target these substrates to the proteasome. Specifically, HECT-type ligases facilitated or expanded the autoubiquitination of immune-suppressive E3 ligases, resulting in their proteasome-mediated degradation and onset of immunity. Our discoveries suggest that during plant immunity, HECT-type ligases and the proteasomes they associate with, control cellular proteostasis by governing the stabilities of both E3 ligases and their substrates.

title: LATEER: Low-Cost Open-Source Platform for Electrical Stimulation and TEER Measurement in Human Cardiomyocytes
abstract: Abstract Electrical stimulation (ES) and transepithelial/transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are essential techniques in cell biology and tissue engineering, yet commercial devices for these applications cost between USD 2,500–9,000 and typically offer only one functionality. We present LATEER (Low-cost Arduino-based TEER and Electrical stimulation device), an open-source hardware platform that combines both ES and TEER measurement capabilities at a total cost below USD 100. The device features four independent channels, configurable pulsatile signals (amplitude up to 8.2 V, frequency 0.1–500 Hz, pulse width ≥0.1 ms), and a resistance measurement range of 300 Ω to 1 MΩ, with <5% error for R □ 4.7 kΩ. LATEER uses commercially available graphite pencil leads as electrodes (∼USD 2 vs. USD 350 for commercial Ag/AgCl electrodes), which demonstrated excellent biocompatibility in cell culture. The system includes 3D-printed electrode holders compatible with standard 12-well and 24-well plates, allowing microscope visualization without electrode removal, and a Python-based graphical user interface for parameter configuration and real-time data acquisition. Because the electrodes remain fixed in the plate lid and only a single cable enters the incubator, both stimulation and resistance measurement can run continuously under standard culture conditions (37 °C, 5% CO□) without removing the plate or repositioning the electrodes, avoiding the temperature excursions and placement variability inherent to manual chopstick measurements. Validation with human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes demonstrated reliable frequency capture (electrical pacing) of the contracting monolayer, with a capture threshold between 250 and 400 mV/mm and controlled pacing across the 0.5–5 Hz range. TEER functionality was verified with mesenchymal stem cells, where the device resolved cell-density-dependent differences in electrical resistance in real time. All design files, firmware, and software are freely available under the CERN-OHL-S v2 license, enabling replication and customization by research laboratories worldwide. Highlights An open-source device combines electrical stimulation and TEER measurement under $100 Graphite electrodes offer biocompatibility at 0.6% cost of commercial alternatives Four independent channels with configurable parameters and real-time data logging. title: Mathematical modeling of SUMOylation reveals tissue-specific and dynamic responses to abiotic stress
abstract: SUMOylation is an essential and evolutionarily conserved post-translational modification that enables rapid cellular adaptation to environmental stress. Despite its importance, how the SUMOylation machinery controls its dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated a mathematical model of the plant SUMO cycle with quantitative imaging and biochemical data to decode the regulatory logic of SUMOylation dynamics. The model reveals a fundamental principle: steady -state SUMOylation levels are determined not by the full complement of SUMO-cycle components, but by the abundance of SUMO modifier proteins and E1 enzymes, together with SUMO protease abundance and activity. Strikingly, when we integrated fluorescence measurements from reporters for SUMO-cycle components in Arabidopsis roots after three hours of abiotic stress, the model predicted decreased SUMOylation levels across several tissues, contrary to prevailing evidence. Motivated by this unexpected prediction, we performed time-resolved imaging to better characterize the dynamics of key SUMO-cycle components after salt and osmotic stress. These data revealed highly dynamic component levels within the first three hours of stress that were not captured in the previous measurements. Incorporating this temporal data into the model uncovered a twin-peaked SUMOylation response to salt stress: an early surge underpinned by protease dynamics, followed by a decline and a second peak driven by elevated SUMO modifier and E2 levels. Western blot analysis revealed a corresponding twin-peaked pattern of SUMOylation. Together, our findings demonstrate that the plant SUMO cycle is a highly dynamic system that achieves tissue- and stress-specific control of SUMOylation through the coordinated interplay of multiple SUMO-cycle components.

title: Interaction-specific early wheat responses to Zymoseptoria tritici share enhanced defense-related transcription during incompatibility
abstract: SUMMARY Despite the recent cloning of RLK-encoding resistance genes and the identification of a common point of hyphal arrest at the stomatal level in incompatible interactions, the molecular mechanisms leading to the establishment of wheat resistance against Septoria tritici blotch (STB) remain poorly characterized. Here, we use long-read RNA-sequencing data to compare the early transcriptomic responses of two wheat cultivars carrying major, isolate-specific resistances to Zymoseptoria tritici via differential expression, differential transcript usage (DTU), functional- and pathway enrichment analyses. We show that both magnitude and composition of the responses depend strongly on the combination of host cultivar and pathogen isolate and that DTU appears to be uncommon at this infection stage. We do not detect a set of genes exclusively differentially expressed across incompatible interactions, but genes coding for proteins involved in several defense-related processes consistently show higher expression levels in incompatible than compatible interactions, including receptors and ROS homeostatic, antifungal hydrolytic, phenylpropanoid and diterpenoid biosynthetic enzymes. Our results suggest that whilst interaction-specific differences in magnitude and composition may also shape resistance, different major STB resistances may quantitatively enhance overlapping defense machinery, providing a basis for its functional investigation.

title: Predicting viral host range for reverse zoonosis surveillance
abstract: ABSTRACT Zoonotic transmission of viruses has triggered major outbreaks throughout history. However, human-to-animal transmission, or “reverse zoonotic” transmission, also represents an underappreciated public health threat. Reverse zoonoses can establish novel animal reservoirs that fuel viral evolution and enable eventual spillback into humans, underscoring the importance of defining viral host range. Current approaches for host range prediction are limited. Experimental methods are retrospective and rely on brute-force testing in a small number of models, whereas computational approaches often lack experimental grounding. Here, we present a platform that integrates high-throughput experimental screening with deep learning to predict viral host range from sequence. We screened a yeast-displayed SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain library against 15 angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) orthologs from diverse species, and deep sequenced the ACE2-binding and non-binding populations to generate an atlas of 8.8 million unique RBD:ACE2 interaction measurements. These data were used to train a transformer-based deep learning model that predicts RBD:ACE2 compatibility across animal species from sequence alone, and generalizes in a zero-shot manner to ACE2 orthologs not observed during training. Critically, the model pairs each prediction with a distance-based uncertainty estimate, allowing hundreds of candidate species to be triaged by both predicted host compatibility and confidence. This framework enables the rapid prioritization of animal species for SARS-CoV-2 surveillance and provides a general strategy for anticipating viral host range.

title: Large-Scale Mutagenesis Identifies Sequence Changes That Bias Tau Toward CTE-like Aggregation
abstract: Tau amyloid fibrils adopt disease-specific structures across tauopathies, yet the sequence determinants that favor one pathological fold over another remain poorly defined. Here we combine computational saturation mutagenesis and energetic profiling, in vitro aggregation, cryo-EM and cellular seeding assays to identify sequence changes that alter tau fold compatibility. Across six tauopathy fibril structures, approximately 12,000 substitutions revealed that mutational sensitivity is concentrated within interaction networks formed by amyloidogenic motifs rather than uniformly distributed across the fibril core. Comparison of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) folds identified residues within the 335-363 region that differentially influence fold compatibility. The S341L/S352I double mutant accelerated aggregation and remodeled packing within the PAM4-containing amyloidogenic region, producing an alternative amyloid architecture in a minimal tau fragment. S341L/S352I biosensors preferentially responded to CTE-derived over Alzheimer's disease-derived seeds, while aggregates generated from recombinant S341L/S352I tau exhibited CTE-like cellular templating behavior. Although these assemblies are not established to reproduce the atomic CTE fold, the results demonstrate that targeted sequence changes can bias tau aggregation and propagation toward a CTE-compatible state. This framework provides a strategy for defining sequence-structure relationships in polymorphic amyloids and developing conformation-selective models and biosensors.

title: Quantitative 3D imaging of intact engineered heart tissues using inverted selective plane illumination microscopy
abstract: Abstract Background Advanced in vitro models of the human heart have become promising tools for studying cardiac diseases and drug discovery. Three-dimensional (3D) engineered heart tissues (EHTs) provide more adult cardiac tissue-like structural organization compared to traditional two-dimensional (2D) in vitro models with straightforward contractile readouts. However, the assessment of the architecture of EHTs, especially the quantification of cellular and tissue structural components, has remained poorly studied. Here we demonstrate the use of light-sheet microscopy for structural imaging of intact EHTs and provide quantification of the EHT cellular and subcellular structures. Methods We developed an in-house inverted selective plane illumination microscopy (iSPIM) platform and combined it with iterative indirect immunofluorescence (IT-IF) staining for better signal acquisition. We developed an image-processing and analysis pipeline dedicated to volumetric EHT analysis. Results With this integrated platform, we achieved volumetric imaging of intact EHTs and quantification of 3D tissue architecture, revealing aligned cardiomyocytes within the imaged volume and increasing cardiac nuclei content towards the core of the tissue. The developed methods allowed the detection of heterogeneities between tissue sections, demonstrating the sensitivity required for future disease modeling or maturation studies. Conclusions The developed integrated platform opens new possibilities for volumetric analysis and characterization of 3D tissue structure using iSPIM, providing new insights into EHT architecture and the use of EHTs as disease modeling tools.

title: Rapid simulation of organ-scale oxygen transport for tissue ischemia prediction
abstract: Abstract A densely vascularized tissue can still be starved of oxygen. Tissue oxygenation depends heavily on vessel arrangement, blood flow distributions, and cellular metabolism. Resolving these effects from individual constituent vessels to whole organs has historically been computationally prohibitive. We introduce the Cardiovascular Analysis and Simulation of Circulatory Advection, Diffusion, and Exchange (CASCADE) toolkit, which makes vessel-resolved oxygen transport tractable at the organ scale through a novel screened Green’s-function formulation. On laptop-class hardware, CASCADE simulates networks containing thousands of vessels in under one second and a full biventricular human heart model in about two minutes. We validate spatial oxygen and cell-survival predictions against experiments in perfused engineered tissues and matched finite-element simulations. In engineered tissues, sweeps across thousands of network designs and physiological conditions reveal when vessel density, oxygen supply, or network architecture limits viability, establishing design rules for sustaining thick constructs. In a human heart model, CASCADE translates coronary occlusion, anemia, polycythemia, and hypoxemia into distinct myocardial oxygenation patterns, revealing where oxygen delivery fails and how much tissue is at risk.

title: Evaluation of Densified Collagen Tubes as an Interposition Graft in Abdominal Aorta
abstract: ABSTRACT A major challenge in vascular tissue engineering is the development of scalable fabrication methods capable of producing vascular grafts with suitable mechanical properties and hemocompatibility for both preclinical evaluation and future clinical translation. Using a recently developed method to generate acellular vascular grafts from densified collagen hydrogel, we present a proof-of-concept in vivo evaluation of the scalable collagen graft technology. Thick-walled, genipin-crosslinked grafts, representative of a fabrication approach applicable to clinically relevant vessel sizes, were implanted as interposition grafts in the rat abdominal aorta. These grafts supported rapid neointima formation and re-endothelialisation of the luminal surface but developed late thrombosis, highlighting the challenges of evaluating clinically scalable grafts in small-animal models. To enable assessment of the platform in millimetre-scale vessels, we developed a thin-walled (∼100 µm), non-crosslinked graft using a constrained densification approach and hyaluronic acid-mediated modulation of collagen fibril assembly to improve compliance matching and hemocompatibility, with the latter providing a matrix-level approach that may complement surface-bound antithrombotic coatings. These grafts remained patent for up to 17 weeks and exhibited neointima formation, re-endothelialisation, and early cellular infiltration into the graft wall. Together, these findings demonstrate in vivo functionality of densified collagen vascular grafts and establish a foundation for future evaluation in larger animal models.

title: MINT: Predicting Enzyme-Cofactor Specificity by Multimodal Knowledge Transfer from Protein–Ligand Interactions
abstract: ABSTRACT Protein-cofactor selectivity prediction is important for enzyme annotation, metabolic engineering, and biocatalyst discovery, but it remains challenging because experimentally supported associations are limited and unevenly distributed, and because biologically relevant differences can be subtler than those captured by general protein-ligand interaction models. Here, we present MINT (Multimodal Interaction Network with Teacher supervision), a multimodal framework for cofactor specificity prediction. MINT combines protein sequence features with cofactor sequence and graph representations and is trained with a gradual adaptation strategy that transfers useful information from a pretrained protein-ligand interaction model to the cofactor prediction task. On a fixed balanced held-out test set, MINT achieved the best overall performance among all compared methods (AUC = 0.932), and this ranking was reproduced in an independent family-stratified evaluation at the natural positive rate (pooled AUC = 0.939). Further analyses suggest that the pretrained model provides transferable structural information, while the gradual training scheme helps adapt that information to cofactor specificity. In a case study of the chemically near-identical NAD/NADP pair, MINT recovered 95.0-98.6% of true binders and resolved a single-phosphate-level distinction with direct relevance to engineering enzyme cofactor specificity. These results show that gradual transfer learning is an effective approach to cofactor specificity prediction when annotation is limited. TOC

title: A minimally modified AAV9 variant (AAV9fyhr) for enhanced CNS gene delivery by intra-CSF administration
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) mediated gene therapies continue to show promise for the treatment of genetic diseases. However, delivery and safety still represent significant prohibitive barriers restricting translation of these delivery modalities to humans. We describe a novel AAV9 variant, "AAV9fyhr" or "FYHR", identified from screening a controlled randomization point mutation AAV9 library in mice and nonhuman primates followed by directed evolution of in vivo CNS-derived libraries screened in human iPSC differentiated cortical neurons. Capsid variants of interest were identified by coupling long read sequencing and computational structure modeling. Structure-function analysis of our lead candidate reveal that two targeted amino acid changes are sufficient to result in beneficial pleiotropic effects across viral stability, cell surface attachment, and gene delivery. We developed a novel multiplexed barcoding reporter system, enabling a time and cost-effective option to gather spatially resolved single cell capsid validation data in mice and nonhuman primates. When administered intrathecally, AAV9fyhr exhibits 2-to-6-fold higher gene delivery across several tissues in the CNS while minimally altering the tropism to peripheral tissues in comparison to AAV9. These findings demonstrate the potential of whole capsid engineering for the rational development of translational next generation AAV capsids.

title: Biohybrid toggle switches: leveraging bistability in muscle-actuated machines
abstract: Abstract Tissue-engineered skeletal muscle offers robotics unique advantages in energy density, adaptability, and self-repair, but current biohybrid machines couple muscle directly to artificial skeletons, limiting net force output and requiring continuous stimulation maintain mechanism positions. Here, we introduce a biohybrid bistable switching mechanism that converts antagonistic muscle contractions to snap-through actuation of an elastomeric four-bar flexure, maintaining stable positions without energy consumption. We decouple passive muscle pre-tensioning from flexure operation with thin-film elastomer “resistance bands,” enabling fine tuning of spring stiffness and force to match muscle mechanical output envelopes. Leveraging mesoscale additive manufacturing, spin coating, and replica molding techniques, components are integrated into a millimeter-scale linear stage to axially align muscles with artificial components. Our prototype achieves reversible toggling between bistable states with a 130 ms switching time, establishing skeletal muscle actuators as viable electromechanical switches, and broadening biohybrid robotics towards novel applications such as grippers, valves, and mechanical computers.

title: Unsupervised 3D classification and characterisation of osteocyte and chondrocyte lacunae in the murine osteochondral unit
abstract: In the murine osteochondral unit, morphology of chondrocyte lacunae (CCL) within calcified articular cartilage and osteocyte lacunae (OCL) within the underlying subchondral bone reflects local biomechanical conditions that are altered in disease, making reliable discrimination of both lacunar populations important for studying osteochondral physiology and pathology. Histology is generally considered the gold standard for identifying CCL and OCL. However, it is inherently limited to two-dimensional assessment and a relatively small tissue section, restricting comprehensive characterisation of three-dimensional lacunar structure. Synchrotron-radiation micro-computed tomography (SR-microCT) enables volumetric quantification of lacunae; where classification is typically based on the position of each lacuna relative to the cement line separating calcified cartilage from bone, requiring manual delineation of this convoluted interface. Such approaches are labour-intensive, operator-dependent, and rely on access to specialised synchrotron infrastructure that is not widely available. To address these limitations, we present a fully automated, annotation-free pipeline for classifying OCL and CCL in the mouse osteochondral unit based on desktop micro-computed tomography (microCT), independent of cement line identification. The proposed unsupervised workflow requires neither tissue separation nor labelled training data, enabling objective and scalable discrimination of lacunar populations directly from volumetric image data. Seven morphometric and positional features per lacuna were extracted from SR-microCT and desktop microCT datasets and analysed using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Validation of the pipeline outcome on SR-microCT against manual classification across specimens yielded very-high agreement, with Gwet's AC1, the Matthews correlation coefficient, and balanced accuracy each approaching 0.99, in both healthy and post-traumatic osteoarthritis specimens. Such a workflow can be readily adapted for the investigation of osteochondral interface in various other species.

title: Synthetic genetic circuits that count developmental cues in plant roots
abstract: Abstract Plants explore soil environments through their roots, which branch repeatedly to access water and soil-borne nutrients. In many plants, root branches are generated by repeated developmental programs and molecular analyses have not identified markers that distinguish primary from later root branches. Consequently, efforts to engineer plant roots for improved water or nutrient acquisition are limited to changes that affect the entire root system. Here, we developed synthetic genetic circuits to count repeating root development cues and enable differential gene expression in successive root branches of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana . The circuits use a root primordium-specific promoter to express large serine recombinases, which irreversibly invert segments of DNA each time a new lateral root is initiated. This converts repeating rounds of root formation into distinct, heritable DNA states. Because root branch specification and outgrowth occur over a ~2 day period, we tested circuit designs for their ability to count long-duration input pulses and developed an architecture that produces distinct fluorescence outputs in primary, secondary, and tertiary roots. By linking repeated developmental cues to distinct genetic outputs, synthetic genetic circuits that count enable root system engineering at the resolution of individual branches and offer a general strategy for dissecting developmental processes that rely on repeated signals.

title: Distinct Strategies for Engineering Bioenergy Traits in Sorghum Drive Divergent Functional Shifts in the Rhizosphere Microbiome
abstract: Abstract Engineering bioenergy crops for enhanced biomass digestibility and high-value co-products is a promising approach to sustainable biofuel production. However, the impact of these engineered crops on the belowground microbiome remains poorly understood. In this study, we characterized the composition and functional responses of the belowground microbiome associated with transgenic sorghum lines: one with reduced cell wall crosslinking (AT10) and another with elevated protocatechuic acid (PCA) production (Qsub). The lines were grown under field conditions with four irrigation levels, and samples were collected twice during the growing season. We found that the two transgenic types drove a subtle but significant divergence in bacterial communities, both compositionally and functionally. Community-wide functional profiling showed that AT10 rhizospheres were consistently depleted in genes associated with mobile genetic elements, while Qsub rhizospheres were enriched in TonB-dependent transport and vanillate monooxygenase, an enzyme that funnels lignin-derived monomers toward PCA degradation, alongside reduced pectin- and cellulose-degradation genes. Genome-resolved analysis linked these community-level shifts to specific taxa: in Qsub, the enriched MAGs were taxonomically diverse, ranging from genome-reduced Patescibacteria with an episymbiotic lifestyle to taxa enriched in lignin-associated auxiliary activity enzymes. In AT10, the depleted Azospirillaceae MAGs carried unusually high mobile genetic element content, consistent with the community-wide pattern. Collectively, these findings offer new insights into how genetic modifications aimed at improving bioenergy traits shapes the composition and function of the rhizosphere microbiome, with potential downstream consequences for soil carbon cycling.

title: FE DEFICIENCY-INDUCED KELCH REPEAT PROTEIN 1 ( FDK1 ) links coumarin metabolism and iron homeostasis during alkaline iron deficiency in Arabidopsis
abstract: Abstract Although iron (Fe) is abundant in soils, its low solubility, particularly under alkaline conditions, often limits plant Fe acquisition. Under these conditions, coumarin-mediated Fe mobilization becomes increasingly important. Arabidopsis thaliana FE DEFICIENCY-INDUCED KELCH REPEAT PROTEIN 1 ( FDK1 , AT3G07720) is strongly induced by Fe deficiency and regulated by the central transcription factor FIT, but its function is unknown. We investigated FDK1 using genetic, physiological, metabolite, and transcriptomic analyses. Loss of FDK1 altered root growth, whereas this phenotype was restored in the FDK1 -Ox overexpression line. Under alkaline Fe deficiency, growth medium from FDK1-Ox contained strongly increased levels of the Fe-mobilizing coumarins fraxetin and esculetin compared with wild type, whereas their induction was attenuated in fdk1-1 . RNA-seq analysis linked FDK1 abundance to coumarin biosynthesis and iron-homeostasis gene expression. FIT and many FIT -associated genes were highly expressed in FDK1-Ox , whereas several upstream iron-homeostasis regulators, including bHLH Ib factors, were highest in fdk1-1 . These findings identify FDK1 as a component of the alkaline Fe-deficiency response that promotes iron-mobilizing coumarin accumulation and is associated with coordinated regulation of iron-homeostasis genes.

title: A Synergistic Terpenoid–Phenolic Defense Network Confers Resistance to Dendrolimus superans in Hybrid Larch
abstract: Abstract To elucidate the resistance of hybrid larch ( Larix spp.) clones to Dendrolimus superans and their chemical defense mechanisms, 46 clones were subjected to field feeding–infestation experiments. Insect resistance was comprehensively evaluated by the membership function method from three perspectives: insect weight change, frass weight and defoliation rate (damage consequences); pre- and post-infestation physiological indices (constitutive and induced resistance). High- and low-resistance materials screened from each perspective were further analyzed by widely targeted LC-MS metabolomics. The three damage indices differed highly significantly among clones ( P <0.01) and were positively correlated, indicating abundant genetic variation in resistance. Clones such as -30-C, -35-A and -21-A showed strong overall resistance, whereas -28-E and -20-A showed high constitutive and induced resistance. Defence enzyme activities (POD, SOD, CAT, PPO and PAL) correlated closely with secondary metabolites (total phenolics, tannins and total flavonoids) and nutrients, and rose synergistically after feeding, reflecting synergy between constitutive and induced resistance. In total, 3,577 metabolites were identified, predominantly terpenoids (>90%). The three groups yielded 1,010, 1,086 and 922 differentially accumulated metabolites, and PCA separated high-from low-resistance materials in all groups. These metabolites were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, monoterpenoid and diterpenoid biosynthesis, and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. In conclusion, resistance of hybrid larch to D. superans is jointly conferred by the defence enzyme system, secondary metabolite accumulation and a “terpenoid–phenolic” metabolic network: terpenoids and phenolics act synergistically via the terpenoid and phenylpropanoid pathways, together forming the core of chemical defense and supporting the breeding of insect-resistant clones.

title: Hidden Medicines in Herbarium Collections: Medicinal Plant Diversity and Ethnopharmacological Knowledge from GSUH, Nigeria
abstract: Abstract Herbarium collections represent an important but frequently underutilized source of information for documenting medicinal plant diversity and preserving ethnomedicinal knowledge. We assessed the medicinal plant diversity represented in herbarium records from the Gombe State University Herbarium (GSUH), Nigeria, and evaluated patterns in taxonomic composition, therapeutic applications, and plant parts reported for medicinal use. We also tested the hypothesis that the plant parts used medicinally are not randomly distributed across therapeutic or ailment categories, but that particular plant parts are disproportionately associated with specific therapeutic applications. The resulting dataset comprised 1,576 specimen records, including 768 recorded as medicinal plant species across 94 families and 1,426 medicinal-use records. Fabaceae was the most species-rich family (15.8%), followed by Asteraceae (9.3%), Malvaceae (4.8%), Lamiaceae (4.4%), Rubiaceae (3.2%), and Apocynaceae (3.2%). The most frequently represented therapeutic themes were infections and sexually transmitted diseases (50.7%), gastrointestinal disorders (41.9%), pain, inflammation, and rheumatism (41.9%), fever and malaria (40.2%), and skin diseases and wounds (40.0%). Individual species had a mean of 2.98 therapeutic themes, with medicinal breadth ranging from 1 to 7 themes. A species-aware permutation test confirmed that the observed plant-part × therapeutic-theme association was significantly stronger than expected under random association (9,999 permutations, P < 0.0001). These findings demonstrate the value of herbarium collections as taxonomically anchored resources for recovering information on medicinal plant diversity. Integrating herbarium records with published ethnomedicinal knowledge provides a reproducible framework for linking plant diversity, taxonomy and traditional medicinal applications and highlights the potential of underutilised African herbaria for ethnopharmacological research.

title: User-friendly software for high-throughput processing of chlorophyll fluorescence images to assess plant stress responses: fvfmPy and fvfmR packages
abstract: Abstract Chlorophyll fluorescence imaging is a powerful tool used to characterize abiotic and biotic stress response of photosynthesis in plants. However, extracting metrics such as F v /F m (maximum quantum yield of photosystem II) from chlorophyll fluorescence images remains a substantial bottleneck in large measurement campaigns, often requiring significant manual effort. To resolve this issue, we developed fvfmPy , a user-friendly program which enables rapid analysis of chlorophyll fluorescence images of arrays of leaf discs. fvfmPy uses algorithmic image segmentation to identify regions of interest and extract fluorescence metrics from tens or hundreds of leaf samples per image with little to no manual input. fvfmPy is developed in Python and includes a graphical user interface enabling intuitive parameter adjustment and real-time quality control checking. We additionally developed fvfmR , an R wrapper package for fvfmPy . F v /F m values extracted with fvfmPy were indistinguishable from those obtained using manual methods ( r 2 > 0.99) but required 94% less time to complete (13 s vs. 200 s per 100 measurements). fvfmPy and fvfmR were built to directly integrate with existing fluorescence software packages and can greatly increase throughput of fluorescence measurements to help address key challenges in agriculture and ecology. Highlight We developed a new, user-friendly tool to rapidly process chlorophyll fluorescence images. This software extracts maximum quantum yield and other metrics with minimal user intervention, enabling ultra-high-throughput image processing.

title: PDF2.2 links constitutive defensin expression to disease resistance in Arabidopsis
abstract: Abstract Background Plant defensins are small cysteine-rich antimicrobial peptides. In Arabidopsis thaliana , the inducible Class I gene AtPDF1.2a is widely used as a transcriptional marker of jasmonate/ethylene immunity, whereas the constitutively expressed Class II members have received less functional attention. AtPDF2.2 was compared with AtPDF1.2a during infection of Arabidopsis by the vascular fungal pathogen Verticillium longisporum , the necrotrophic fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000. Results Profiling of the AtPDF family showed that AtPDF2.2 , together with the Class II genes AtPDF2.3 and AtPDF2.5 , was significantly reduced during V. longisporum infection, whereas AtPDF1.2a was induced. A promoter-reporter line showed a corresponding decrease in AtPDF2.2 promoter activity during V. longisporum infection, strongest in infected roots. KD- pdf2.2 plants contained more V. longisporum DNA, whereas OE-PDF2.2 plants contained less. The same reciprocal disease pattern was observed during S. sclerotiorum and Pst DC3000 infection. Histochemical Prom:: AtPDF2.2 :: GUS reporter signal decreased during S. sclerotiorum infection but increased following Pst DC3000 infection. Basal AtPDF2.2 expression was lower in JA- and ET-signaling mutants and higher in the SA-deficient sid2 background, while the analyzed promoter lacked the GCC-box that mediates inducible AtPDF1.2a regulation. AtPDF1.2a overexpression reduced symptoms across the three pathosystems, but loss of AtPDF1.2a increased disease only during V. longisporum infection under the conditions tested and did not alter Pst DC3000 DNA abundance. AtPDF2.2 overexpression was not associated with reduced vegetative growth under the conditions tested, whereas AtPDF1.2a overexpression reduced rosette size and leaf number. Conclusions AtPDF2.2 is a constitutively expressed Class II defensin whose expression level is associated with disease outcome across two fungal pathogens and a bacterium. Its promoter shows tissue-dependent regulation during V. longisporum infection, while histochemical reporter signal decreases during S. sclerotiorum infection and increases during Pst DC3000 infection. This regulatory behavior differs from that of the inducible reference gene AtPDF1.2a . The reciprocal disease phenotypes of the AtPDF2.2 transgenic backgrounds support a protective association that may involve direct antimicrobial activity, modulation of host responses or both. The absence of reduced vegetative growth in OE-PDF2.2 under the conditions tested supports further evaluation of PDF2 -type genes in Brassica .

title: ATP synthase deficiency promotes prolonged hydrogen production in Chlamydomonas
abstract: Abstract Photosynthetic electron transport is tightly regulated to balance ATP and NADPH production and prevent over-reduction of the photosynthetic machinery. How this balance is maintained under severe ATP limitation, particularly under anoxia, is not fully resolved. Here, we used several deletion mutants of chloroplast ATP synthase subunits from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii to examine how electron flow is reorganized under anoxic conditions through the interplay between linear electron flow, cyclic electron flow, and alternative electron sinks. Using a combination of optical spectroscopy methods and membrane inlet mass spectrometry, we characterized changes in photosynthetic electron transport, proton motive force relaxation and gas exchange. Under oxic conditions, the ΔatpH mutant (lacking the c-subunit) showed strong acceptor-side limitation at photosystem I (PSI), whereas atpC1-2 (lacking the γ-subunit) resembled the wild type. Under anoxia, this limitation was partially relieved, coinciding with sustained electron transport and prolonged hydrogen production. In particular, the Δ atpH mutant exhibited increased cyclic electron flow under oxic conditions and maintained PSI activity under anoxia despite impaired ATP synthesis. Prolonged hydrogen production was also observed in atpC1-2 , which did not share the increased respiration of ΔatpH. Hydrogenase activity under anoxia is consistent with a role as an electron sink that may help alleviate PSI acceptor-side limitation and rebalance the redox state of the electron transport chain. These findings show that ATP synthase deficiency reorganizes photosynthetic electron flow and promotes prolonged hydrogen production, and point to hydrogenase as a candidate electron sink under energy-constrained conditions.

title: The CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON 2 - MIR164A regulatory feedback loop directs leaf morphogenesis
abstract: Abstract Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) establish the spatio-temporal gene expression patterns necessary for reproducible development of organisms. MicroRNAs have emerged as important regulators of gene expression controlling either target gene levels, spatial patterns or timing. These molecular functions may vary depending on how they are integrated into GRNs. Here we used the Arabidopsis leaf as a model to study the genetic and molecular interactions between the CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON 2 (CUC2) transcription factor and its negative regulator, miR164A. Quantitative morphometric analyses showed that miR164A acts from early stages during leaf development regulating CUC2 expression dynamic rather than the spatial distribution of CUC2. At the molecular level, CUC2 directly activates MIR164A expression, forming a single negative feedback loop. Further, using a ratiometric approach, we identified a cis -regulatory element (CRE) sufficient to drive CUC2-dependent MIR164A expression at the leaf sinus. Ordinary differential equation (ODE) modelling suggests that CUC2-CRE may control the timely accumulation of CUC2. Accordingly, quantification of CUC2 protein accumulation dynamics using a spatio-temporal mean cartography strategy in CRISPR cis -regulatory variants at the MIR164A locus revealed that CUC2-dependent MIRA164A expression is required to maintain both the precise timing of CUC2 expression and CUC2 levels. Altogether, our work provides experimental evidence for a specific role of the CUC2-MIR164A module in shaping leaf development, highlighting the contribution of network topology to GRN functions.

title: Mitochondrial dynamics can resolve stoichiometric challenges in plant mtDNA repair
abstract: Although mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is subject to damage and high mutation rates in many eukaryotes, plants have a variety of mtDNA repair pathways that somehow result in exceptionally low mutation rates. However, the stoichiometry of biomolecules in plant mitochondria raises challenges for the DNA repair process. The protein complexes responsible for repair pathways contain subunits present at low copy numbers per mitochondrion. Mitochondria on average contain less than a full genome, limiting the capacity for templated repair, and raising the risk that repair machinery is localised to a DNA-empty mitochondrion where it cannot be used. Here we build on recent experimental characterisation of the copy numbers and physical processes involved to model the capacity for DNA repair in plant mitochondria. We find that targeted import of protein machinery, biased fusion of mitochondria bearing DNA, and exchange of biomolecules upon fusion can improve repair capacity through different mechanisms. Specifically, our model indicates that base excision repair can keep ∼95% of mtDNA intact even without targetting or exchange rules and that targetting protein import to DNA-bearing mitochondria or exchanging protein content drives this to effectively 100%. In contrast, template repair cannot keep a majority of mtDNA intact unless mtDNA is shared across mitochondria through fusion, in which case its efficacy increases. Exchanging of metabolons (repair protein complexes) increases repair efficiency across all circumstances. We discuss the implications of our model for plant development and organelle inheritance.

title: Evolutionary stabilisation of stressful metabolism via integrated biocomputing and essential-gene metabolic locking circuits
abstract: Synthetic genetic circuits enable microbial differentiation from growth to production, yet metabolic burden, imbalance and toxicity frequently drive strain degeneration. Here, we use omics analyses and single-cell biosensors to investigate genetic responses in Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains engineered with stressful terpene biosynthetic pathways. Under metabolic stress, despite divergent stress responses, cells commonly and progressively lose induction of synthetic genetic circuits. In the prenyl pyrophosphate-accumulating strain, this loss is coupled with activation of amino acid biosynthesis and ribosome biogenesis. Accordingly, the essential glutamine synthetase gene GLN1 was coupled to induction of heterologous terpene synthesis through integrated two- and three-input biocomputing circuits that enable stringent, patterned ON/OFF switching. The integrated biocomputing and metabolic locking systems not only alleviate production degeneration but also enable non-degenerative adaptation of toxic terpene synthesis, allowing interrogation of evolutionary shifts for further metabolic optimisation.

title: Directed evolution of a thermostable family-A DNA polymerase into a reverse transcriptase for 2’-modified RNA
abstract: Abstract RNA-based therapeutics increasingly rely on nuclease-resistant xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs), but engineering polymerases capable of reading and amplifying these non-canonical substrates remains a major challenge. Natural DNA polymerases cannot process C2’ sugar modifications, and the complete structural determinants governing this limitation remain poorly understood, limiting rational design strategies. In this study, we apply directed evolution methods to Thermus thermophilus DNA polymerase using a microfluidic implementation of the Compartmentalized Self-Replication (CSR). We identify an engineered variant, termed E5, capable of reverse transcribing C2’-modified RNA, a previously inaccessible activity for this enzyme. Next-generation sequencing allow us to track evolutionary trajectories across nine rounds of evolution. Through an integrated analysis combining statistical methods, protein language models, and crystallographic data, we reveal unknown epistatic networks controlling polymerase function. This large-scale experimental dataset (>196,000 thermostable enzyme variants) provides a robust basis for predicting sequence-to-function relationships, accelerating development of enzymes for aptamer discovery and synthetic biology applications.

title: Sense-and-response to intracellular signaling via nucleocytoplasmic localization control of a synthetic transcription factor platform
abstract: Many therapeutically relevant signaling pathways are sensed inside the cell, yet a modular synthetic biology platform for responding to intracellular signaling at the post-translational level is lacking. Signaling pathways control the nuclear localization and activity of native transcription factors via phosphorylation of nuclear localization/export or cytoplasmic anchor sequences. Here, we apply this concept to develop a platform of nucleocytoplasmic localization tags (NCtags) that control the nuclear translocation of a synthetic transcription factor (synTF) for transgene induction in engineered cells. We identify human-based synTF components that are basally cytoplasmic and induce transgenes under the control of NCtags with minimal background. We demonstrate the modular nature of this platform through transcriptional reporter induction in response to a calcium-inducible NFAT-derived NCtag, and development of novel NCtags responsive to hyperosmolarity, cAMP, or logical combinations of cAMP and calcium. Multiple factors in the tumor microenvironment elevate cAMP in T cells, leading to reduced function. We demonstrate that NCtag-synTF fusions expressed in T cells can respond to endogenous sources of cAMP or calcium in breast cancer spheroids to induce transgene expression. Our use of human components and an all-in-one lentiviral vector encoding the NCtag-synTF-transgene system establishes this as a novel platform for sense-and-response inside therapeutic cells.

title: High-throughput in vivo DNA data encoding by multiplexed conjugation and orthogonal base editing
abstract: Abstract Bacterial conjugation and CRISPR base editing offer complementary routes for programmable DNA transfer and heritable genomic writing, but their combined potential for information encoding in living cells remains unexplored. Here, we introduce CONCORD, a bacterial encoding platform that couples multiplexed bacterial conjugation to genomic base editing for synthesis-free in vivo DNA data writing. A recipient ‘Writer’ strain expresses the base-editing machinery and is equipped with a writing template, whereas reusable donor ‘Guide’ strains deliver the encoding sgRNA signals by conjugation. Using this setup, we encode binary information into genomic DNA in a high-throughput manner. Moreover, we systematically evaluated multiple orthogonal base editors for an expanded encoding repertoire and improved data recovery through redundancy encoding. We deploy the system to encode 45,689 bits into DNA including two culturally and historically significant artifacts: a greeting from NASA’s Voyager Golden Record and a photograph of Navajo petroglyphs and recovered these datasets with 100% and 99.5% accuracy, respectively, without computational error correction. Connecting and engineering the unique mating and immune system of microbial cells we have established a framework for programmable information writing in bacterial populations, with applications for biological event recording and sustainable DNA data storage.

title: Certified Design Regions under Parametric Plant Uncertainty with Application to Antithetic Integral Feedback
abstract: Abstract Kinetic parameters in engineered biomolecular circuits are typically known only within intervals and are not precisely tunable; controller synthesis is therefore naturally posed over sets of gains rather than at a single nominal design. We formulate robust controller tuning under parametric plant uncertainty as a universally quantified set-inversion problem: given a plant-parameter box, compute the controller gains that stabilize every plant in the box. Robust stability is decided by Hurwitz sign conditions, which are bounded over the joint gain–parameter domain using validated range enclosures, yielding machine-checkable certificates of local exponential stability of the deterministic equilibrium. Numerical experiments show that the certified region depends strongly on the range enclosure. For an antithetic integral feedback (AIF) controller acting on a two-species gene-expression cascade, a tensor-product Bernstein enclosure certifies 83.2% of the design plane at bisection tolerance ε = 0.05 with 324 terminal boxes, whereas four baseline enclosures certify between 50.9% and 58.9% on the same paving. For a fifth-order loop, the certified fraction increases from 34.4% to 73.8%, and the certified and excluded terminal boxes confine the robustly stabilizing area to a window of about 2.1 percentage points. Finally, for a refining variant of the algorithm in which the plant box is refined alongside the design box, the undecided area satisfies | U ( ε )| = O ( ε ) under a non-degeneracy assumption on the stability boundary.

title: Mapping Mesoscale Cardiac Architecture with Axially Swept Dithered Light-Sheet Microscopy
abstract: Understanding cardiac microstructure and vascular networks in their entirety is critical for assessing cardiovascular development, disease progression, and therapeutic interventions. Light-sheet microscopy combined with tissue clearing enables high-resolution volumetric imaging of intact organs but faces limitations in trabeculated myocardium due to trade-offs among light-sheet thickness, effective range, and frame rate. We exploit temporal dynamics that govern illumination-detection interplay to maintain uniform resolution across specimens. Building on this, we implemented high-speed dithered light-sheet (DiLS) illumination, extending the confocal region by over 40% and enhancing the space-bandwidth product while preserving optical sectioning. Integration of DiLS with a sweeping approach establishes the axially swept dithered light-sheet (AS-DiLS), which enhances imaging throughput while preserving axial resolution and enables uniform illumination up to 12.5-millimeter range. AS-DiLS delivers near-isotropic resolution (~2.5 μm) for investigating intricate ventricular trabeculae, vasculature, and extracellular matrix, providing a scalable platform for comprehensive cardiovascular morphology and topology assessment from embryos to adults. Teaser: Volumetric imaging reveals microstructure and vascular networks in their entirety with near-isotropic resolution.

title: Powdery mildew fungi block plant vacuolar traffic to suppress immunity
abstract: ABSTRACT Plant immunity can be activated by membrane-localized pattern recognition receptors or by cytosolic nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) receptors, while it can be counteracted by pathogen secreted effectors. Manifestation of immunity often involves endomembrane traffic. However, limited evidence is available for such an involvement in NLR-mediated immunity, which typically includes a hypersensitive reaction (HR)-programmed cell death response. Here we show that the barley powdery mildew fungus uses several effectors to target and inhibit the vacuolar trafficking pathway, which causes endomembrane markers to stall in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). We used this ER-stalling phenotype as a proxy to track fungal manipulation of the vacuolar pathway during different stages of the actual infection. Our data indicate that powdery mildew fungi interfere with the vacuolar pathway, but only temporarily, as the stalling is lifted once the fungal haustorial feeding structures are well-developed for nutrient uptake in epidermal cells. Notably, we show evidence that blocking the vacuolar pathway causes a general inhibition of NLR-mediated HR, and that this mechanism is taken advantage of by the pathogen. Finally, we provide an example that the fungus can secrete a different set of effectors at the haustorial stage that result in the re-opening of the vacuolar pathway by inhibiting the initial vacuolar traffic-suppressing effectors.

title: Cell-free systems enable mechanistic characterization of genetically encoded RNA strand exchange circuits for programmable protein expression, logic, and biosensing
abstract: Nucleic acid circuits are powerful tools for programming biology, but the design principles for operating these circuits in complex cellular environments remain poorly understood compared to simple in vitro settings. Cell-free expression systems (CFES) are uniquely suited to address this challenge, as they can integrate measurements ideal for either test tube or cellular settings. Further, because CFES are open systems, they enable a level of control over component concentration unattainable in cells. Here, we use CFES to characterize genetically encoded RNA circuits that operate via toehold-mediated strand exchange (TMSE). These circuits have been extensively characterized in in vitro transcription (IVT) reactions and were recently deployed as translational riboregulators in Escherichia coli , revealing key differences between the two environments. By systematically modulating the design parameters of these RNA circuits in both purified protein and lysate-based CFES, we elucidate the mechanisms linking TMSE to protein expression. Further, we combine measurements and alterations in CFES composition that are infeasible in cells to investigate interactions between cellular components and RNA circuit components that inform circuit design. Leveraging our mechanistic insights, we demonstrate how a single gate design can achieve multi-level and bidirectional gene regulation, logical operations, and small molecule biosensing. Our results establish a unified set of principles for designing and operating genetically encoded TMSE circuits across IVT, CFES, and bacterial environments, which should catalyze the widespread adoption of this platform for new applications in molecular programming, synthetic biology, and biotechnology.
