title: From Network Topology to Parameterization: An Optimized Model of Endothelial Mechanobiology
abstract: Abstract Endothelial cells integrate biomechanical and biochemical cues to regulate vascular function, which can be modeled using cell signaling networks. Yet, the extent to which their signaling behavior is determined by network topology versus reaction-specific parameterization remains unclear. We developed a continuous logic-based ordinary differential equation model of vascular endothelial signaling containing 70 species and 123 regulatory reactions assembled from the literature. Model predictions were evaluated against 78 literature-defined directional responses to increased wall stress, wall shear stress, hypoxia, and TNF α . We first tested whether a single global parameter triplet describing reaction weight ( w ), Hill coefficient ( n ), and half-maximal activation ( EC 50 ) could reproduce these observations. Investigator-selected global parameters reproduced 62 of 78 responses (79.49%). Monte Carlo sampling of 100,000 globally constant parameter sets improved agreement to 69 of 78 responses (88.46%), indicating that network topology alone captured most qualitative signaling behavior but remained sensitive to parameter choice. Allowing reaction-specific parameters increased the best agreement to 75 of 78 responses (96.15%). We then used a genetic algorithm to identify the smallest subset of reactions requiring reaction-specific specification while retaining a common constant-parameter spine for the remainder of the network. Complete agreement (100%) with all 78 literature-defined responses was achieved with reaction-specific parameterization of only 10 of 123 reactions. The optimized model was subsequently used to simulate continuous changes in wall shear stress, revealing pathway-dependent nonlinear responses, including monotonic increases in nitric oxide and pSmad1/5, nonmonotonic responses in endothelin-1 and NF-κB, and a biphasic pSmad2/3 response. These findings show that most observed endothelial signaling behavior can be reproduced by a fixed network topology with broadly shared reaction parameters with only a limited subset of interactions requiring quantitative specialization. This framework provides a compact endothelial signaling model for investigating mechanobiological regulation and for future integration with multiscale models of vascular adaptation and disease.

title: Colocalization between bone loading and metabolic activity in the human tibia in response to acute exercise
abstract: Abstract Bone strain and remodeling are important factors for bone health. Improved characterization of relationships between these factors in response to acute loading will improve our understanding of bone maintenance, adaptation to load, and pathophysiology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate colocalization between finite-element-estimated bone strain and [ 18 F]sodium fluoride positron emission tomography imaging-estimated subchondral bone remodeling in the tibial diaphysis in response to acute exercise. We hypothesized that the exercise-induced change in standardized uptake values would be greatest in regions of higher strain. 26 participants underwent bilateral positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance scans before and after a bout of stair ascent and descent exercise. Finite element analysis was performed to calculate principal strain distributions in the tibial diaphysis. [ 18 F]sodium fluoride standardized uptake values were calculated from pre- and post-exercise positron emission tomography data and mapped to the tibial surface. Mean pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in standardized uptake values were calculated and compared between regions defined by strain percentile. Both normalized mean pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in standardized uptake values increased with maximum principal strain in a pattern suggesting an exponential relationship. Pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in standardized uptake value were notably much greater in the region of highest maximum principal strains (estimated marginal means = 76.9 and 71.0 percentile, respectively) when compared to all other regions of the tibial diaphysis (≤ 61.1 and ≤ 57.0 percentile, respectively, p < 0.001). This study is the first to directly show a relationship between bone mechanical loads and acute [ 18 F]sodium fluoride uptake in humans in vivo . Our results highlight the influence of tensile strain magnitude on bone metabolic activity in response to acute loading. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of a combined finite element analysis and positron emission tomography approach to interrogate relationships between bone loading and bone metabolic response to acute exercise. Lay summary This study aimed to understand the relationship between bone loading and bone metabolic activity, important factors influencing bone health. Before and after exercise, 26 participants underwent imaging following injection with [ 18 F]sodium fluoride, a radiotracer that localizes to areas in bone with increased perfusion and/or increased remodeling activity. Tracer uptake was spatially compared to bone loading distribution, calculated using personalized models. Exercise-induced change in tracer uptake was increased in regions of high tensile strain, highlighting the importance of loading magnitude in bone metabolism. This combined imaging and modeling approach is a promising method to interrogate relationships between loading and bone metabolism.

title: Bottom-up engineering of EV-mimetic vesicles reveals selective protein loading and modulates cellular uptake and biodistribution
abstract: Abstract Biological systems such as extracellular vesicles (EVs) are highly sophisticated and functionally diverse. Despite growing recognition of EVs’ roles in health and disease through mediating intercellular communication, their inherent heterogeneity and challenges in purity and yield hinder their mechanistic research and clinical translation. To address this gap, we sought to translate essential EV properties into a controllable and simplified platform by engineering biomimetic synthetic vesicles (SVs) incorporating defined proteins and lipids. Using microfluidics, we generated SVs loaded with bulk membrane and cytosolic proteins from cancer cells, as well as individual organotropism-associated integrins. Bulk membrane protein incorporation into SVs reduced surface charge, modified lipid profiles, and enhanced cellular uptake, while integrin incorporation altered biodistribution. To investigate protein loading, we profiled input materials and SVs by mass spectrometry, identifying features linked to high incorporation, such as low molecular weight, positive charge, high isoelectric point, and predicted stability, globularity, lipidation, and amphipathic helices. This work presents a synthetic platform for dissecting the roles of EV-associated features and cargo, while providing insights into protein properties relevant to the optimization of delivery systems.

title: Prime editing enables high-throughput identification and characterization of selective MutSβ inhibitors
abstract: ABSTRACT DNA mismatch repair (MMR) maintains genome stability but paradoxically drives expansion of pathogenic repeats responsible for trinucleotide repeat disorders. Attenuating repeat instability through targeted inhibition of MMR is therefore a therapeutic strategy of interest; however, progress is constrained by a lack of robust methods for defining and isolating MMR subpathways. We exploited features of prime editing to profile the effects of core MMR genes on thousands of programmed DNA mispairs in cells and resolved distinct MMR processes, including a noncanonical “loop-directed” mechanism. Guided by these results, we built a set of scalable reporters that detect loss of separable MMR processes and screened ∼72,000 small molecules for activity against MutSβ-directed MMR. This effort identified a novel series of MutSβ inhibitors that reduced (CAG) n expansion in a cell model. Altogether, this study establishes several methods for systematically interrogating MMR, with demonstrated capacity to identify inhibitors of therapeutic value.

title: Blood-brain barrier-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap for anti-cancer immunomodulation of gliomas
abstract: Clinical studies have revealed that glioblastoma (GBM) is refractory to immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) primarily intensified by intratumoral upregulation of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ). Primary GBM tumor bulks are surgically removed in clinic, but invasive tumor cells infiltrated into surrounding normal brain tissue cannot be eradicated by systemic therapy due to the integral blood-brain barrier (BBB), leading to near-inevitable tumor recurrence. To address these translational challenges, we have engineered a TGFβ-inhibiting protein nanocage comprising human heavy-chain ferritin protein and TGFβ receptor II ectodomain that enables BBB penetration and multivalent TGFβ entrapment, respectively. We demonstrate that the nanocage platform, denoted TβR2-HFt, following systemic administration, traverses the BBB, and extensively modulates immunosuppressive TME, both stromal and immune components, thereby potentiating the therapeutic efficacy of a clinically used ICI in multiple mouse glioma models. Notably, a majority of the glioma-bearing animals that received surgical tumor resection, followed by treatment with TβR2-HFt and the ICI, survived the tumor and resisted tumor rechallenge, providing a potential means to control GBM in a durable manner. Teaser: BBB-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap reverses the immunosuppressive TME to rescue therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade against GBM.

title: Differential Adaptation of Osteocyte Lacunar Morphology at Bone (Re)modeling Sites under Mechanical Loading and Pharmacological Therapies in a Mouse Model of Osteoporosis
abstract: Abstract Postmenopausal osteoporosis is a highly prevalent disease characterized by low bone mass and structural deterioration of bone tissue leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. Osteocytes orchestrate local bone (re)modeling and therefore, characterizing their 3D morphological and spatial distribution across distinct (re)modeling microenvironments is essential for understanding the cellular mechanisms underlying divergent tissue-level responses. To address this, we used a 3D-3D multiscale registration framework mapping endpoint osteocyte lacunae onto dynamic, time-lapsed in vivo ( re)modeling sites. Ovariectomized 15-week-old mice were subjected to 4 weeks of anabolic parathyroid hormone (PTH) or anti-catabolic bisphosphonate (BIS) treatment as monotreatment or combined with cyclic mechanical loading (ML). Biweekly in vivo micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) to identify (re)modeling sites and endpoint ultra-high resolution (ultra-HR) micro-CT to characterize osteocyte lacunae was performed. Osteocyte lacunae were characterized by lacunar density, volume and sphericity. Our findings showed that physical and pharmacological therapies differentially regulate the osteocyte lacunar network through distinct perilacunar adaptations across functional microenvironments. While BIS stabilizes local lacunar architecture, PTH drives asymmetrical lacunar expansion (increased volume with reduced sphericity) through perilacunar remodeling that supersedes any added ML effects. Crucially, estrogen loss disrupts the natural spatial maturation gradient by inducing rounding of lacunae in newly formed bone. Therapies counteract this disruption, restoring the healthy gradients in lacunar morphometry between spatially distinct microenvironments. Additionally, despite restoring tissue-level bone volume, physical and pharmacological osteoporosis therapies do not fully recover persistent lacunar density deficits. The overall lacunar morphological spatial signatures confirm active osteocytic tuning to endocrine, physical and matrix cues.

title: Slice, Subtract, Segment: Efficient 2D and Physiologically Informed 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Background Automated segmentation of glioma subregions on multiparametric MRI can be improved by changing either the network architecture or the information presented to the network. These two design levers are usually studied together, which makes their individual contributions difficult to see. We present an integrated analysis of two completed, independent studies, each of which isolates one lever. Methods In the architecture-level study ( Slice ), SIBA-UNet—a 2D U-Net combining depthwise separable convolution, inverted-bottleneck blocks and attention-guided skip fusion—was trained on 128 × 128 multimodal slices from BraTS 2020 with a patient-level split, and a sigmoid decision threshold was selected on validation data. In the representation-level study ( Subtract ), CMSR-3D augmented the four standard MRI sequences with four voxel-wise cross-modal subtraction maps (T1 − T1CE, T2 − FLAIR, FLAIR − T1CE, T2 − T1CE) and evaluated 4-, 6- and 8-channel inputs with an identical 3D U-Net on 1,251 BraTS-GLI 2023 cases (1,001/125/125 split). Results SIBA-UNet reached an overall validation Dice of 0.8601 at a validation-selected threshold of 0.51, with reported subregion Dice of 0.8795 (necrotic core), 0.8501 (edema) and 0.9125 (enhancing tumor); the source ablation was only partially reported. With the architecture held fixed, the 8-channel CMSR-3D configuration gave the highest mean Dice among the evaluated inputs (0.8699 vs. 0.8534 for the 4-channel baseline) and the lowest mean HD95 (5.9859 vs. 8.2308), whereas either two-map subset alone changed mean Dice by at most 0.0037. Conclusions Architecture design and input-representation design are separable levers for brain tumor segmentation. The controlled representation ablation indicates that the complete set of subtraction maps was more informative than either subset under a fixed 3D U-Net. Both studies were evaluated internally on their respective datasets, and their numerical results are not directly compared because the datasets, dimensionality and evaluation protocols differ.

title: Benchmarking cartilage regeneration across ten chondrogenic cell sources using native tissue references
abstract: Abstract A persistent challenge in cartilage tissue engineering is identifying cell sources capable of regenerating cartilage with native-like properties. Variability in chondrogenic potential among human- and animal-derived cells complicates graft development and disease modeling. Here we benchmarked ten chondrogenic cell sources under standardized culture conditions using hyaluronan-alginate biomaterials and implementing a functionality index combining histological and mechanical metrics referenced to native tissue. Mesenchymal stem cells and fetal chondroprogenitors demonstrated superior regenerative capacity, achieving 103% and 95% of native cartilage functionality, respectively. In contrast, adult articular chondrocytes from healthy and osteoarthritic donors produced fibrocartilaginous tissue with functionality scores below 50%. These findings provide a quantitative framework to guide cell source selection and optimize cartilage graft standardization for clinical applications and physiologically relevant disease models, addressing regulatory demands for product characterization.

title: Extending the least-cost theory of stomatal regulation to include soil moisture stress
abstract: Abstract Terrestrial biosphere models commonly use empirical scaling factors to represent soil moisture constraints on carbon and water fluxes, but these lack mechanistic grounding and produce inconsistent estimates of soil moisture limitations on primary production and transpiration across models. Here we extended the least-cost hypothesis for optimal stomatal conductance to account for soil moisture limitations by allowing soil water availability to modulate the carbon cost of water transport, drawing on the observed temperature dependence of stem respiration, and derived a simple empirical approximation to the theory using global δ 13 C and eddy covariance data. The empirical analysis shows moderated thermal acclimation of stem respiration and a weak increase in water transport costs with aridity, supporting the interpretation that the decline in light-use efficiency (LUE) under arid conditions is primarily attributable to non-stomatal limitations. Validation against an independent global dataset of sapflow-derived canopy conductance and transpiration shows that the revised scheme significantly improves the predictive power of the least-cost hypothesis, offering a more mechanistically coherent alternative to existing soil moisture parameterisations.

title: Epidemic potential of Maravalia cryptostegiae , a classical biological control agent of rubber vine, in Northeastern Brazil
abstract: Abstract Rubber vines ( Cryptostegia madagascariensis and C. grandiflora ) are highly invasive weeds in the semi-arid landscapes of many tropical regions. The rust fungus Maravalia cryptostegiae has provided a spetatular and sustainable control of invasive C. grandiflora populations in Australia, after its scientific and quarantine-authorized release in the context of a classical biological control program. The Caatinga biome of Northeastern Brazil is under a devastating invasion by C. madagascariensis . This species is also susceptible to M. cryptostegia but its epidemic potential towards C. madagascariensis in Brazil remains unknown. We developed a weather-driven epidemiological model integrating experimentally derived relationships for infection as a function of temperature and wetness duration and temperature-dependent latent development. Three infection-response models were fitted to 20 experimental temperature × wetness combinations found in the literature and evaluated using information criteria and grouped cross-validation. The selected model incorporated wetness-dependent thermal breadth and provided the best overall fit ( R 2 = 0.931), with prolonged wetness significantly broadening the thermal range favorable for infection. The infection and latent-development models were coupled with 25 years (2001–2025) of hourly meteorological data from 65 grid cells representing rubber-vine-infested locations in Northeastern Brazil. May–July accounted for >60% of annual infection potential, with the highest epidemic potential in Central Ceará and Western Paraíba, overlapping major host-infestation areas. Cross-continental evaluation at 13 historical monitoring sites in Queensland, Australia, reproduced documented wet-season epidemic patterns and differentiated high-impact coastal/riparian from drier inland environments. These results demonstrate strong seasonal and geographic structuring of epidemic potential, providing a quantitative basis for identifying locations and periods favorable for M. cryptostegiae establishment and epidemic development following its future release in Brazil.

title: Beyond seed counts: what two decades of seed testing reveal about European beech in Poland
abstract: Abstract Forest regeneration depends on a long chain of processes, of which the number of seeds produced is only the first link. Climate-driven changes in seed production and masting in temperate trees are well documented, whereas long-term changes in the quality of the seeds produced have been examined far less often. Using a nationwide operational dataset for European beech ( Fagus sylvatica L.) from Poland (13,387 seed lots from 380 forest districts, 1996 to 2024; temporal analyses on 5,381 freshly harvested lots from 352 districts, 2004 to 2023), we followed three dimensions of seed quality: seed mass, the proportion of filled seeds (purity) and the viability of filled seeds. The three dimensions were nearly uncorrelated (ρ ≤ 0.11 at the district-year level) and changed over time in different ways. Adjusted annual mean seed mass declined by 1.48 g per year (29.6 g, or about 10%, over 20 years), with the whole distribution shifting downwards uniformly across the country. The median proportion of filled seeds remained stable, but the frequency of lots with fewer than 85% filled seeds rose from about 1% to 14% between 2006 and 2023. The viability of filled seeds showed no temporal trend, although it was the only dimension associated with seasonal climate: warmer previous summers and harvest-year autumns were associated with higher viability, and warmer harvest-year springs and summers with lower viability, and these associations were unchanged after controlling for annual crop size. Seed fill was not associated with seasonal climate, and seed mass showed at most a weak negative association with seasonal temperature that could not be assigned to any seasonal window. The decline in seed mass was not related to the masting history of the districts, nor to the local rate of decline in the interannual variability of seed production reconstructed from collection records. In cold storage, viability declined with storage duration and the rate of loss varied among harvest years more than the mean rate itself, but climate during seed development did not modify the rate of loss. Summer and autumn temperatures increased over the study period whereas spring temperature did not; the dimension of quality that responds to climate therefore remained stable, while the two dimensions that changed were at most weakly related to seasonal climate. It seems that the decline in seed mass and the increasing frequency of fill failure are driven by processes that seasonal climatic means do not capture, and their consequences for regeneration remain to be tested.

title: Quantitative modelling of biological response dynamics reveals novel patterns in plant volatile signalling
abstract: Abstract Biological responses to environmental stimuli are inherently dynamic. Recent technological advances enable detailed time-resolved measurements of such responses across biological systems. However, a consistent, universal standard for quantifying temporal response dynamics is lacking, thus limiting biological insights and comparisons. We developed an unbiased mathematical model structure that allows for the quantification of biological response dynamics without a priori knowledge of underlying biochemical mechanisms. Using the model to quantify the dynamics of stress-induced plant volatiles, we uncover a range of novel patterns in volatile signalling, including i) a strong light-independent impact of the time of day of wounding on the onset, duration and shape of the volatile induction responses, ii) an accentuation of volatile-specific induction curve shapes by herbivory-associated molecular patterns (HAMPs) and iii) independent regulation of the strength and duration of volatile induction across genotypes. We also demonstrate that our approach performs well across diverse plant and animal systems, potentially indicating universality across responses. The model is also robust to partial response curves, low resolution data and complex multi-modal responses arising from overlapping stimuli, enabling identification of priming events from otherwise convoluted curves. As all responses measured conform to a common model structure, yet parameter values diverge markedly, we conclude that biologically meaningful information is ignored when temporal dynamics of responses are not quantified. The presented approach will pave the way to identifying new response patterns, and their function, across the tree of life.

title: Root Age Structure Governs Long-Term Architecture and Hydraulic Function in Perennial Plants: a Modelling Framework
abstract: Summary Background and aims Perennial root systems develop over decades and exhibit continuous turnover of structural and absorptive components, yet most root architecture models treat woody roots as permanent and neglect root age structure. We developed an empirically constrained modelling framework that explicitly represents age-structured demography, growth regulation and dormancy in perennial root systems. Methods We extended the functional–structural plant model CPlantBox to simulate perennial root development over decades by integrating age-dependent survival, secondary radial growth and climate-driven dormancy. The model was parameterised using unique three-dimensional root system data from young and mature grapevines, together with dendrochronological root age measurements, and coupled to root hydraulic properties. Key results Empirical analyses revealed multi-cohort age distributions and substantial turnover of lignified structural roots, contradicting the assumption of a static woody scaffold. The model reproduced age distributions, order-specific survival probabilities and fine-to-structural root length ratios, and generated realistic, genotype-specific three-dimensional architectures. Simulated uptake profiles and hydraulic scenarios showed strong age- and architecture-driven effects. Conclusions Explicitly representing woody root age distributions and age-dependent processes may fundamentally change predictions of perennial root system architecture and function. The framework advances root modelling beyond annual paradigms and provides a transferable tool for analysing long-term architectural and hydraulic consequences of genotype × climate interactions in perennial crops.

title: Molecular characterization of a cytochrome P450 involved in the skeletal diversification of tricyclic coumarins in Angelica keiskei
abstract: Abstract Tricyclic coumarins (TCs) exhibit defensive properties against herbivorous insects and possess valuable pharmacological properties for humans. They are mainly distributed in the Apiaceae, Rutaceae, Moraceae, and Fabaceae families. The chemical structural diversity of TCs in these families primarily arises from differences in skeletal variety and attachment position of the third ring, as observed in unsaturated furanocoumarins (FCs) and saturated dihydrofuranocoumarins (DHFCs). In TC biosynthesis, the FC and DHFC pathways diverge through distinct oxidation patterns. The product specificity of the reported cytochrome P450 monooxygenase at the branching point suggests that these TC groups are produced in nearly identical ratios; however, some species of the genus Angelica (Apiaceae) accumulate DHFCs at higher levels than FCs. In this study, we investigated the enzymatic mechanism responsible for forming these two TC groups using A. keiskei , a Japanese native species used as a medicinal and edible herb. Organ-specific transcriptome analysis highlighted a P450 member CYP71AJ62 that exhibited a close correlation with TC accumulation across organs. Enzymatic characterization demonstrated that CYP71AJ62 predominantly forms a hydroxylated DHFC, vaginidiol, which may promote DHFC over FC skeletal formation in TC biosynthesis. Phylogenetic analysis suggested that CYP71AJ62 has been derived from a gene responsible for FC formation by functional shift without gene duplication. Subsequent three-dimensional structural modeling and site-directed mutagenesis revealed that two amino acid residues on substrate recognition sites cooperatively determine the product specificity of this P450 enzyme. This study provides new insights into the molecular evolutionary process underlying ring-structure diversification and, more broadly, the adaptation of plants to their environments.

title: Overexpression of Active or Inactive RNase J Disrupts Chloroplast RNA Quality Control in Arabidopsis
abstract: SUMMARY The chloroplast is a semi-autonomous organelle with a compact genome encoding ∼100 expressed genes. Numerous and widespread promoters coupled with inefficient transcription termination leads to a highly complex primary transcriptome that undergoes extensive RNA quality control orchestrated by RNA binding proteins and ribonucleases. Among the ribonucleases, only RNase J (RNJ) is absolutely required for plant germination and survival, likely because its deficiency leads to massive accumulation of antisense RNA which inhibits translation. As one approach to understanding the selectivity of RNJ for antisense RNA and noncoding regions, we created Arabidopsis lines overexpressing catalytically inactive versions of the enzyme designed to trap its substrates. Initially, transgenic plants appeared phenotypically normal. However, crosses used to generate homozygous transgenic lines yielded progeny that developed varying degrees of chlorosis within 2-3 weeks. Concomitantly, these plants exhibited chloroplast transcriptome alterations similar to RNJ-silenced lines, along with mRNA changes consistent with retrograde signaling. This chlorosis could be correlated to the likely decay of RNJ protein, but not its endogenous transcript. The result could be replicated by attempting to overexpress a wild-type version of RNJ, in which case even one transgene copy was sufficient to induce chlorosis. Our results suggest that RNJ is under protein expression level surveillance to prevent wholesale destruction of the plastid transcriptome.

title: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of PtaAGL16 improves post-drought recovery and shoot vitality in hybrid poplar
abstract: Abstract Drought stress severely limits tree growth and survival, a problem intensifying under climate change due to the rising frequency of extreme weather events. Identifying genetic variants that modulate drought stress responses and enhance resilience is therefore of great interest for developing climate-adapted trees. While the MADS-box transcription factor AGL16 has been implicated in drought responses and stomatal regulation in herbaceous species, the function of its homolog in woody perennials remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the role of PtaAGL16 in the poplar hybrid Populus tremula × P. alba . We generated CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines of PtaAGL16 in the poplar clone INRA 717-1B4. Plants were subjected to a severe drought stress regime followed by a re-watering recovery phase. Morphological and physiological traits, including growth, stomatal conductance, shoot vitality, and stomatal density, together with stress-associated metabolites and drought-responsive gene expression, were analyzed. All agl16 knockout lines exhibited significantly reduced drought-induced damage compared to the wild-type. While the wild-type suffered extensive defoliation and persistent stem necrosis, the knockout lines retained higher shoot vitality and resumed growth after re-watering, including the formation of new leaves. Consequently, vitality in the knockout lines reached up to 86%, compared to only 34% in the wild-type. This improved resilience was accompanied by reduced persistent oxidative membrane damage, as indicated by lower MDA levels after recovery. These findings indicate that the disruption of PtaAGL16 is associated with enhanced drought resilience in a woody perennial species and highlight its potential as a genetic target for improving climate adaptation in fast-growing forest trees.

title: A decision-based criterion and a resolution threshold for ranking genomic prediction models within trials
abstract: Abstract Breeding programmes choose genomic prediction models by accuracy rankings, and the metric behind a ranking decides which model wins. Selecting the best genotypes within a trial depends only on the order of the predictions, so a metric that guides the choice must be unchanged by any order-preserving change of the predictions and respond when their order is reversed. Of the 22 official metrics of the Genomes to Fields maize competition, one meets both conditions, the within-environment rank correlation; the within-environment Pearson correlation is protected against rescaling only; and twenty fail, including the root mean squared error that decided the 2022 ranking. Switching between the competition’s two official metrics reverses 27 % of team pairs, and an exact decomposition shows why pooled metrics mislead: in three constructed panels, 94–95 % of the attainable square of pooled correlation is carried by the environment means. The accuracy difference a trial can resolve falls as about 3/√ N with its N genotype–environment cells: at least 0.03 at the competition’s design and 0.04–0.12 once calibrated on real panels, against 0.003 between the first two teams; tests that two correlations differ declare far smaller differences, which do not reliably change selection. In soybean, where the two most accurate methods stand clear of most others by more than the trial resolves, ranking by either within-environment correlation selects better material, 98–99 % of the attainable selection gain in held-out environments against 13–34 % for error-magnitude rankings; in common bean and a Chinese maize population, where the leading methods lie within the resolvable gap, all rules pick material of similar value. GPverdict runs these checks on any programme’s cross-validated predictions.

title: Dynamic 2′-O-Me of rRNA regulates ribosome translation in Arabidopsis nucleolin1 mutants and during seed-to-seedling transition
abstract: ABSTRACT Across all kingdoms of life, 2′- O -ribose methylation ( 2 ′ -O- Me) is the most abundant modification of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), which are central to ribosome assembly and function. The 2′- O -Me of specific rRNA sites is catalysed by C/D-box small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) complexes. However, how and when the landscape of plant rRNA 2′- O -Me modifications is remodelled remains largely unexplored. To study the regulation of rRNA 2′- O -Me and its impact on ribosome translation, we characterised Arabidopsis NUCLEOLIN 1 (NUC1)-depleted plants, which exhibit reduced 2′- O -Me at dozens specific rRNA sites, and investigated the impact of 2′- O -Me in ribosome translation during plant development. We demonstrated that 2′- O -Me is dynamically regulated during seed-to-seedling transition. Our analysis identified differentially methylated rRNA sites, which are specifically located in structurally critical regions of the ribosome. Notably, this hypomethylation is uncoupled from the global expression, assembly, or subcellular localisation of C/D-box snoRNPs. We further observed that polysomes with low 2′- O -Me levels not only accumulate but also exhibit differential mRNA loading. These polysomes characterised by reduced 2’- O -Me at specific rRNA sites, influence multiples aspects of translation, including ribosomes stalling at the initiation, elongation and termination steps. Together, these findings advance our understanding of the dynamic regulation of rRNA 2′- O -methylation and its functional role in ribosome-mediated translation in plants.

title: “Myosin-Driven Nuclear Movement Generates Stromules in Arabidopsis thaliana ”
abstract: Abstract Plastids form stroma-filled tubular extensions, termed stromules, that are implicated in inter-organellar communication. In pathogen-challenged Nicotiana benthamiana , stromule formation is driven by kinesins acting along microtubules. However, whether this mechanism also operates in unstressed plants or in other species remains unknown. Using systematic genetic analysis of all class XI myosin genes and quantitative time-lapse imaging in Arabidopsis ( Arabidopsis thaliana ), we show that basal stromule formation is predominantly myosin dependent through two distinct mechanisms. Myosin XI-I generates most stromules by driving oscillatory nuclear movement that mechanically pulls stromules from stationary plastids within the approx. 8µm wide stromule-promoting zone. Myosins XI-K, XI-1, and XI-2 additionally drive a movement-independent, nucleus-associated stromule subpopulation within the same zone, establishing two mechanistically distinct pathways. We propose that movement-coupled stromules function as dynamic tethers maintaining plastid–nucleus proximity during nuclear oscillations, while movement-independent stromules expand the plastid membrane area within the perinuclear space, increasing the potential contact surface with the nucleus and surrounding environment. Together, both populations are proposed to enhance signal and metabolite exchange at the plastid–nucleus interface. These findings indicate that stromule biogenesis is both mechanistically and functionally context dependent, challenging the universality of the kinesin–microtubule model across plant species and physiological states.

title: Studying the role of climate and sex in flowering dynamics of black poplar across time and space
abstract: Abstract Global change has a major impact on rivers and their associated terrestrial compartment, the riparian forest. The black poplar ( Populus nigra L.), the dominant species of the European riparian forest, is considered an indicator of the biodiversity dynamics of these ecosystems, but is threatened with extinction in several parts of its range. The species is dioecious and shows wide variability in many traits, enabling it to adapt to a broad range of environmental conditions. A detailed characterization of this natural variability is therefore a key issue both for the conservation of natural populations and for biological engineering aimed at restoring riverbanks. Phenology is both an indicator of climate change and an adaptation lever for populations, particularly in perennial species such as trees. In this study, we characterized the spatial and temporal variability in flowering phenology by studying 13 natural black poplar populations along the Loire River, France. Flowering date and duration showed substantial variability both within and between populations, and males generally flowered earlier than females. Despite this variability, the ranking of individual trees’ flowering dates was highly consistent across years. Most male-female pairs shared several days of overlapping flowering each year, and this overlap was moderately stable across years. Flowering dates advanced by about five to six days per degree Celsius during early spring, with no detectable difference in sensitivity between sexes. This work contributes to the characterization of flowering variability in an economically important tree species and may inform both the conservation of genetic resources and breeding. Highlights Flowering phenology varied substantially within and among black poplar populations. Male black poplars generally flowered earlier than females. Flowering advanced by 5–6 days per °C increase in early spring temperature. Phenological diversity informs black poplar conservation and breeding.

title: Jasmonate restrains the enhanced growth response of lateral roots induced systemically by a local water deficit
abstract: Abstract Water availability in drying soils is most often spatially heterogeneous, requiring plants to adjust their root system architecture to sustain water uptake. This acclimation response to water deficit (WD) relies on the integration of local and systemic signals. The later and their mode of action remain poorly understood. Using hydroponic split-root systems in maize and Arabidopsis, we show that, with respect to control well-watered plants, a local WD does not affect shoot biomass but suppresses lateral root (LR) growth in the water-deprived compartment while promoting LR elongation in the well-watered compartment. Spatiotemporal analyses in maize revealed an early and transient (<2h) transcriptomic response of LRs triggered by both local and systemic WD signals. This response involved activation of jasmonate (JA) biosynthesis and signaling components, including MYC2 like regulators and JAZ repressors. It occurred in both the water-deprived and well-watered root halves of split roots, with no evidence of long-distance transport of JA. Furthermore, exogenous methyl jasmonate locally inhibited LR elongation, whereas the Arabidopsis JA insensitive jar1-1 mutant showed an enhanced systemic LR growth response to a local WD. Together, these findings demonstrate that JA acts as an early negative regulator that counterbalances the systemic enhancement of LR growth induced by a local WD, thereby fine-tuning root system architecture and water uptake during local soil drying. Significance Statement Plants growing in heterogeneous soils must coordinate local and systemic responses to optimize water acquisition, yet the underlying signaling mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using hydroponic split-root systems in maize and Arabidopsis, we show that local water deficit rapidly suppresses root growth in the stressed root half while stimulating lateral root elongation in the unstressed half. Spatiotemporal transcriptomic analyses reveal a rapid, transient activation of jasmonate biosynthesis and signaling. Genetic evidence further demonstrates that jasmonate restricts systemic lateral root elongation, acting as a negative regulator of developmental plasticity. These findings uncover a balanced interplay between positive and negative effectors and an unexpected role for jasmonate as an early integrator of systemic root responses to heterogeneous water availability, expanding its established functions beyond defense and canonical drought signaling.

title: Unfolded Protein Response signaling restricts PTI and limits salicylic acid-dependent cell death under ER stress
abstract: Abstract The Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) maintains endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis during proteotoxic stress while also contributing to plant immunity. However, the functional relationship between UPR signaling, pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP)-triggered immunity (PTI) and salicylic acid (SA) remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated this interplay using Arabidopsis mutants impaired in the two major UPR branches. Mutants defective in the INOSITOL-REQUIRING ENZYME 1 (IRE1)-bZIP60 branch displayed enhanced resistance to Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 and to the type III secretion-deficient strain hrcC − , indicating potentiation of PTI. Consistently, the ire1a ire1b double mutant exhibited increased flg22-induced callose deposition, whereas reactive oxygen species production was unaffected. Despite enhanced basal resistance, all UPR mutants retained full responsiveness to benzothiadiazole, demonstrating that downstream SA signaling remains functional independently of UPR integrity. Conversely, acute ER stress induced by tunicamycin promoted SA accumulation and extensive leaf necrosis. Reverse genetics revealed that SA-deficient mutants were largely protected from ER stress-induced cell death, whereas mutants over-accumulating SA exhibited enhanced susceptibility, demonstrating that endogenous SA is required for the full execution of this response. Analysis of an independent transcriptomic dataset further showed that loss of IRE1 de-represses genes involved in SA biosynthesis, PTI and defense under ER stress. Together, our results identify IRE1 as a key regulator coordinating ER homeostasis with immune signaling by limiting SA-dependent defense activation during ER stress, while simultaneously preventing excessive cell death. Highlights UPR deficiency primes PAMP-triggered immunity and increases resistance to bacterial pathogens. The UPR acts as a brake on PTI, inverting the view of the UPR as a simple positive regulator of immunity. Acute ER stress drives salicylic acid accumulation ER stress-induced cell death is dependent on SA IRE1, bZIP60 and bZIP28 are the principal UPR actors mitigating acute tunicamycin-induced ER stress. BTH-induced resistance is independent of the UPR, separating induced resistance from ER stress control.

title: EdiProPred: Prediction of Edible Plant Tissue-Associated Proteins Using Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract Ensuring the safety and suitability of proteins considered for food and biotechnology applications is an important challenge. Computational approaches can facilitate the prioritisation of candidate proteins for further investigation, particularly given the rapid growth of genomic and metagenomic sequence datasets. In this study, we developed computational models to distinguish edible plant tissue-associated (EPTA) proteins from non-EPTA proteins. The positive class comprised 939 proteins with experimentally validated evidence of expression in plant tissues commonly consumed by humans, hereafter referred to as EPTA proteins. The negative class comprised 939 proteins annotated in UniProt as toxic, allergenic, or antinutritional, hereafter referred to as non-EPTA proteins. Models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation with a cluster-based partitioning strategy, ensuring that no protein in the validation set shared more than 40% sequence identity with proteins in the corresponding training set. First, composition-based sequence features were evaluated to establish a baseline for EPTA or non-EPTA classification, with the Extra Trees (ET) classifier achieving a validation AUROC of 0.848. To incorporate evolutionary information beyond amino acid composition, PSSM profiles were subsequently evaluated, yielding an AUROC of 0.842 with an SVM classifier. Finally, to capture richer sequence patterns and contextual information using protein language modelling, we evaluated ESM2-based models. The fine-tuned ESM2-T33 model achieved the highest validation AUROC of 0.925 and was selected as the final predictive model. The resulting approach was implemented as the EdiProPred web server ( https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/edipropred/ ) and standalone software for computational classification of plant proteins. The EdiProPred framework provides a useful computational tool for prioritising candidate plant proteins and facilitating the exploration of novel protein resources for food and biotechnology applications. Highlights Proteins expressed in the edible parts of plants are considered edible proteins. Toxins, allergens, and anti-nutritional proteins are considered non-edible proteins. All models were trained, tested, and evaluated using non-redundant datasets. The evolutionary language model achieved the highest performance. A platform for the Prediction, Design, and Screening of Edible Proteins. Author’s Biography Pushpendra Singh Gahlot is currently pursuing a PhD in Computational Biology at the Department of Computational Biology, Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, New Delhi, India. Akshay Shendre is currently working as a Research Assistant in the Computational Biology Department at the Department of Computational Biology, Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, New Delhi, India. Gajendra P.S. Raghava is currently working as a Professor and Director of Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, New Delhi, India.

title: Towards an understanding of the taxonomy of the Eurasian montane riparian genus Myricaria (Tamaricaceae) through Angiosperms353 herbariomics
abstract: ABSTRACT Myricaria Desv. (Tamaricaceae) is a genus of shrubs that play a keystone role in montane riparian ecosystems across Eurasia, shaping riverine habitats and supporting ecological function. The genus has a centre of origin in the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau and exhibits a broad distribution, but many species boundaries are unresolved. Here, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Myricaria using the Angiosperms353 target enrichment bait set, with sampling across its full geographic range. Off-target plastid loci were extracted from next-generation sequencing data using the CAPTUS bioinformatics pipeline. We infer species relationships using ASTRAL-IV and network analysis with SplitsTree, in conjunction with morphology. We also provide a taxonomic treatment of the genus, integrating our morphological observations and phylogenomic analyses for species delimitations. Based on our analyses, recognise two infrageneric sections: sect. Parallelantherae (containing only M. elegans ) and sect. Myricaria (the remainder of the genus, with type species M. germanica ). We also propose synonymising M. davurica , M. bracteata and M. squamosa with M. germanica . Although species boundaries in the Asian highlands remain unresolved, we conclude that the species M. elegans , M. germanica , M. laxiflora , M. longifolia , M. platyphylla , and M. pulcherrima are well-supported both phylogenomically and morphologically.

title: An Aphid Protein Interferes with Plant endomembrane Trafficking Machinery to Promote Aphid Survival and Plant Growth
abstract: Aphids deplete their host plants of amino acids and other essential nutrients by feeding on phloem sap. Autophagy, a conserved process across eukaryotes, maintains cellular homeostasis during starvation and environmental stress by recycling damaged or excess cellular components. Here, we identified and characterized a previously uninvestigated aphid salivary protein, termed Aphid Autophagy-Related Factor 1 (AAF1), that is secreted into plant cells and manipulates plant physiology in a manner that benefits the aphid. We show that AAF1 interacts with four known or putative host autophagy-related proteins: RABD1 and RABD2a (plant homologs of Ypt1/RAB1), ATG8, a ubiquitin-like protein required for autophagosome formation, and PI3PT, a previously uncharacterized ER-localized putative lipid-binding or lipid-transfer protein annotated as a phosphoinositide 3-phosphate transfer protein. We further demonstrate that the RAB-binding domain of AAF1 and its interaction with RABD2a may be specifically required for AAF1 function. In addition, we identified unique, highly mobile compartments containing interacting AAF1 and RABD2a that are associated with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and dynamically traffic with autophagosomes. We propose that these compartments may be derived from endosomes or endosome-ER contact sites (EERCSs) and serve as platforms for autophagosome trafficking and/or biogenesis. We further propose that AAF1, RABD2a, and PI3PT function together to regulate the formation or function of these compartments, thereby supporting autophagosome formation and trafficking. Finally, we show that stable expression of AAF1 in plants enhances growth and biomass in an autophagy-dependent manner.

title: Emergence of tunneling nanotube-like intervesicular connections
abstract: Abstract Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are actin-supported membrane bridges that mediate long-range intercellular communication and direct transfer of signaling molecules, organelles, and pathogenic cargo, yet the physicochemical mechanisms underlying their formation and organization remain poorly understood. Here we show that TNT-like intervesicular connections emerge from minimal physicochemical interactions between actin filaments and lipid membranes. Upon Mg²⁺ exposure, actin-encapsulating vesicles spontaneously generated actin bundle-embedded lipid nanotubes (AT-LNTs) that formed stable intervesicular networks. Mg²⁺ simultaneously induced actin polymerization, filament bundling, and electrostatic recruitment of F-actin to phosphatidylcholine membranes, enabling membrane tubulation without actin-binding proteins. Systematic perturbation of membrane phase, membrane tension, Mg²⁺ concentration, ionic strength, and actin concentration revealed that AT-LNT formation occurs only within a narrow physicochemical regime where membrane deformation and actin-membrane coupling are simultaneously permissive. The resulting AT-LNTs reproduced key structural and dynamic features of cellular TNTs, including bundled organization, helical unwinding, lumenal diffusion, and spontaneous bridging between synthetic vesicles and living cells. These findings establish a minimal biophysical framework for understanding the emergence of intercellular membrane connections in living systems and provide a foundation for engineering communication between synthetic and living cell.

title: Targeted tumor desialylation by engineered probiotic reprograms the tumor microenvironment to potentiate immunotherapy
abstract: Abstract Tumor hypersialylation drives immunosuppression and limits immunotherapy efficacy by shielding tumor cells and engaging inhibitory immune receptors. Here, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN Δpgi -SAS) as a metabolically confined “desialylation catalyst” to remodel the tumor microenvironment. This strain combines HER2-directed adhesion, hypoxia-inducible surface sialidase display for targeted glycan cleavage, and sialic acid catabolism to prevent glycolytic recycling. Critically, disrupting glucose metabolism (Δ pgi ) restricts bacterial proliferation to sialic acid-rich tumor microenvironment, significantly enhancing biosafety. In mice, EcN Δpgi -SAS colonized tumors and effectively desialylated tumor cells, synergizing with anti-PD-L1 to suppress growth of immunologically “cold” tumors. Mechanistically, desialylation reversed immunosuppression by broadly enhancing antitumor immunity. Orally administered EcN Δpgi -SAS substantially inhibited colorectal carcinogenesis, repaired epithelial barrier integrity by restoring tight junctions, and prevented adenoma formation. This integrated strategy establishes a clinically translatable platform for reversing immunosuppression in solid tumors.

title: The p53-Mdm2 interaction through the lens of antithetic feedback
abstract: Abstract We show that the p53-Mdm2 gene interaction can be understood as a form of antithetic feedback, but with mixed feedback loops. In particular, we show that this viewpoint sheds light on the emergence and robustness properties of p53’s oscillatory behaviour, as observed experimentally.

title: Biotin-operated ligand trapping enables dynamic spatial redistribution of protein and organelle in living cells
abstract: Controlling protein localization through chemical biology tools is essential for mechanistic interrogations, functional perturbations, and therapeutic development. While existing tools cover a wide range of applications, no single approach simultaneously enables inducible trapping, controlled release, and visualization of a protein of interest (POI). To address this gap, we developed Biotin-Operated Ligand Trapping (BOLT), which combines a HaloTag-fused POI with a streptavidin trap. Desthiobiotin-conjugated Janelia Fluor HaloTag ligands enable POI visualization, trapping, and biotin-operated release. We demonstrate BOLT's capacity in synchronized secretory cargo release, microtubule-directed organelle movement and hitchhiking, and ectopically localizing nuclear transcription factor. Importantly, pulse-chase BOLT further reveals bidirectional endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking of an endogenous Golgi enzyme and distinguishes recycled from newly synthesized enzyme populations using distinct HTLs. Altogether, BOLT provides an all-in-one platform to interrogate how subcellular localization regulates protein function across HaloTag-compatible systems.

title: Evaluating low-cost hyperspectral and RGB fusion with PSNet for presymptomatic detection of Albugo candida in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: Abstract Plant pathogens cause substantial yield losses worldwide, threatening food security and livelihoods. Because early infection is difficult to diagnose, management often relies on prophylactic pesticide use, increasing costs and environmental impacts. Here we evaluate PSNet, a multimodal framework that fuses hyperspectral and RGB imaging for presymptomatic plant disease detection, together with a low-cost Raspberry Pi hyperspectral camera. We tested the system using Arabidopsis thaliana inoculated with the oomycete Albugo candida in a controlled experiment comprising 96 plants imaged at 2, 4 and 6 days post inoculation (dpi). PSNet achieved 90.00% overall accuracy on the four-class task comprising Healthy, 2 dpi, 4 dpi and 6 dpi. Collapsing the same true and predicted labels into healthy versus inoculated yielded 97.50% binary accuracy across all dates. Supplementary date-specific binary analyses compared inoculated and mock-inoculated plants separately, using plant-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, three training seeds and within-plant probability aggregation. PSNet achieved balanced accuracies of 55.79%, 83.56% and 95.37% at 2, 4 and 6 dpi, respectively. The 4 dpi observations preceded visible symptoms, whereas at 6 dpi abaxial sporulation was present despite the imaged adaxial surface remaining symptom-free. RGB-only models also performed strongly at 4 and 6 dpi, while HSI-only discrimination weakened after 2 dpi, and no consistent advantage of hyperspectral fusion over RGB alone was demonstrated. Whole-cube spectral analysis identified significant treatment-group differences across 269 of 313 spectral positions at 2 dpi, but none at 4 or 6 dpi after within-time-point Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Because treatment was confounded with tray and acquisition order, these spectral differences cannot be attributed specifically to infection. Together, these results support the use of low-cost multimodal imaging for controlled-condition plant disease classification, while highlighting the need for independent validation before diagnostic deployment.

title: Domesticated pennycress is a predominantly self-pollinated crop
abstract: Abstract Domesticated pennycress ( Thlaspi arvense L.) is an emerging winter annual oilseed crop developed from field pennycress to deliver commercial agronomic performance, low-carbon feedstock for biofuel production, and value-added animal feed. Effective breeding, seed production, and stewardship of this newly domesticated crop requires a clear understanding of its potential for pollen-mediated outcrossing. Although prior evidence suggests that field pennycress is predominantly self-pollinated, direct experimental evidence remains limited. Here, we integrate laboratory, greenhouse, and field experiments to rigorously evaluate pollen viability, pollen movement, and outcrossing potential in domesticated pennycress. Pollen viability declined rapidly with increasing temperature and environmental exposure: pollen stored at 4°C reached 50% viability after 12 h, whereas pollen held at 37°C reached the same threshold after 2.5 h. Exposure to outdoor conditions with natural light and wind reduced viability to 50% within 1.6 h. Under greenhouse conditions, no cross-pollination was detected among plants flowering in close proximity within an agitated pollen-containment covering. Detectable cross-pollination occurred primarily when emasculated flowers were directly exposed to donor pollen, demonstrating that intact flowers strongly favor self-fertilization. Field trials using a trackable knockout gene edit provided no detectable evidence of pollen movement under field conditions across two locations, even at short distances from donor plots. Together, these results provide strong, multi-environment evidence that domesticated pennycress is predominantly self-pollinated and that outcrossing is rare under practical greenhouse and field production conditions.

title: Effector-host networks in the barley powdery mildew pathosystem reveal significant targeting of ubiquitin-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators
abstract: Summary The ascomycete fungal pathogen Blumeria hordei ( Bh ) is predicted to secrete over 530 effector proteins to infect barley and cause powdery mildew disease, yet their individual and collective functions are largely unexplored. We used yeast two-hybrid next-generation interaction screening (Y2H-NGIS) to probe the host targets of 48 Bh candidate secreted effectors (CSEPs), including multiple AVR A effectors that are recognized by MLA nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) receptors. Y2H-NGIS and subsequent binary retesting identified 356 high-confidence protein-protein interactions (PPI) among Bh CSEPs, MLA NLR fragments, and barley proteins. We uncovered unique and shared host targets, including numerous proteins involved in ubiquitin-associated processes, gene expression, immune and kinase signaling, metabolism, and vesicle trafficking. We identified a host protein ( Hv CAP2) that interacts with MLA and at least five Bh effectors, as well as additional effector-host PPI that correlate with loss of recognition of AVR A13 and AVR A6 by MLA13 and MLA6, respectively. Results were integrated with an interolog-based barley interactome (HvInt) to assemble a host-pathogen network of 1248 proteins and 1701 interactions. This PPI resource can serve as a platform for functional investigations into the molecular basis of powdery mildew pathogenesis and host recognition.

title: Arabidopsis cysteine protease RD19 limits RBOHD-generated ROS production in pattern triggered immunity
abstract: Abstract Plants perceive pathogenic threats through receptors localized at the plasma membrane and inside cells to initiate pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) and effector-triggered immunity (ETI), respectively. PTI and ETI pathways are interconnected and partially converge on the EDS1-PAD4-ADR1 branch which stimulates anti-pathogen defence. Besides these canonical immune pathways, proteolysis plays a pivotal role in immunity by regulating the abundance and activities of diverse components. We previously identified Arabidopsis papain-like cysteine protease RD19 as a PAD4 interactor and showed that RD19 promotes resistance to host-adapted pathogens. Here, we investigated the contribution of RD19 to bacterial flg22 and nlp20 elicited PTI responses which exhibit, respectively, partial and high PAD4 dependence. We show that although PAD4 and RD19 both promote PTI, they have separate functions. In resting (non-triggered) and nlp20-triggered tissues, RD19 limits RBOHD protein accumulation and consequently ROS production. Using N-terminomic enrichment and protease cleavage site identification methods we identify candidate RD19 substrates in resting and nlp20-responding tissues. Our analysis shows that two immune-related aspartyl proteases AED3 and AED2/ASPG1 are likely direct RD19 targets. This study reveals a role of RD19 in ROS regulation and advances our understanding of proteolysis and dynamic RD19 substrate targeting in plant immunity. Highlight Arabidopsis RD19 cysteine protease modulates accumulation of the immune signalling hub protein RBOHD and its generation of ROS. RD19 processes multiple immune-related proteins and promotes defence potentiation in pattern-triggered immunity.

title: Pancreatic progenitor cells respond to laminar shear stress with transcriptomic changes, accompanied by reduced YAP1 activity
abstract: Abstract The human pancreas secretes digestive fluid that flows through an extensive ductal network before emptying into the duodenum. However, little is known about how hydrodynamic forces influence pancreatic function and development. We hypothesized that pancreatic cells respond to physiological levels of fluid shear stress. In this study, we developed a microfluidic system featuring reversible sealing between the device layer and the cell culture substrate, enabling (1) conventional open-well cell culture prior to fluid shear stress application and (2) selective patterning of proteins and cells for migration studies. Channel dimensions were chosen to support 24-hour perfusion using standard syringe pumps. Using this platform, we investigated effects of physiological shear stress levels representing basal and activated pancreatic function (2, 8 and 33 mPa) on human iPSC-derived pancreatic progenitor cells. Pancreatic progenitor cells exhibit graded sensitivity to shear stress at the transcriptomic level. Specifically, shear stress upregulated expression of cell cycle-related gene sets; endocrine-associated genes including NEUROG3 ; and Notch receptor ligands ( DLL1 , DLL3 ) in a magnitude-dependent manner. The exposure to unidirectional fluid flow also resulted in a reduction in YAP1 protein content, decreased WWTR1 gene expression, and downregulation of YAP/TAZ target genes. Furthermore, barrier-based migration assays under shear stress revealed that cell patches expanded their boundaries both along and against the flow, with greater distance in the direction of flow. Our system and findings may help lay the foundation for understanding biophysical regulation of developmental processes in a physiologically important, yet hard-to-access, epithelial model system.

title: Interconnected Macroporous GelMA Scaffolds for Cell Culture through Temperature Controlled Spinodal Decomposition
abstract: Abstract Developing biomaterials that faithfully recapitulate the complex architecture of native tissues is central to tissue engineering. Conventional hydrogels typically exhibit nanoscale porosity, which limits mass transport and cell migration and thereby constrains tissue development. Here, we exploit liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) to generate interconnected macroporous gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) scaffolds with tunable pore sizes ranging from 2 to 50 µm under physiological pH conditions. By mapping the GelMA/dextran phase diagram, we identify a composition range in which LLPS occurs through spinodal decomposition, resulting in a spontaneous bicontinuous, trabecular-like architecture. Pore size can be further tuned by varying polymer concentrations and temperature. We advantageously combined thermal gradients and photopatterning to enable spatial control over pore morphology to fabricate hierarchically structured materials. The biological relevance of these architectures is assessed using fibroblasts cultured within controlled porosity gradients. We show that pore size strongly influences cell infiltration, growth, and spatial organization, with larger pores providing sufficient space for cell migration while reducing the dependence on matrix degradation. Pore size of 7–15 µm is identified for maximizing fibroblast growth. Overall, our approach provides a versatile platform for porosity screening, enabling the engineering of biomimetic hydrogels with optimized microarchitectures tailored to specific biological contexts for three-dimensional cell culture.

title: Designed nanofiber immunogens prime antibody responses to diverse conformations of the HIV-1 fusion peptide
abstract: Focusing antibody responses towards known neutralizing epitopes is a major strategy for protective immunization. Targeting flexible antigenic regions represents a unique challenge because functional antibodies must be able to bind the epitope of interest in multiple conformations. The fusion peptide (FP) of HIV-1 is a flexible peptide critical to viral entry of host cells for which broadly neutralizing antibodies have been identified. Because elicitation of potent, functional antibodies toward this epitope remains an unmet challenge in HIV-1 vaccination, we introduce a designed immunogen platform capable of raising anti-FP-antibodies with increased conformational tolerance relative to a traditional carrier protein. Antibodies induced by these immunogens bind heterologous FP sequences when elicited in mice and infant non-human primates. This platform shows promise for preclinical development to prime antibody responses toward FP of the HIV-1 envelope and can likely be translated to peptide immunofocusing for other viral pathogens.

title: Enriching microlaser-labelled cells by commercial flow cytometry-based cell sorting systems
abstract: Abstract Microlasers based on whispering-gallery modes (WGMs) provide bright, spectrally narrow emission, making them ideal optical probes for high-resolution cellular tagging, single-cell tracking, and biosensing. To reproducibly apply WGM microlasers in biomedical or tissue-engineering contexts, control over the number of lasers in a cell population is highly desirable. Here we use a commercial instrument for flow cytometry-based cell sorting to obtain HEK293T cell populations with a controlled number of polystyrene laser particles (LPs). By modifying the particle surface with poly(ethyleneimine) (PEI) or lipofectamine, we enhance LP-association to cells. We demonstrate that our sorting procedure yields viable cells showing unchanged proliferation rates. Manufacturer-dependent differences in particle-cell interactions were observed and investigated by scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) and flow cytometry. Finally, we show that the same sorting approach enables the generation of multi-cellular spheroids with a defined ratio of LP-containing and LP-free cells. This work lays the foundation for larger tissue engineering studies with defined LP populations and control over LP-placement with respect to the cell.

title: Engineered mRNA-packaging virus-like particles enable efficient and precise mitochondrial base editing in vitro and in vivo
abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) base editors (mtBEs) are promising tools for studying and correcting pathogenic mtDNA mutations. However, the application of mtBEs is often hindered by substantial mtDNA-wide off-target editing that accumulates with prolonged mtBE expression resulting from plasmid DNA or viral delivery. To overcome this limitation, we developed mtBE-VLPs, a virus-like-particle (VLP) platform for transiently delivering mtBEs in vitro and in vivo with minimal off-target effects. While canonical protein-packaging VLPs yielded undetectable mtDNA base editing, engineered mRNA-packaging VLPs enabled efficient but transient mtBE cargo delivery. By iteratively engineering mRNA-packaging VLP compositions, we improved mtBE-VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies from less than 1% to greater than 50% across multiple target mtDNA loci in bulk populations of treated cultured cells. To further improve the packaging and delivery of certain mtBEs, we developed a strategy to selectively reduce mtBE cargo expression in VLP producer cells but not transduced cells, which increased VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies for certain mtBEs by 7.1-fold. Compared to plasmid DNA delivery in vitro , mtBE-VLPs exhibited equivalent on-target editing but 23- to 41-fold lower mtDNA-wide off-target editing, highlighting the improved editing specificity offered by transient mtBE delivery. mtBE-VLPs efficiently installed a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (88% efficiency) and corrected a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in a human patient-derived cell line (41% efficiency). Additionally, a single subretinal injection of mtBE-VLPs yielded 6–20% (average 12%) mtDNA base editing in the mouse retinal pigment epithelium with minimal mtDNA-wide off-target editing. These findings establish mRNA-packaging mtBE-VLPs as promising vehicles for efficient and precise mitochondrial base editing via transient mtBE delivery.

title: Agentic campaign control for high-throughput de novo binder design
abstract: Abstract Progress in artificial intelligence has produced a rapidly growing ecosystem of methods for de novo protein design. With access to many specialized and often complementary tools, how does one use them effectively, especially with a finite compute budget? Here, we introduce Target-adaptive Rescue–Explore–eXploit (T-REX) , an agentic protein binder design framework that orchestrates multiple state-of-the-art protein generative models and structure evaluators. Over the course of a design campaign, T-REX leverages large language model (LLM) agents to reason over accumulating outcomes and decide whether to rescue promising candidates, explore alternative settings, or exploit productive routes, while a deterministic controller validates and schedules proposed actions. Across seven targets, we find that T-REX adaptively allocates its compute across methods in a target-dependent manner and achieves the highest throughput of structurally distinct hits compared to all baselines. These results suggest that adaptive orchestration can complement increasingly powerful protein design models, and we openly release T-REX to support compute-efficient binder design workflows.

title: Answering clinicians’ questions over trial evidence tables with verifiable, feedback-driven language models
abstract: Abstract Systematic reviews condense clinical trials into evidence tables, yet clinicians can interrogate these tables only through database queries, and many questions concern attributes that the table does not record, such as a drug’s target class or a harmonised endpoint. Here we introduce FD-SCoPE, a language-model framework that answers both kinds of question, exposes the query, the selected trials and the derivation rule behind every answer, and learns from expert corrections. On an oncology evidence table of 159 immune checkpoint inhibitor trial records, FD-SCoPE completed all 140 clinician-style tasks (alternatives, 90.7–97.9%). For questions needing derived attributes it retrieved 99.3% of relevant trial records at a positive predictive value of 89.8% and outperformed four alternative approaches (derived-value F1 77.7% versus 64.8–73.4%). Corrections on 299 questions, simulated from reference answers, raised F1 on 1,201 unseen questions from 77.9% to 84.9%. Language models coupled with executable queries, verified programs and expert feedback can give clinicians auditable access to trial evidence.

title: A 4D GelMA-Cad/Gelatin Hydrogel for High-Resolution DMD Bioprinting of Vascularized Soft Tissue Models
abstract: Digital micromirror device (DMD)-based bioprinting enables high-resolution fabrication of hydrogel-based tissue constructs, but print fidelity and hydrogel mechanics are typically coupled through polymer concentration, light exposure, and crosslinking density. This creates a materials constraint for vascular bioprinting, where constructs must preserve microscale architecture during fabrication while supporting multicellular remodeling, lumen formation, and long-term tissue organization. To meet these requirements, we developed a 4D GelMA-Cad/gelatin hydrogel with time-dependent mechanics that maintains print fidelity while providing a soft, cell-permissive matrix. GelMA-Cad provides a covalently photocrosslinked, bioactive network containing an N-cadherin-mimetic peptide, while uncrosslinked gelatin serves as a transient matrix-modifying component that diffuses from the hydrogel after fabrication, producing further softening without bulk degradation of the GelMA-Cad network. We characterized hydrogel chemistry with NMR, quantified time-dependent changes in stiffness, visualized pore morphology with cryo-SEM, and evaluated the platform in retinal and pulmonary constructs. The 4D hydrogel supports 3D-patterned accuracy, cell viability, inner blood-retinal barrier vasculature, and vascularized lung-alveolar tissue models. Single-cell RNA-sequencing of the pulmonary vascular-alveolar model demonstrated compartment-specific transcriptional responses, including enrichment of lung capillary-associated endothelial features and AT1-like epithelial states. Overall, this platform decouples DMD print fidelity from post-print matrix mechanics for vascularized soft tissue bioprinting and tissue modeling.

title: Timing Determines Fate: Temporal Dynamics of Jasmonate Signaling Distinguish Adaptive from Maladaptive Salt Stress Responses in Rice
abstract: Abstract Plant encounters with saline conditions trigger a phase of osmotic stress, followed by ionic stress as salt accumulates in plant tissue. Jasmonate (JA) signalling plays a vital role in both phases, but its role for adaptation depends on timing. Using wild-type rice ( Oryza sativa L. cv. Kitaake) and a JA-deficient allene oxide cyclase ( aoc ) mutant, we followed whole-plant physiology (growth, biomass, photosynthesis, ion distribution) with expression analysis for genes of jasmonate signalling, ion transporters and redox balance to separate adaptive from maladaptive JA effects. The aoc mutant sustained shoot and root growth more effectively than the wild type, maintaining cell expansion in the shoot and cell proliferation in the root under saline conditions. Likewise, stomatal conductance in the mutant was more persistent under salinity, accompanied by improved shoot K /Na homeostasis and reduced sodium in young leaves. In the wild-type, prolonged saline conditions were linked with induction of OsJAZ13 and OsNHX1 , stomatal closure and chlorophyll degradation. We discuss these findings in the context of a model, where the function of JA signalling does not merely depend on its accumulation, but on its temporal dynamics. Here, OsHAK16 emerges as a marker of early adaptive responses, whereas OsNHX1 and OsJAZ13 characterize later maladaptive stress states, emphasising the potential of modulating JA dynamics to improve salt resilience in rice breeding. Highlight Time-resolved physiology and transcript profiling show that jasmonate signalling promotes salt tolerance in rice when transient but drives ionic damage when sustained.

title: Genetic control of leaf carbon- and water-related traits in grapevine under greenhouse and field conditions
abstract: Abstract Understanding the genetic architecture of ecophysiological traits related to carbon gain and water loss is crucial to develop cultivars tolerant to abiotic stresses and that maintain productivity in the context of climate change. This can be achieved both through experiments in the greenhouse on potted plants under controlled conditions and in the field. However, the stability of genetic determinism of ecophysiological traits across environmental conditions has rarely been evaluated. We studied a grapevine diversity panel grown both in a greenhouse and in the field, to investigate the impact of growing conditions on leaf ecophysiological traits related to leaf morphology, fluorescence, gas exchange and water use efficiency. The correlation structure between traits was conserved within each environment even though, for most traits, cultivars ranking was not conserved between both environments. However, a set of cultivars, sharing the same functioning pattern in terms of gas exchange and fluorescence in both environments, was identified. Single-and multi-environment Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS), based on a dense genotyping matrix, were used to dissect the genetic architecture of leaf traits. The Quantitative Trait Loci (QTLs) identified through single-environment analyses differed substantially from those detected using multi-environment ones. Multi-environment approaches highlighted shared QTLs across environments for gas exchange and fluorescence traits. Candidate genes associated with carbon- and water-related functions were further identified in these genomic regions. Despite the weak correlation between greenhouse and field trait values, combining both environments enabled the identification of robust genetic regions associated with ecophysiological traits of interest.
