title: Evolutionary signatures of self-incompatibility genes in grasses: high diversity, trans-generic polymorphism and co-evolution
abstract: Abstract In many flowering plants, self-incompatibility (SI) is a genetically controlled recognition system that prevents self-fertilization, thereby promoting outcrossing and maintaining genetic diversity within populations. The gametophytic SI system in grasses (Poaceae) is governed by two multiallelic loci, S and Z , each locus comprising of three genes governing the initial recognition between pollen and stigma. Identifying these genes establishes the molecular basis of SI in grasses, but how its unique two-locus architecture has shaped the evolution of the underlying loci and recognition genes remains largely unexplored. Here, we report targeted sequence capture of SI genes in 362 genotypes across nine forage grass species, revealing extensive allelic richness and sequence diversity. The SI genes exhibited elevated nucleotide diversity (π) (0.134 < π < 0.403) and great amino acid sequence divergence, ranging between 48.2-58.0% for the female determinants (sS and sZ) and 66.5-83.4% for the male determinants (SI-DUF247). The SI-DUF247 proteins also displayed trans-generic polymorphism, indicating that alleles predate speciation. Phylogenetic analysis of SI determinants showed congruence at both S - and Z -locus, consistent with co-evolution of recognition partners. Our results demonstrate that the unique two-locus SI system in grasses shares evolutionary characteristics with other SI systems, suggesting that their reproductive function is shaping their evolution. These findings also indicate that the grass SI loci are under long-term balancing selection to maintain recognition specificity while creating sufficient allelic diversity. Our study provides comprehensive sequence resources for SI genes and new insights into the evolution of the unique two-locus SI system of grasses.

title: Cross-scale Imaging of Live Botanical Specimens using Fourier Ptychographic Microscopy
abstract: Abstract Light microscopic imaging of botanical specimens is typically performed using diffraction-limited methods which can image either a small field of view (FOV) with a shallow depth of field (DOF) at high resolution, or a large FOV and large DOF at low resolution. As such, many of the important small features, such as cells in the root cap of Arabidopsis , chloroplasts in algae and leaf guard cells, cannot be resolved in high numbers for meaningful statistical interpretation of results. Fourier ptychographic microscopy (FPM) is an accessible low-cost solution for large format bioimaging which makes use of multiangle illumination and iterative phase retrieval to recover high-resolution estimates of sample phase and amplitude. To date much FPM research has focused on optimising hardware and image reconstruction techniques with biological and biomedical applications limited primarily to mammalian cell cultures and histological tissue sections. We have, for the first time, applied FPM for label-free imaging of these large, living botanical specimens to investigate cellular and sub-cellular structures over multiple length scales simultaneously, with the aim of resolving structures that cannot be seen with diffraction-limited methods over a large field of view. With our FPM system we demonstrate imaging of living samples mounted in water with a half-pitch resolution of 615 nm over a 3.6 mm diagonal FOV, producing a measured 9-fold improvement in resolution compared to conventional brightfield imaging. This allows for individual root cap cells of Arabidopsis thaliana to be resolved within the context of larger root structures, individual chloroplasts identified in large section of Spirogyra varians, and high-resolution colour imaging of Tradescantia zebrina stomata and chloroplasts across large leaf sections.

title: Genetic Mapping Reveals a Major Locus for Boron Exclusion in Wild Vitis
abstract: Abstract Boron toxicity constrains grapevine ( Vitis ) production in irrigated arid and semi-arid regions, yet most available rootstocks are sensitive to excessive boron. Although underutilized Vitis species may harbor sources of adaptation, the genetic basis of natural variation in boron exclusion remains poorly understood, limiting the development of boron-tolerant rootstocks. We screened 267 wild Vitis accessions representing 16 species for their ability to limit leaf boron accumulation under excess boron conditions. Leaf boron concentration varied 190-fold among accessions and was highly heritable (entry-mean H² = 0.71). Its correlation with stomatal conductance was modest (r = 0.34), indicating that transpiration rate explained only a small proportion of the variation in leaf boron accumulation. Leaf boron was correlated with leaf chloride (r = 0.36), but their largely non-overlapping association profiles supported distinct genetic control. Genome-wide association analysis identified a suggestive association on chromosome 11. Independent quantitative trait locus mapping in a full-sib F 1 population (n = 158) derived from Longii-9018 ( V. acerifolia ) × GRN3 (commercial rootstock) identified qBEx11.1 in the same syntenic region on chromosome 11, which explained 19.5% of the phenotypic variance. Positional candidate genes near the association peak included a pectinesterase and a MATE efflux transporter, suggesting roles for cell wall modification and membrane transport. Leaf spectral reflectance was associated with leaf boron concentration in both populations, particularly at visible and red-edge wavelengths, indicating potential for high-throughput phenotyping. Together, these findings identify qBEx11.1 as a priority locus for boron exclusion and support integrated genetic and spectral approaches for breeding boron-tolerant grapevine rootstocks. Plain Language Summary Boron is needed by plants in small amounts, but too much can damage them, especially in dry regions irrigated with boron-rich water. Grapevine rootstocks, the root systems onto which fruiting grape varieties are grafted, may help limit boron uptake. We screened 267 wild grapevines and offspring from two parent vines for their ability to limit boron buildup in leaves. Leaf boron levels differed nearly 190-fold. Genetic analyses of both groups identified the same region of chromosome 11 as important for limiting leaf boron. Transpiration rate explained only a small part of this variation, and boron and chloride buildup appeared to be controlled largely by different genetic factors. Measurements of how leaves reflected light also detected boron-related changes and may allow faster screening. These findings could help breeders develop grapevine rootstocks better suited to boron-affected soils and irrigation water.

title: CropStabDB: a protein stability resource and Engineering Atlas of orthologue-supported substitutions for 30 plant proteomes
abstract: Abstract Protein stability, the capacity to maintain a folded structure and function, matters as much for transporters and regulators as for enzymes, and heat erodes it. Wheat, rice, maize and soybean supply two-thirds of human caloric intake, and warming reduces yields. Rubisco activase variants selected for thermostability increased photosynthesis, biomass and yield under heat. They came from gene shuffling; no method proposes residues at proteome scale. Genome editing has made such changes routine, yet predictors estimate melting temperature, name no residue, and have not been reported for a plant proteome. Here we present CropStabDB: 1,425,716 proteins from 30 plant species scored on six interpretable components, with an Engineering Atlas of 2,097,576 candidate substitutions in 51,440 proteins, 785,622 at Engineering Confidence Score ≥ 0.70. Every candidate is a residue a more stable orthologue carries at that column. Substitution-type scores match the direction of measured folding free energies in 842 of 926 domains (90.9%). On three proteomes from families absent from training, the model reaches an area under the curve of 0.919. Applied blind to wheat, the score reproduces the measured thermostability ranking of the Rubisco activase isoforms in all three subgenomes. CropStabDB is freely available without registration at https://cropstab.org .

title: Designing enzymes for new-to-nature chemistry and non-natural substrates with AlphaProtein Novo
abstract: Abstract Creating highly active enzymes for arbitrary reactions is a transformative goal for the molecular sciences 1 . Traditional protein engineering 2,3 is constrained by a reliance on existing natural starting points, which are often challenging to discover. De novo design offers the potential to overcome this by creating enzymes from first principles 4 , but has yet to achieve practically relevant catalytic properties. Here we present AlphaProtein Novo (AP Novo), a machine-learning pipeline that demonstrates, for the first time, that de novo enzyme design can outperform natural sequence mining in addressing challenging chemistry. We used AP Novo to design new-to-nature nitrene transferases to synthesise the pharmacophore piperidine with unprecedented product selectivity, and to create enzymes that degrade the environmental toxin DEHP under conditions that denature natural enzymes. We also obtained state-of-the-art catalytic efficiencies on two well-studied model reactions, and through iterative design and analysis found that key enablers of success were mechanism-inspired metrics based on AlphaFold 3 5 predictions and sequence-ensemble-based scoring of designed backbones. Our results show that de novo design has become a powerful complement to natural enzyme diversity for discovering catalysts for a range of applications.

title: AtaA as a Self-Immobilizing Scaffold for Enzymatically Active Surfaces through Oxidative Tyrosine Coupling
abstract: Abstract Protein nanofibers hold great promise as genetically programmable scaffolds for constructing functional material interfaces. AtaA, a giant trimeric autotransporter adhesin from Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5, forms an elongated architecture from the bacterial cell surface, enabling the cells to adhere directly to a wide variety of abiotic surfaces. However, the potential use of AtaA as a scaffold with additional biological functions remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated the use of AtaA as a self-immobilizing scaffold for constructing enzymatically active surfaces via horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-catalyzed tyrosine coupling. We prepared a recombinant AtaA nanofiber fragment (NhNs-AtaA) and its derivative containing two tyrosine-containing loop structures (YL-NhNs-AtaA). Both recombinant proteins retained their adhesive properties. Treatment with HRP and H₂O₂ generated high-molecular-weight products from both proteins, and dityrosine fluorescence emission indicated the formation of tyrosine-derived covalent cross-links. Y-Loop insertion further increased the consumption of monomeric AtaA and promoted the formation of high-molecular-weight products. The removal of arginine, which was included during purification, further increased the loss of monomeric AtaA in both constructs, indicating that intermolecular protein association influenced productive AtaA cross-linking. NhNs-AtaA and YL-NhNs-AtaA were combined with Y-tagged bacterial alkaline phosphatase (BAP-Y). HRP-mediated coupling generated high-molecular-weight products consistent with the cross-linked AtaA-BAP-Y conjugates and enabled the retention of BAP activity on AtaA-coated surfaces without prior chemical modification. Although Y-Loop insertion enhanced polymerization in solution, it reduced AtaA adhesion and consequently lowered surface-bound phosphatase activity, revealing a trade-off between cross-linking reactivity and native adhesive function. These findings establish AtaA as a self-immobilizing protein nanofiber scaffold for constructing enzymatically active surfaces, and suggest the potential extension of this strategy to other AtaA-based interfaces. title: Genome-wide association mapping of sudden death syndrome resistance in germplasm from the USDA soybean collection
abstract: Abstract Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS), caused by Fusarium virguliforme , can significantly impact soybean yields. To advance the understanding of SDS resistance in diverse plant introductions, we conducted genome-wide association studies (GWAS) on a set of 351 accessions from the USDA National Plant Germplasm System (NPGS) Soybean Germplasm Collection. The analysis revealed seven single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) significantly associated with foliar SDS resistance; three significant QTL (on chromosomes 3, 9 and 11) were detected with Fixed and Random Model Circulating Probability Unification (FarmCPU) and four (on chromosomes 5, 6 and two on chromosome 7) with Bayesian-information and Linkage disequilibrium Iterative Nested Keyway (BLINK). Localized linkage disequilibrium blocks were estimated for these regions. Notably, all of them overlapped with regions where QTL associated with SDS resistance had been previously reported and were within, or close to, sequences annotated as implicated in plant defense mechanisms, such as toxin transporters and transcription factors. The architecture of SDS resistance appears quantitative and polygenic, with most loci explaining only modest phenotypic variance. Six plant introductions in this study—PI 175188, PI 307889A, PI 323559, PI 578307C, PI 445683, and PI 323558— harbor favorable alleles at all seven loci, providing high-value resources for resistance introgression. This study underscores the value of leveraging the USDA Soybean Germplasm Collection for the discovery of resistance loci and provides a foundation for marker-assisted breeding to enhance SDS resistance in elite soybean lines.

title: Mechanochemically-reprogrammed stem cell exosomes reconcile the biogenesis internalization trade-off for pulmonary fibrosis therapy
abstract: Abstract Matrix stiffness serves as a pivotal biophysical cue of extracellular vesicle (EV) function and cellular uptake, yet the mechanical cues that enhance EV function may not simultaneously favour cellular uptake. Through comparative analyses across pulmonary cell populations, we identified macrophages as the predominant EV recipients in our experimental system and as a functionally relevant effector population in pulmonary fibrosis. Herein, we developed a mechanochemical reprogramming strategy to coordinate the immunomodulatory function of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived EVs with their uptake by macrophages. We found that soft-matrix conditioning of MSC-derived EVs enhanced immunomodulatory activity and promoted an anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype. By contrast, increasing matrix stiffness upregulated ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), increased EV membrane cholesterol, and enhanced macrophage uptake. Guided by these complementary mechanical responses, we combined soft-matrix conditioning with ABCA1 modulation to generate mechanochemically programmed MSC-EVs. This strategy preserved the immunomodulatory advantages associated with the soft matrix while enhancing macrophage uptake and increasing EV production. In a murine model of pulmonary fibrosis, mechanochemically reprogrammed EVs produced higher and more persistent EV-associated signals in lung tissue and were preferentially associated with pulmonary macrophages. Treatment promoted anti-inflammatory and reparative macrophage responses and was accompanied by reduced pulmonary inflammation and fibrotic remodelling. Together, these findings establish a mechanochemically reprogrammed strategy that coordinates MSC-EV immunomodulatory function with macrophage uptake while increasing EV production, providing a framework for engineering EV-based therapies for pulmonary fibrosis.

title: The Sorghum Lipid Database (SoLD): population-scale lipidomics linking environmental and genetic variation in the Sorghum Association Panel
abstract: ABSTRACT Sorghum ( Sorghum bicolor ) is a climate-resilient crop whose acclimation to nutrient limitation and low temperature likely involves extensive lipidome reconfiguration. Lipids are key membrane components, carbon and energy stores, and mediators of stress signaling, yet population-scale lipidomics data for sorghum are limited. We present the Sorghum Lipid Database (SoLD), a curated lipidomics resource from the Sorghum Association Panel grown under two field regimes, (i) a nutrient-sufficient with usual planting date environment (control) and (ii) a low input treatment with reduced nitrogen and phosphorus, earlier planting, and no pesticide application (low input). Using high-resolution LC–MS, we quantified 266 lipid species and found the lipidome broadly similar across trials, with four low-input-associated signatures relative to control, (i) depletion of sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol, (ii) triacylglycerol enrichment, (iii) phospholipid redistribution centered on phosphatidylserine, and (iv) a shift in the lysophosphatidylcholine-to-lysophosphatidylethanolamine ratio. Genomic heritability was zero at the median under control against 0.171 under low input, and more of the lipidome could be mapped under low input. GWAS of lipid species, class sums, and class ratios recovered loci that were largely trial-specific, with candidate genes assigned by linkage disequilibrium and prioritized by LD-aware ontology enrichment and reaction mapping. Control-associated loci yielded twenty enriched gene sets, all confined to triacylglycerol traits and led by cutin biosynthesis, whereas low-input-associated loci yielded fifty-one across five lipid classes, centered on nutrient transport and signaling, cold-responsive regulators, and jasmonate and oxylipin genes, and including a chromosome 3 block carrying two LOW PHOSPHATE ROOT homologues. SoLD thus connects sorghum lipid diversity to environmental and genetic variation, and lets users move from lipid class to individual species and associated candidate loci. It is freely accessible at https://nirwan.shinyapps.io/SAP-Lipidomics-Database/ .

title: Rational design of intrinsic transcription terminators with programmable strength
abstract: SUMMARY Intrinsic terminators are widely used in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, yet their strength must be selected empirically from characterized libraries. We therefore developed a framework for designing intrinsic terminators with programmable strength. TK, designed to maximize termination strength, exceeded both B0010, a widely used standard, and the strongest terminator in a 582-member reference library when assayed in parallel. To establish that these gains reflect intrinsic termination rather than cellular context, we developed a cloning-free in vitro transcription assay using fluorescent light-up aptamers; TK again ranked highest. The framework improved the canonical T7 terminator and recovered strength rankings across three other bacterial species. Designs were generated using an interpretable sequence-to-function model trained from primary-sequence descriptors alone. The framework is available as open web tools, TerSP for strength prediction and TerFac for target-driven design. Model interpretation revealed previously unreported determinants, including a preference for compositionally diverse hairpin stems.

title: Design-Evolution Synergy Enables New-to-Nature Enzyme Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Directed evolution and machine-learning-assisted evolution have transformed biocatalysis by enabling rapid optimisation of catalytic performance within compatible protein scaffolds. In parallel, advances in deep-learning-driven de novo protein design have expanded accessible protein architectural space, enabling the generation of functional catalysts for increasingly challenging transformations. We herein report a synergistic design-evolution strategy to encode new-to-nature regio- and enantioselective C–H amination reactions using engineered de novo haemproteins to synthesise chiral piperidines, a privileged pharmacophore in drug discovery. By integrating motif scaffolding, computational re-design, and directed evolution, we demonstrate de novo enzyme design can enable challenging, high-energy-barrier enzyme chemistry with programmable regio- and enantioselectivity, high catalytic efficiency, excellent enzyme stability, and scaffold diversity.

title: Reversing transgene silencing via targeted chromatin editing
abstract: Mammalian cell engineering offers the opportunity to uncover biological principles and develop next-generation biotechnologies. However, epigenetic silencing of transgenes hinders the control of gene expression in mammalian cells. Here, we use chromatin editing of an integrated reporter in CHO-K1 and human induced pluripotent stem cells to study the molecular interactions driving silencing and its reversal. After transient induction of either DNA methylation or H3K9me3, stable silencing was exclusively observed with both marks. Due to the positive feedback between DNA methylation and H3K9me3 and the relative low stability of H3K9me3, our model predicts that removing DNA methylation is sufficient for transgene reactivation. Accordingly, targeted DNA demethylation reactivated the reporter irrespective of whether silencing was achieved by inducing DNA methylation, H3K9me3, or by the endogenous cellular machinery. These results shed light on molecular mechanisms at play during silencing and provide engineering tools for potent and specific transgene reactivation in mammalian cells.

title: Impact of noise on optical redox ratio estimation
abstract: Optical redox ratio (ORR) is a commonly used metric to quantify the metabolic state of biological samples based on autofluorescence of NAD(P)H and FAD. Despite its relevance and popularity, little work has been done to quantify the estimation error of ORR, especially in low-photon count data. Here, we provide an analytical solution to determine ORR variability in the presence of shot noise and dark counts. We then validate this analytical model with simulated and experimental data. This work will enable researchers to quantify the uncertainty in their ORR measurements, aiding in more accurate and efficient experimental design and data analysis.

title: A synthetic gene circuit confers salt tolerance in plants
abstract: Abstract Soil salinity exerts a major constraint on global crop production, while seawater intrusion impacts coastal aquifers and surface waters. Using a blueprint from nature, we designed and implemented genetically encoded circuits that confer high salt tolerance to Arabidopsis and rice plants. Endodermal-like barriers, duplicated to the root epidermis and distally expanded to protect sensitive regions, provide tolerance to salinity levels comparable to seawater. Two additional genetic modules were added to reduce adverse effects of the epidermal barriers on ion uptake (aquaporin module) and to provide osmotic protection (osmolyte module). Arabidopsis and rice containing all three genetic modules can grow with continuous 600 mM NaCl treatment for extended days and reproduce. Transcriptomic analysis suggests that our rational engineering approach primes plants for salt tolerance, even without salt exposure, while detailed ionic analysis uncovers leakage suggesting means for improvement. Our results, duplicating suberin and the Casparian Strip in the epidermis while addressing adverse effects and osmotic stress demonstrate a new approach to enhancing salt tolerance while offering additional insights into plant responses to high salinity. One Sentence Summary A bio-inspired approach engineering epidermal barriers, symplast transporters and osmotic protection produce salt tolerance in Arabidopsis and rice.

title: Associations of age, sex, and bicuspid aortic valve with biaxial mechanical properties and circumferential residual stress in ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm
abstract: Abstract Background Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) is characterized by progressive biomechanical remodeling that is incompletely captured by maximum aortic diameter. The relationships between age, sex, aortic valve phenotype (BAV vs TAV), and aneurysmal mechanics remains incompletely understood. Methods Ascending aortic specimens from 54 patients undergoing elective ATAA repair were evaluated. Biaxial testing quantified Green strain and local stiffness at membrane tensions of 60 and 120 N/m. Opening angle was used to assess circumferential residual stress and stretch. Associations with age were evaluated using Pearson correlations, and differences between sex and valve phenotype were also explored. Multivariable linear regression models including age, sex, and valve phenotype were used to evaluate their adjusted associations with each mechanical outcome. Results Increasing age was associated with increased local stiffness and reduced Green strain and remained the strongest determinant of biaxial mechanical properties after adjustment. Compared with tricuspid aortic valve specimens, BAV specimens exhibited lower Green strain together with lower local stiffness. Females demonstrated greater Green strain in unadjusted analyses; however, after adjustment, sex remained associated only with longitudinal Green strain at 60 N/m. None of the evaluated clinical characteristics consistently explained opening angle or residual stretch. Conclusions Age was the predominant clinical determinant of biaxial mechanical remodeling in ATAA, whereas valve phenotype demonstrated selective associations and sex contributed comparatively little after adjustment. Circumferential residual stress appeared largely independent of these clinical characteristics, suggesting that residual stress and biaxial mechanics capture complementary aspects of aneurysmal remodeling.

title: Passive Cell-Flux Partitioning Enables Single-Cell-Constrained Impedance Sensing From High-Density Microbial Cultures
abstract: Fermentation is a process through which microorganisms are used to transform basic molecules into high value substances in various applications such as biopharma, food production, and biofuel generation. In such processes, monitoring the health of microbial cells is essential, as it is a key factor in the final product yield. Traditional methods of assessing the health of fermenter populations have involved manually extracting samples from the fermenter for benchtop testing, which lacked the accuracy and efficacy of real-time continuous measurements. This has opened the door for inline sensors to be integrated into fermenters for continuous measurement; including microfluidic based Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS). EIS utilizes a range of frequencies to gain insight into the characteristics of microbial populations, such as cell size and membrane capacitance. EIS cytometry, in particular, has emerged as a relevant tool, as it enables single-cell level detection in real-time. However, current EIS cytometry devices cannot be deployed directly within fermenters due to the high cell density conditions. This has limited EIS analysis in fermenters to bulk measurements averaged across a population. Here, we present a microfluidic chip that uses passive cell-flux-partitioning geometry to direct cells from high-density culture through a single-cell-constrained flow path containing integrated impedance-sensing electrodes. The proposed chip combines geometric channel design and embedded electrodes to enable continuous impedance measurements from cell-containing flow while operating at input cell densities on the scale of 10 9 CFU/mL. This work demonstrates a first step toward integrating single-cell-constrained microfluidic handling with impedance sensing for inline monitoring in industrial biomanufacturing.

title: An L-threonine-inducible biosensor derived from the tryptophan-repressed trp promoter of Escherichia coli for high-throughput screening of L-threonine overproducers
abstract: Abstract L-Threonine is an essential amino acid widely used in the feed, food, and pharmaceutical industries, and microbial fermentation is now the dominant route for its production. Further increases in producer titers depend on random mutagenesis coupled with high-throughput screening (HTS), but progress has been limited by the lack of a biosensor with a broad operating range, high sensitivity, and target specificity. Here, we show that L-threonine induces the tryptophan-repressed trp promoter of Escherichia coli , a response that, to our knowledge, has not been described previously. Deletion analysis showed that both the trpO operator and the trpL attenuation element contribute to induction, and that the lowest basal expression occurs only when both elements are present. By optimizing the ribosome-binding site, the promoter –10 region, and TrpR expression, we constructed an L-threonine biosensor on a pACYC backbone. The sensor responded linearly to L-threonine from 0.1 to 30 g/L (R² = 0.9895), with an induction ratio of up to 51.7-fold. Among the 20 proteinogenic amino acids tested, only L-threonine produced a detectable response. The biosensor distinguished strains with different L-threonine production capacities and guided the directed evolution of homoserine kinase (ThrB) at a conserved motif, yielding variants with brighter reporter fluorescence and increased L-threonine production. This work provides a high-performance biosensor based on native E. coli regulatory elements for screening L-threonine overproducers.

title: Electroencephalography for Radiation-Free Orientation Estimation of Directional Deep Brain Stimulation Leads
abstract: Abstract Background Programming segmented deep brain stimulation (DBS) leads requires knowledge of their rotational orientation, but current postoperative workflows rely mainly on radiographic imaging. Objective To develop and evaluate a radiation-free electroencephalography (EEG) framework for directional lead orientation estimation, in a realistic phantom and postoperative human data. Methods A realistic head phantom containing a directional DBS lead was mounted on a rotating tray and stepped through known orientations in 5° increments to evaluate EEG-based orientation estimation. Stimulation artefact topographies were compared with forward-model predictions using Pearson correlation, and a tri-montage approach combined estimates from all three same-ring electrode pairs to improve accuracy. Robustness was tested by adding brain noise and reducing the electrode count. The method was then applied to a patient with bilateral directional DBS leads implanted in the globus pallidus. Robustness in the human data was assessed by reducing the sampling rate and the number of EEG electrodes. Results In the phantom, the best simplified forward model was a tangential BEM dipole positioned midway between the active contacts. The tri-montage reduced the maximal mean orientation error to 0.59° (95% CI: 4.48°). A conservative tray-position analysis yielded a pooled mean error of 2.05° (95% CI: 3.20°). In the human dataset, EEG-derived orientations differed from imaging-based references by about 8° for the right lead and 15° for the left lead, and remained stable after downsampling and montage reduction. Conclusions Phantom validation established the key modelling assumptions, and postoperative human recordings showed that EEG can recover clinically plausible directional lead orientations under realistic conditions.

title: The “osteostat”: a theory of bone mechanosensing and setpoint adaptation based on osteocytes
abstract: Abstract The osteocyte network in bone is believed to play an important role for how bone tissues sense and respond to mechanical stimulation. Yet, bone adaptation to mechanical loads is often conceptualised as a simple response to mechanical stimuli, such as Wolff’s law, which is based on mechanical variables only and takes no account of the cellular basis of mechanosensation. Wolff’s law presumes the existence of a reference mechanical stimulus, the mechanical setpoint, above which bone is added , and under which bone is removed. In this paper, we develop a theory of bone tissue sensing and adaptation based on osteocytes to provide new understanding of the role played by osteocyte signals in mechanical adaptation. In this theory, the mechanical setpoint of Frost’s mechanostat is explicitly embodied as osteocyte properties involved in mechanotransduction. The mechanical setpoint is allowed to adapt due to the replacement of osteocytes during remodelling, making the setpoint space and time dependent. We propose a mathematical model to implement this new theory of bone adapation and present numerical simulations of this model to explore how mechanobiological response curves (effective Wolff’s laws) are modulated by setpoint adaptation during remodelling. By accounting for varying osteocyte populations within bone tissue, we explore bone adaptation under osteocyte disruptions, which is particularly relevant to age-related bone loss. Our model suggests that biological disruptions of remodelling balance cannot always be compensated by mechanical feedback, and that setpoint adaptation during remodelling may have significant observable consequences, such as hysteresis in bone response signatures that resemble lazy zones.

title: Proximal tubule-enhanced kidney organoids with S3-like cell enrichment model physiological responses
abstract: ABSTRACT Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health challenge affecting >840 million people, with rising prevalence driven by common conditions including diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and drug toxicity. The proximal tubule (PT) is central to kidney function yet is highly injury-prone, particularly within the S3 segment which plays key roles in CKD progression. Despite decades of in vitro PT model development, achieving accurate functional and structural segmentation of the PT with distinct PT sub-cell types has remained challenging. Here, we report an enrichment of S3-like cells within PT-enhanced kidney organoids (PT-EKO) that confers segment-specific functionality. This advanced platform facilitated modelling of physiological responses to environmental changes, including glucose levels, fatty acid substrate availability, and fluid sheer stress. Integrating with both static and organ-on-chip culture systems, the translational potential of S3-enriched PT-EKOs was underscored by their amenability to scale-up via cryopreservation of day 13 progenitors with retained differentiation capacity. PT-EKO applications were further broadened as an expandable high-yield source of S3-like PT cells, retaining transporter functionality across multiple passages. Together, these findings represent an advance towards more physiologically relevant, human-specific modelling of PT responses supporting therapeutic approaches for CKD, including drug development, toxicity evaluation and cellular therapy. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Advancing stem cell-based proximal tubule models, here we identify proximal tubule-enhanced kidney organoids (PT-EKO) as an enriched source of the most injury-prone cell type in the nephron; S3 proximal tubule cells. This advanced platform provides physiologically-relevant modelling of tubular responses to changes in the metabolic and biophysical environment, as well as a scalable source of high-quality PT cells, paving the way for more accurate modelling, screening, and cellular therapy applications.

title: Deep learning models detect neuromuscular disease and quantify functional impairment from video-derived biomechanics data
abstract: Measurements of human movement are critical for evaluating patients with neuromuscular diseases. However, current clinical tools are limited in sensitivity and can fail to detect the full spectrum of movement changes patients may exhibit. These limitations can obscure early signs of decline, delaying interventions that could preserve function and independence. OpenCap-a smartphone application that performs video-based markerless motion capture-can help address this gap by enabling scalable, out-of-lab measurements of human movement. Here, we present a method for both detecting disease and quantifying the severity of impaired movement from smartphone videos of a patient's motion. We used OpenCap to measure kinematics from 337 individuals with diagnoses spanning 12 rare, genetically-defined neuromuscular diseases and 78 age-matched healthy controls. Our dataset is the largest existing publicly available resource of body segment kinematics for this class of diseases. These data were collected in neuromuscular clinics during regular clinic visits as well as at conferences and community events across the United States. We trained deep learning models on these kinematic time series to differentiate between participants with neuromuscular disease and controls (AUROC = 0.97 [0.93-1.00]). We also developed a movement impairment severity score that correlates with both participants' ratings of their own functional abilities (ρ= -0.81, p<0.001) and existing clinical tests of movement capabilities such as run speed (ρ= -0.83, p<0.001). Our methods for detecting disease and deriving quantitative biomarkers of movement impairment from smartphone videos have the potential to complement clinical assessments, inform screening protocols, and improve clinical trial endpoints.

title: Sensitivity of Pulmonary 4D Flow MRI Biomarkers to Controlled Spatial and Temporal Degradation in a CFD Benchmark
abstract: Abstract Purpose To quantify, in a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) benchmark, how spatial degradation, temporal acquisition and noise change the error of plane-based pulmonary-artery flow endpoints. Methods Twenty-two historical, non-converged CFD simulations (11 geometry families) were voxelised at 2 mm with 80 frames per cycle. Simulations with numerical divergence were excluded, leaving 13 (7 families). Fields were degraded to 4 and 8mm and with noise, plane waveforms were sampled at 20 phases with one-interval averaging, and errors were computed against the noise-free reference waveform on 66 geometric planes. Family-mean paired differences are reported with t-based 95% confidence intervals under an analysis plan fixed in advance. Results Spatial degradation from 2 to 4mm increased full-waveform nRMSE by 0.0032 [0.0021, 0.0043], in 7 of 7 families; cycle-mean flow bias accounted for 23% of the squared error, against 60% at 8 mm. With SNR scaled to voxel volume, the increase was not resolved (0.0002 [−0.0012, 0.0015]). Twenty-phase acquisition increased PI error (0.0223 [0.0214, 0.0233]) and diastolic-trough timing error (0.63 [0.52, 0.74] frames) more than spatial degradation, and its point estimates for these endpoints were larger with every recovery method; the nRMSE ordering and peak timing depended on the recovery method. The implementation of the downsampling operator mattered: an alternative, corner-aligned implementation of the same 4mm degradation gave a larger spatial effect (nRMSE difference 0.0010 [0.0002, 0.0017]). Conclusion In this benchmark, a 2 to 4mm degradation produced a small, consistent, mostly shape-related nRMSE increase that depended on the noise model, whereas 20-phase acquisition changed PI error and trough timing more. The results describe benchmark behaviour, not clinical acquisition requirements.

title: Synergistic Combination of Bioengineered MicroRNA and Chemotherapy Across High-Risk Neuroblastoma Subtypes
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite intensive treatment, high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNB) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children. Current treatment paradigms include multimodal systemic treatments and multi-agent chemotherapy, which is limited by substantial acute and long-term toxicities. Platinum-based chemotherapy is a cornerstone of this treatment but is fraught with side effects and stands to benefit from dose reduction strategies. MicroRNA (miR)-based therapeutics represent an attractive strategy to simultaneously moderate multiple oncogenic pathways, providing a potential avenue to enhance the efficacy of current treatment regimens. However, the development of miR therapeutics has largely relied on chemically synthesized ones, which are limited by issues of inconsistency and poor in vivo stability. Biologically produced, tRNA/pre-miR containing bioengineered miRs (bioRNAs) address these limitations. We investigated the therapeutic potential of bioRNA encoding miR-124 and miR-34a across molecularly distinct HRNB models and evaluated their ability to enhance cisplatin efficacy. Both bioRNAs significantly suppressed neuroblastoma cell viability in vitro, with proteomic analyses demonstrating preferential induction of neuronal differentiation by miR-124 and apoptotic signaling by miR-34a. Combining bioRNA with cisplatin produced robust synergy across multiple HRNB lines, enhancing apoptosis while simultaneously promoting differentiation-associated phenotypes. In vivo, both bioRNAs suppressed tumor growth as monotherapies, while combination with low-dose cisplatin produced the strongest responses across multiple xenograft models with different HRNB subtypes. Notably, low-dose cisplatin combined with bioRNA therapy frequently achieved tumor control comparable to, or greater than, that observed with high-dose cisplatin monotherapy while maintaining favorable tolerability. These findings establish bioRNAs as potent cisplatin sensitizers and support bioRNA-based combination therapy as a strategy for improving HRNB treatment while reducing chemotherapy-associated toxicity in children.

title: Phase-noise tolerant fully-coherent optical coherence tomography angiography for high-contrast 3D microvasculature mapping
abstract: Abstract Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) has been extensively explored for the detection of pathological retinal changes arising in various ophthalmological diseases. Due to phase instability of conventional systems, most OCTA signal processing methods to date have relied on intensity-based averaging, despite the resulting lower contrast and dynamic range compared to coherent averaging approaches. In this work, we (1) present a novel computation pipeline that enables fully-coherent processing in any phase-stable or phase-unstable system, and (2) demonstrate the first angiography metric with integrated signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) correction and coherent spatiotemporal ensemble averaging effective in any OCT system. Our method does not rely on 2D en face projections or binarization to produce high-contrast en face views and it significantly enhances the contrast-to-noise ratio of computed OCTA volumes, particularly in regions with reduced SNR levels. Our OCTA volumes also have high cross-sectional quality, enabling the use of single-depth en face views and the localization of capillary paths in the axial dimension. We can now identify capillaries below the retinal pigment epithelium, near the lamina cribrosa in the optic cup, which was not previously possible due to low SNR. We also conducted an analysis of strategies for bias reduction in OCTA and developed the optimal method utilizing coherent spatiotemporal ensemble averaging. Because our method leverages coherent averaging across all dimensions, it provides flexibility in shaping the averaging kernel to target specific workflows. The value of this additional degree of freedom is illustrated in our vessel tracing investigations, in which the depth resolution was maximized by limiting coherent ensemble averaging to the two lateral dimensions even in presence of strong phase noise, enabling the identification of 3D features such as overlapping capillary paths.

title: BrightEyes-Scope: A Reference Implementation for Image Scanning Microscopy with SPAD Array Detection
abstract: Image scanning microscopy (ISM) is emerging as the natural evolution of confocal laser-scanning microscopy, combining optical sectioning and a two-fold improvement in lateral resolution with high signal-to-noise ratio. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) array detectors enable an effective implementation of ISM by recording a micro-image at each scan position with single-photon sensitivity, negligible read-out noise, and without the fixed frame-readout constraints of conventional cameras. Nevertheless, SPAD array-based ISM remains largely confined to laboratories with expertise in microscope development. Here, we present BrightEyes-Scope, a reference implementation of a SPAD array-based ISM system. We provide step-by-step guidelines for optical design, system construction, alignment, calibration, data acquisition, and image reconstruction. Presented as a complete ISM microscope, BrightEyes-Scope also serves as a reference for upgrading existing laser-scanning microscopes. We anticipate that it will accelerate the adoption of ISM for quantitative super-resolution imaging.

title: Avidity-controlled biotherapeutic delivery systems for the treatment of ischemia-reperfusion acute kidney injury
abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are key mediators of immune resolution and tissue repair following acute kidney injury (AKI), yet strategies to selectively enrich Tregs within the renal microenvironment remain limited. Interleukin-2 (IL-2) is essential for Treg survival and function, but systemic IL-2 delivery is constrained by a short half-life, narrow therapeutic window, and risk of off-target activation of cytotoxic T cells. Effective Treg-based immunomodulation may therefore require both localized cytokine signaling and targeted recruitment of precursor immune populations. Here, we present a sequential, biomaterial-based immunomodulatory strategy that integrates immune cell recruitment with sustained cytokine delivery. An injectable granular hydrogel physically encapsulating the chemokine CCL21 was used to initially recruit CD4+ T cells to the injured kidney. Subsequently, supramolecular guest-host interactions were leveraged to deliver IL-2 modified with the hydrophobic "guest" moiety adamantane, enabling prolonged local cytokine release over 28 days. In healthy mice, we observed early CD4+ T cell recruitment, followed by a pronounced increase in Treg frequency, consistent with immune reprogramming driven by our sequential delivery system. In a murine model of bilateral ischemia-reperfusion (BiAKI), this injectable biomaterial induced a local increase in the proportion of FOXP3-expressing Tregs and a concomitant decrease in the levels of AKI markers. This two-step immunomodulatory approach minimizes acute immune activation while promoting long-term enrichment of Tregs within the renal microenvironment. Together, these findings demonstrate that granular hydrogels with supramolecular host capability can orchestrate immune recruitment and differentiation in a spatiotemporally controlled manner, providing a versatile immunomodulatory platform for applicability in kidney disease.

title: Venous Angiogenesis and Dermal Fibroblast Augmentation of Decellularized Dermis: Towards Transplantable Dermal Substitutes
abstract: Abstract The ability to generate vascularized tissue constructs supplied by surgically accessible vessels remains a major limitation in reconstructive tissue engineering. Previous work demonstrated that positioning porous biomaterials around a vein can induce extensive vascular sprouting and generate a vascularized tissue volume without creation of an arteriovenous loop. However, this phenomenon has principally been demonstrated using rigid calcium-phosphate scaffolds, limiting its direct relevance to soft-tissue reconstruction. Here, we investigated whether a flexible decellularized dermal matrix could similarly be vascularized around a single unmodified vein and whether autologous dermal fibroblasts could further enhance this response. Decellularized rat dermis, with or without autologous dermal fibroblast seeding, was implanted either subcutaneously in the dorsal region or around the femoral vein for 8 weeks. Following Microfil perfusion, three-dimensional micro-CT demonstrated an extensive branching vascular network within perivenous constructs. Vessel volume relative to tissue volume was 0.206 ± 0.055% in subcutaneous constructs without fibroblasts (n = 11) and 0.598 ± 0.190% with fibroblasts (n = 9), compared with 6.131 ± 1.413% in perivenous constructs without fibroblasts (n = 10) and 7.329 ± 1.215% with fibroblasts (n = 10). Histology and immunohistochemistry similarly showed greater cellular repopulation and substantially higher CD31-and α-SMA-positive vessel densities following perivenous implantation. Integrated two-way ANOVA of the same 8-week data confirmed a dominant effect of implantation site across the vascular outcomes, while fibroblast seeding significantly affected vascular volume, dermal remodeling, and nuclear density. The effect of fibroblast seeding on vascular volume was site dependent, with a significant implantation site × fibroblast interaction. At 8 weeks, the vascularized dermal construct was completely dissected free from the surrounding tissues while maintaining its connection to the femoral vein. A small superficial incision into the isolated dermis produced visible bleeding, supporting an acute functional connection of the intradermal vascular network to the host circulation while the femoral venous connection was preserved. After flap elevation, perivenous constructs retained substantially greater vascular volume and showed more complete surface healing and organized skin architecture than subcutaneous constructs. Fibroblast seeding accelerated wound closure, while its effect on post-elevation vascular volume depended on implantation site: VV/TV decreased in subcutaneous constructs but increased in perivenous constructs. These findings show that single-vein vascularization can extend from rigid calcium-phosphate biomaterials to a compliant biological extracellular-matrix scaffold and may provide a simplified axial vascularization strategy without arterialization or incorporation of an arterial vessel.

title: Angiotensin (1-7)-based Proteomimetic Polymers as Topicals for the Remediation and Repair of the Cornea following Injury
abstract: The cornea is the outermost layer of the eye, most vulnerable to injury including from chemical exposure, either environmental, industrial or chemical weapons. For example, exposure of the eye to sulfur mustard (SM) can cause mustard gas keratopathy, resulting in devastating consequences for vision. Available treatments for corneal mustard keratopathy are either ineffective, or if used for a prolonged time, have deleterious side effects. Here, we aimed to harness the anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic peptide angiotensin-(1-7), known as Ang-(1-7), that is derived from the renin-angiotensin system (RAS). We designed and developed a protein-like polymer (PLP) displaying a brush of norleucine modified Ang (1-7) peptides (NLE Ang (1-7) PLP), which is a more potent derivative of Ang-(1-7), for administration as an eye drop. In a mouse model of nitrogen mustard (NM)-induced corneal injury, topical treatment and intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of NLE Ang (1-7) PLP persistently minimized: (i) corneal haze; (ii) edema; (iii), expression of pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic genes; and (iv) neovascularization and conjunctivalization as evidenced after a prolonged treatment and recovery period. Collectively, our observations have demonstrated the efficacy of this novel polymer proteomimetic based eye drop treatment in reducing chemical agent-induced corneal injury as well as indicating its potential application in other ocular surface diseases associated with inflammation and angiogenesis.

title: High-throughput microfluidic encapsulation of cells in extracellular matrix microbeads for microtissue engineering
abstract: Abstract Microfluidics-assisted encapsulation of cells in hydrogel microbeads has found diverse applications in tissue engineering, disease modelling, and drug testing. However, upscaled production of submillimeter-sized microbeads, each encapsulating optimally tens to hundreds of living cells, remains a challenge. Excessive viscous stresses or non-homogeneous crosslinking reactions hamper droplet monodispersity, hydrogel integrity, and/or cell viability. Herein, we present a device consisting of (i) tens of parallel step-emulsifiers arranged radially around the hydrogel inlet and (ii) an in-flow UV crosslinking system capable of continuous generation and crosslinking of up to around 45000 microbeads/min, each encapsulating N ∼50 cells, at cell viability exceeding 80%. We use gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) as the biomaterial of choice and establish a unique “sweet spot” in terms of UV wavelength, irradiance, and exposure time—the latter controlled via the net applied flow rate and the length of the UV-exposed microchannel—at which we achieve an optimal balance between long-term microbead stability and cell viability. In particular, we observe a strong correlation between reduced cell viability and poor crosslinking efficiency, the latter attributed to the presence of a spontaneous core-shell structure. We further study the impact of added methacrylated hyaluronic acid (HAMA) and extracellular matrix (ECM) on cell proliferation and microtissue formation in the case of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells for future application in drug testing. The upscaled production of the encapsulated microtissues demonstrated here provides new perspectives for both drug testing and cell therapies where the precision in microenvironment formulation as well as production throughput remain of primary importance.

title: Rewiring systemic nodulation control to engineer heat-tolerant nitrogen fixation in Medicago truncatula and chickpea
abstract: Abstract Root nodule symbiosis allows legumes to meet their nitrogen requirements. However, the causes of symbiosis failure at high temperatures remain unknown. We demonstrated that elevated temperatures affect both the host and the microbial partner in Medicago truncatula and chickpea. Rhizobial viability and nod gene expression persisted under heat stress, but plant transcriptome analysis revealed a strong downregulation of the nodule organogenesis machinery. Nodule organogenesis was restored by constitutive overexpression of NIN-LBD16-NFYA1-NFYB16 , miR2111, and CLE5 knockdown but failed to restore nitrogen fixation. In contrast, the genetic manipulation of the competence pathway involving CEP peptides significantly improved both nodulation and nitrogen fixation. Constitutive loss of the autoregulation of nodulation (AON) pathway in the SUNN alleles also rescued root nodulation and nitrogen fixation. Therefore, heat stress perturbs the balance between AON and the competence pathway, and genetic manipulation of these pathways is a promising approach to engineer thermotolerant nitrogen fixation in crop legumes.

title: Distinct infection and colonization strategies in cowpea leaves by three Colletotrichum species recently reported in Nigeria
abstract: Abstract Cowpea, a crop of great importance in several regions in West Africa, faces many biotic and abiotic challenges. Several species of the genus Colletotrichum cause cowpea anthracnose disease (CAD), a major constraint to cowpea production severely affecting foliage and yield. Three Colletotrichum species— C. cliviicola, C. truncatum , and C. chrysophilum recently reported as causal agents of CAD in Nigeria were investigated in their infective processes and pathogenicity on cowpea leaves using histopathological and microscopic examination of stained leaf tissues. Inoculated leaves were examined at intervals to monitor fungal establishment, colonization, and reproductive development within host tissues. The three species completed the infection cycle, progressing from conidial germination and host penetration to tissue colonization, and sporulation. However, differences in both infective ability and pathogenicity were observed in representative isolates of each species. C. truncatum isolate was the most virulent, had extensive branching hyphae, produced severe tissue necrosis, abundant acervuli, and prominent seta formation. C. cliviicola also had substantial colonization and sporulation ability with dense conidial masses and mature acervuli. In contrast, C. chrysophilum had moderate infectivity with less extensive reproductive structures and tissue degradation. Here we provide the first histopathological report of infection and pathogenic development of these three species recently reported as causal agents of CAD.

title: A Natural qE- and qZ-Deficient Alga Retains Functional Plant-Like and Chlorophycean Violaxanthin De-Epoxidases
abstract: Abstract Photosynthetic organisms protect themselves from excess light through non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), a process that safely dissipates excess light energy as heat. Current understanding of NPQ is largely drawn from a few model systems, leaving it unclear how universal NPQ mechanisms are across the green lineage. We characterize the slow, sustained NPQ of the green alga, Auxenochlorella protothecoides x symbiontica (UTEX 250-A). The Auxenochlorella genome lacks Light-Harvesting Complex Stress Related (LHCSR), one of the two proteins required for the fast energy-dependent quenching (qE) component of NPQ. Mutants lacking the Photosystem II Subunit S (PSBS)-like gene ( psbsl1 ) in Auxenochlorella had no effect on NPQ, indicating this alga lacks canonical qE. We identified two candidate enzymes associated with zeaxanthin-dependent quenching (qZ), which has slower kinetics: a plant-type Violaxanthin De-Epoxidase (VDE) and an algal-type Chlorophycean Violaxanthin De-Epoxidase (CVDE). High light did not trigger the expected conversion of violaxanthin to zeaxanthin, a pigment change that is a hallmark of qZ. Mutants lacking VDE ( vde1 ), CVDE ( cvde1 ), or both enzymes ( vde1 cvde1 ) still displayed slow, reversible NPQ. However, when the Auxenochlorella VDE1 and CVDE1 were expressed in a VDE-deficient mutant of Nicotiana benthamiana, both enzymes restored zeaxanthin production and NPQ, confirming they are catalytically functional de-epoxidases. Together, these results reveal an alga that retains two functional, evolutionarily distinct xanthophyll-cycle enzymes yet does not rely on typical xanthophyll pigment dynamics for photoprotection. This points to a biological function that is decoupled from de-epoxidase activity, highlighting unexplored diversity in green algal photoprotection.

title: Jasmonate-induced expansion of the MYC2 cistrome occurs within a preconfigured chromatin landscape
abstract: ABSTRACT The transcription factor (TF) MYC2 is a central regulator of jasmonate (JA) signaling, yet its genome-wide occupancy has primarily been characterized using transgenic lines expressing tagged MYC2 proteins, leaving the dynamics of the native MYC2 cistrome unresolved. Here, using a MYC2-specific antibody, we define the wildtype MYC2 cistrome in Arabidopsis thaliana under basal and JA-induced conditions. Native MYC2 showed minimal genome-wide occupancy under control conditions but underwent a pronounced expansion following JA treatment, resulting in more than 3,000 binding sites enriched at core components of the JA signaling network. Cistrome expansion coincided with increased MYC2 protein abundance, while elevated basal MYC2 levels in a transgenic line were associated with extensive MYC2 occupancy even in the absence of JA, supporting a dosage-dependent relationship between MYC2 abundance and genome-wide binding. Despite this extensive cistrome expansion and transcriptional reprogramming, ATAC-seq revealed remarkably limited remodeling of chromatin accessibility following JA treatment. MYC2 recruitment occurred predominantly within pre-existing accessible chromatin regions that remained largely intact in myc2 myc3 myc4 mutants. Together, our findings reveal that JA-dependent expansion of the native MYC2 cistrome occurs within a largely pre-established accessome and identify MYC2 dosage as an important determinant of the extent of genome-wide occupancy.

title: Divergence in wilt tolerance across the range of Mimulus guttatus in the absence of stomatal regulation
abstract: Whether phenotypes and environments predict performance under stress is central to ecology and evolution and can reveal species' vulnerability to global change. We sampled Mimulus guttatus range-wide to test whether reproductive, morphological, and physiological traits predict drought responses. Surprisingly, we find that stomatal response, a key mediator of water balance, did not change as drought intensified. Climate, however, predicted survival after turgor loss: plants from regions with large daily relative to seasonal temperature ranges survived wilting longer. Stress responses also depended on life history: where summers are dry, perennials withstood lower water potentials, whereas annuals increased leaf cooling as they wilted. Known trait associations were not fixed: although many baseline traits tracked climate, none predicted drought responses. Drought performance therefore cannot be inferred from traits measured under well-watered conditions. Lacking stomatal regulation, riparian drought escapers like M. guttatus may be vulnerable if shorter growing seasons bring drought before reproduction.

title: Cytokinin Mediates Photosynthesis and Senescence Action Through CHLOROPLAST IMPORT APPARATUS 2 (CIA2) and CIA2-like (CIL)
abstract: Abstract Progression of leaf senescence is regulated by internal factors like the plant hormone cytokinin (CK) that acts to delay senescence and retain photosynthesis by maintaining chloroplast-functionality. While initial CK-signaling components controlling senescence have been described, downstream targets regulating physiological performance have remained less characterized. Here we present the CHLOROPLAST IMPORT APARATUS 2 (CIA2) and CIA2-like (CIL) transcription factors (TFs) as mediators of CK senescence activity, enabling chloroplast-function. Utilizing loss-of-function mutants, we show CIA2 and CIL negatively regulate senescence progression and alter physiological performance in Arabidopsis thaliana . Integrated transcriptomic-metabolomic analysis shows that CIA2 and CIL action is distinct from other known chloroplast-related TFs (like GLKs/GATAs) and can boost antioxidant response over senescence. We find that CIA2 and CIL are essential in relaying CK activity during chloroplast biogenesis, photosynthesis, rubisco function, and metabolite accumulation. In turn, ARR10/12 CK signaling components were needed for CK induction of CIA2 and CIL themselves - a cascade that induced chloroplast- and photosynthesis-associated nuclear genes, to boost chloroplast-function and metabolism. We also show that CK acts to repress senescence through accumulation of the polyamine, spermidine, in a CIA2/CIL dependent manner. This work presents a CIA2/CIL-cascade as a new anterograde signal for CK antisenescence effects, indicating a mechanism through which CK prolongs leaf function. This fundamental understanding of CK action has implications towards engineering plants with elevated photosynthesis performance and delayed senescence.

title: Heterologous engineering of receptors using OrthoRep (HERO) for directed evolution of GPCRs in yeast
abstract: ABSTRACT Engineering G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) for biosensing applications remains challenging due to structural and functional constraints when such proteins are expressed in a heterologous host. OrthoRep offers the continuous accumulation and selection of signal-enhancing mutations in yeast, yet it has not been applied to GPCR evolution. We apply OrthoRep-driven mutagenesis to evolve opioid GPCRs and improve yeast-based biosensors: first, we express the human μ-opioid receptor (OPRM1) on the OrthoRep p1 plasmid and couple ligand activation to growth. Serial cell passaging of the biosensor generated functionally diverse mutants. However, mutations that decouple receptor activation from selection arose over longer passaging campaigns, halting evolution. We resolve this issue using a site-specific recombinase that re-introduces evolved variants onto the p1 landing pad of an unmutated biosensor, allowing continued selection. This led to an ∼18-fold improvement in sensitivity of a mutant OPRM1 over wt-OPRM1. Additional polymerases were added to the platform, broadening the mutational profiles available. Assembling these components forms the platform we call HERO (Heterologous Engineering of Receptors using OrthoRep). Lastly, we deploy HERO using automation to improve the human δ-opioid receptor’s weak response to an agonist by ∼40-fold. Sensitivity also improved for a structurally dissimilar ligand assayed on the same evolved variants.

title: Rice blast fungus hijacks a rice RALF peptide to initiate infection
abstract: Abstract Plant-derived peptides regulate immunity and host–microbe interactions, but whether fungal pathogens exploit endogenous plant peptides for infection-site selection remains largely unknown. Rapid alkalinization factors (RALFs) are a family of plant peptide hormones that contribute to plant development, reproduction, stress responses, and cell-wall organization. Here, we show that OsRALF7, which is an immune-activating peptide in rice ( Oryza sativa ), is co-opted by the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae as a host-derived cue for appressorium formation, specialized infection structures required for host penetration. While synthetic OsRALF7 peptide induced defense responses in rice suspension cells, the same peptide induced appressorium formation in M. oryzae . OsRALF7-induced appressorium formation was associated with activation of the cAMP/PKA and Pmk1 MAPK pathways and required a hydrophobic surface. M. oryzae inoculated onto Osralf7 knockout plants formed fewer appressoria, and the positioning of these appressoria relative to the boundaries between two adjacent plant epidermal cells was altered. These findings suggest that OsRALF7 provides positional information for infection initiation for M. oryzae . OsRALF7 localized to the plasma membrane and cell wall in rice, and its appressorium-inducing activity required a conserved YISY motif and cysteine residues. This activity was not conserved in Colletotrichum higginsianum , as RALF23 from Arabidopsis thaliana did not induce appressorium formation but instead showed antifungal activity. Together, these findings uncover a dual function of endogenous plant immune-modulating RALF peptides at the plant–pathogen interface, where they can be exploited by M. oryzae as a host-derived cue for infection initiation while also retaining antifungal activity against other fungal species.

title: Fed-batch production of antiviral „OP7 chimera” defective interfering influenza A particles
abstract: Abstract Influenza A virus (IAV) defective interfering particles (DIPs) are regarded as promising broad-spectrum antivirals due to their high efficacy demonstrated in animal trials. Previously, an “OP7 chimera” DIP was generated that showed markedly enhanced antiviral efficacy compared to conventional IAV DIPs. In addition, a high-yield cell culture-based production process for OP7 chimera DIPs was established in perfusion mode. However, due to the technical complexity of this technology, we aimed to combine the advantages of perfusion in terms of yield with that of a simple and less complex batch process. In the present work, we established a fed-batch production process for OP7 chimera DIPs that allows a more straightforward implementation into existing production facilities. Using a feeding regime that was able to overcome the cell density effect, we achieved productive virus infection in stirred tank reactors until a cell density of 10E+6 cells/mL. Furthermore, we obtained a high virus titer of 3.8 log 10 (HAU/100 µL), corresponding to a 3.4-fold increase compared to a reference batch production. Moreover, the produced material demonstrated a significantly increased interfering bioactivity shown by an in vitro potency assay. Interestingly, this efficacy was similarly high as compared to OP7 chimera DIP material previously produced in perfusion mode, despite twofold lower virus titers. Finally, we demonstrate robustness of OP7 chimera DIP seed virus trains, which is significant step towards later pharmaceutical production. Further, corresponding GMP “MDCK-PB2(sus)” cell and “OP7 chimera” virus banks are now available for later biomanufacturing further use. In conclusion, the established fed-batch process offers a valid n additional option for pharmaceutical grade OP7 chimera DIP GMP manufacturing production under GMP conditions required for subsequent clinical testing and for later large-scale manufacturing. Key points - Robustness of OP7 chimera DIP seed virus production confirmed for GMP manufacturing - Scalable fed-batch process enabled high infectious virus titers up to 7E+9 PFU/mL - OP7 chimera DIP material harvested demonstrated very high antiviral activity

title: Argonaute 15 regulates immunity of potato to filamentous pathogens through transposon-derived small RNAs
abstract: Summary Canonical ribonucleases such as Argonaute (AGO) participate in RNA-based gene regulatory processes. They are important for small RNA (sRNA) association and the formation of RNA-induced RNA silencing complexes. Potato ( Solanum tuberosum ) has 14 AGO -encoding genes, including the Solanum -specific StAGO15 , which is activated upon infection by filamentous pathogens. The resistant phenotype conferred by ectopic expression of StAGO1 5 was abolished in plants in which a 21-nt sequence in the PAZ-encoding region of StAGO15 was targeted using an artificial miRNA. We then analyzed the sRNAs associated with StAGO15 in Phytophthora infestans leaf infection. Small RNAs were coimmunoprecipitated, subjected to deep sequencing, and analyzed against the P. infestans and potato genomes, in which cleavage sites were predicted by applying the R package, smartPARE. The most notable difference between pathogen-and water-inoculated StAGO15 samples was observed in the transposon (TE) category. Here, two categories of nonautonomous TE dominated: the miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements ( MITEs ) and short interspersed nuclear elements. The StAGO15 -associated sRNAs bind and target complementary endogenous potato RNAs. One example is siRNA122, which acts on a cleavage site in the resistance gene PGSC0003DMG400015681 ( StRES1 ). siRNA122 is derived from a MITE ; upon deletion of this source sequence, resistance is restored. Our findings provide new insights into the plant immune surveillance network and demonstrate that deleting a 21 nt RNA sequence from a MITE transposon restored a defense response against two important filamentous pathogens. Significance Statement Potato is a major food crop in the world with increasing importance in the developing countries due to its high adaptive capability to variable climate conditions. The potato plant is known to be attacked by many pathogens and insects during its growing season. Here we demonstrate the importance of a small RNA affecting the defense level to the late and early blight diseases which provides new possibilities for crop improvement.

title: An AI-powered cloud biofoundry for autonomous biological research
abstract: Abstract Autonomous experimentation, where an automated system designs, performs, analyzes, and iteratively improves experiments with minimal human intervention represents a transformative scientific research paradigm. However, it remains hampered by the disconnect between computational design and experimental execution. Here we present iCloudBiofoundry, a cloud-accessible, scalable, and self-evolving platform that bridges this divide. A scientific multi-agent system, iBioGenie, plans research workflows by converting natural language research objectives into testable hypotheses and experimentally grounded protocols using literature, databases, and computational tools. A physical AI layer, BiofoundryAI, translates them into executable workflows that run autonomously on distributed robotic biofoundries, and collects the data for iterative design. We demonstrate the end-to-end capabilities of iCloudBiofoundry across three representative case studies spanning enzyme retrieval, protein engineering, and metabolic engineering. By integrating agentic AI with physical AI, iCloudBiofoundry provides a cloud accessible platform that unifies computational design and robotic execution, enabling autonomous biological research. The iCloudBiofoundry platform is available at: https://icloudbiofoundry.illinois.edu

title: NO VEIN is an ancestral immunity protein involved in plant-virus interaction
abstract: Abstract The conservation of immune systems from prokaryotes to eukaryotes can guide discovery of immunity genes across the tree of life. Most studies to date have focused on metazoan systems, while the extent of ancestral immunity conservation in plants remains underexplored. Here we show that NO VEIN (NOV), a plant protein previously characterized for its essential developmental roles in Arabidopsis thaliana , shares domain composition and structural similarity with Tiamat, a bacterial antiphage protein. In light of the antiviral function of the bacterial protein, we asked whether NOV is involved in plant–virus interactions. We found that NOV knockdown in the model plant Nicotiana benthamiana resulted in an impaired transcriptional response to tobacco rattle virus, including reduced induction of defense genes, and observed increased potato virus x accumulation in a secondary infection. We also reveal that NOV, previously considered plant-specific, has homologs in animals - pointing to a shared origin. Together, these findings uncover a deeply conserved protein involved in plant-virus interaction, and demonstrate the power of prokaryote–eukaryote homology to reveal new aspects of plant biology.

title: Lactate:propionate molar ratio and substrate concentrations shape valerate production in secondary lactate fermentations
abstract: Abstract Odd-chain carboxylates such as valerate and heptanoate are ecologically relevant metabolites and promising platform chemicals, yet the factors leading to their formation during secondary lactate fermentations remain poorly understood. Here, a continuous anaerobic bioreactor was operated for 297 days at pH 5.5 to evaluate how lactate:propionate molar ratios shape product spectrum in lactate fermentations. Valerate was the predominant odd-chain product under all conditions, reaching concentrations up to 110 mM, while heptanoate accumulated only at low levels (<10 mM). At low lactate concentrations (110-220 mM), product selectivity strongly depended on the lactate:propionate ratio. When lactate:propionate ratios were around 1.2 mol/mol, odd-chain products were favored, whereas higher ratios (up to 4.8 mol/mol) shifted metabolism toward caproate and butyrate formation. However, this trend was not maintained at higher lactate concentrations (330-440 mM; lactate not fully consumed), where odd-chain selectivities remained high even at lactate:propionate ratios of 4.8 mol/mol. Pathway analysis allowed to infer that under high-lactate conditions, up to 30% of lactate was used for propionate and acetate formation. Microbial community analysis revealed a stable dominance of Caproiciproducens spp. when valerate was the main product. Overall, this work provides mechanistic insights into the ecology of lactate fermentations and offers a framework for steering product selectivity in engineered anaerobic systems. Highlights Valerate was the dominant product in most tested conditions, reaching up to 110 mM. Lactate:propionate ratio and substrate concentrations drive product selectivities. High lactate concentrations were associated with inferred endogenous propionate formation. Caproiciproducens dominance was associated with sustained valerate production.

title: AMP: An Automated Marker Based Motion Capture Processing Pipeline for Kinematic Trajectory Label Scrubbing and Gaps Filling
abstract: Abstract Marker-based optical motion capture remains the gold standard for kinematic analysis across biomechanical research. However, when tracking dynamic movements, severe occlusions often create missing data and noisy signals that require time-consuming manual cleaning. Existing automated methods usually rely on predefined skeleton models or need massive training datasets for machine learning solutions. This study presents the AMP: an automated marker based motion capture processing pipeline. The AMP is a fully analytical approach that uses hierarchical algorithms including 1) rigid-body constraint, 2) Kalman Filter state estimation and 3) kinematic pattern match to label markers and fill data gaps without manual human intervention. First, the algorithm identifies and removes mislabeling markers before any data scrubbing. During the data cleaning process, our hierarchical algorithm uses a translation-based step to track segments even when there are insufficient donor markers to form a full rigid body. To reconstruct missing marker trajectories, the pipeline initially uses Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomial (PCHIP) interpolation for short marker gaps. However, the PCHIP creates massive spatial errors during long occlusions, the system automatically switches to rigid-body tracking for gaps over 40 ms. Results showed the pipeline drastically reduced processing time compared to manual human expert methods by 73.5%. In addition, the AMP kept spatial errors within 10 mm of the manual ground truth. By using this combined hierarchical approach to match marker processing accuracy, the pipeline provides a fast, general-purpose tool that fully automates data cleaning and saves hours of manual effort.
