title: Digital Empowerment of Vocational Geology Education: A Case Study of the "Mineralogy and Petrology" Online Course.
abstract: The digital transformation of vocational education provides opportunities to address persistent challenges in geology teaching. This study uses the national online course "Mineralogy and Petrology" as a case study to examine digitally supported teaching reform in vocational geology education. To address highly abstract course content, relatively passive student learning, and insufficient alignment between course content and industry development, the course team collaborated with industry, enterprises, schools, and research institutions to develop digital teaching resources, including animations, virtual simulations, three-dimensional (3D) models, and micro-videos. The traditional lecture-centered approach was reorganized to integrate digital resources with physical specimens, blended online and offline learning, and a dual-mentor system involving on-campus and off-campus instruction. The curriculum was structured into three progressive modules: Crystallography Fundamentals → Mineral Identification → Rock Identification. A closed-loop teaching cycle of Pre-class Diagnostic Exploration → In-class Skill Consolidation → Post-class Extension and Enhancement was implemented to track students' learning status and support timely adjustment of instructional strategies. A comprehensive evaluation system integrating process, outcome, and value-added assessments was adopted to evaluate students' learning and professional skill development. These components were organized within the "One Body, Two Combinations, Four Connections and Dual Integration" teaching paradigm. Professional values, including the "Three Glories Spirit of Geology" and craftsmanship spirit, were integrated throughout the teaching process. Following implementation, course observations and platform data showed positive trends in student engagement and academic performance, while vocational certification and competition outcomes provided additional indicators of practical skill development. Overall, the findings indicate that the digitally supported teaching model was associated with positive trends in student engagement and academic performance and supported the integration of digital visualization, physical specimens, practical training, professional values, and industry collaboration in vocational geology education.

title: Leveraging machine learning to uncover broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptides from pathogenic fungal genomes: A case study
abstract: The growing crisis of antimicrobial resistance highlights the urgent demand for innovative therapeutic solutions. Although genomic data for thousands of pathogenic fungi are publicly accessible, their potential in drug discovery remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce a machine learning-based approach to mine these fungal genomes for antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), focusing particularly on the critical stage of fungal spore germination. Using the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae —ranked first among the top ten fungal pathogens in molecular plant pathology—as a case study, we developed an integrated computational platform to predict peptides capable of inhibiting spore germination in the wheat scab fungus Fusarium graminearum , a pathogen capable of infecting multiple crop species. From a library of 20 synthesized candidates, phenotypic screening identified two peptides with potent antifungal activity. These peptides disrupt fungal membrane integrity, induce abnormal cellular morphology, and function in a dose-dependent manner. Notably, they also display broad-spectrum efficacy by inhibiting spore germination in multiple filamentous plant pathogens and suppressing the growth of yeast-like human fungal pathogens. In plant models, the peptides provided effective protection against fungal infection. Moreover, they demonstrated unexpected antibacterial activity, inhibiting bacterial pathogens both in vitro and in planta . By integrating artificial intelligence with fungal genomics, this work uncovers a rich and underexplored resource for antimicrobial discovery. Our findings underscore the transformative potential of machine learning in identifying novel therapeutics to counter antimicrobial resistance, with significant implications for global health and food security.

title: OsNOMT Contributes to Rice Blast Resistance and Viral Defense and Is Associated with Altered Jasmonate Homeostasis
abstract: Sakuranetin (SAK), a flavonoid phytoalexin synthesized by naringenin 7-O-methyltransferase (NOMT), contributes to rice immunity. However, the relationship between OsNOMT-dependent SAK accumulation, resistance to fungal and viral pathogens, and jasmonate (JA) homeostasis remains unclear. Here, we combined genetic, metabolite and transcriptomic analyses of OsNOMT-overexpression (OsNOMT-OE) and knockout (osnomt) lines. Loss of OsNOMT abolished SAK accumulation and was associated with increased susceptibility to Magnaporthe oryzae and Southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus, whereas OsNOMT-OE lines accumulated high levels of SAK and exhibited enhanced resistance to both pathogens. Co-expression network analysis identified a susceptibility-associated module containing OsWRKY62, OsFBX148, and a putative ACC oxidase as candidate hub nodes. OsNOMT-OE plants exhibited increased expression of JA-related genes and higher JA levels but lower basal levels of JA-Ile than wild-type ZH11 plants. In osnomt mutants, basal JA-Ile levels were reduced, whereas JA-Ile levels after M. oryzae infection were comparable to those in ZH11 plants, indicating that OsNOMT-dependent SAK accumulation is linked to a reconfiguration of JA homeostasis rather than a uniform increase in all JA metabolites. In addition, short-term exogenous SAK application promoted JA and JA-Ile accumulation. Collectively, these findings associate OsNOMT-mediated SAK biosynthesis with rice resistance to fungal and viral diseases and altered JA homeostasis.

title: Discovery and Optimization of MoEno1-Targeting Antifungal Compounds for Rice Blast Control
venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Developing fungicides with novel modes of action is essential for sustainable rice blast management. Here, we investigated the glycolytic enzyme MoEno1 in Magnaporthe oryzae as a potential antifungal target. Deletion of MoEno1 impaired vegetative growth, melanin production, conidiation, and pathogenicity. Deep-learning-assisted affinity prediction and structure-based virtual screening identified isobavachalcone (IBC) as a MoEno1-binding hit. Structure-guided optimization of IBC yielded 59 derivatives, among which II-24 showed enhanced antifungal activity, stronger MoEno1 binding, and greater inhibition of enolase activity. II-24 treatment was associated with reduced melanin accumulation and acetyl-CoA levels, together with perturbations in energy metabolism. II-24 also showed in planta efficacy, broad-spectrum antifungal activity, low phytotoxicity, low toxicity to zebrafish, predicted low mammalian toxicity, and enhanced activity in combination with tebuconazole. These findings support MoEno1 as a potential antifungal target and II-24 as an early stage lead for rice blast control.

title: Guideline adherence and expert-rated potential safety concerns in AI-generated dietary advice for patients with cirrhosis: a comparative evaluation of large language models
abstract: Background Patients with cirrhosis require complication-specific nutritional counseling. Large language models are increasingly used for health information seeking, but the guideline adherence and potential safety concerns of their dietary advice for cirrhosis remain uncertain. Methods Thirty-six standardized simulated cases represented compensated cirrhosis, cirrhosis with ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy recovery. Each case was submitted once to DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Qwen, and Claude through their official web interfaces, generating 144 English-language recommendations. Three reviewers performed de novo model-blinded assessments using a locked framework. The primary outcome was response-level Guideline Adherence; secondary outcomes included Error Count, Any Major Error, and Harm Flag. Results Mean Guideline Adherence was 7.00 ± 0.00 for ChatGPT, 6.97 ± 0.17 for Claude, 6.94 ± 0.19 for DeepSeek, and 6.44 ± 0.84 for Qwen (Friedman p < 0.001). In hepatic encephalopathy recovery, Qwen scored 5.36 ± 0.54 and was lower than each other model after Holm adjustment (all adjusted p = 0.009). Any Major Error occurred in 0 ChatGPT, 2 Claude, 4 DeepSeek, and 11 Qwen responses; corresponding Harm Flag counts were 0, 1, 2, and 8. Most events occurred during hepatic encephalopathy recovery and involved protein-related recommendations. Conclusion Under standardized English-language structured prompting, all four models generally reproduced core cirrhosis nutrition principles. However, Qwen showed lower adherence and more frequent protein-related errors in hepatic encephalopathy recovery. Expert verification remains necessary before patient-facing or individualized use.

title: Protein–Protein Interface Residue Prediction by Integrating Protein Language Representations and Structural Graph Attention
abstract: Accurate residue-level prediction of protein-protein interaction interfaces is important for elucidating molecular recognition mechanisms and guiding targeted drug design. However, interface residues are relatively sparse and governed by complex spatial dependencies, making their accurate identification challenging. In this study, we developed EvoStruct-GAT, a multimodal graph attention model based on the PDBbind v2020.R1 data set. To reduce information leakage arising from sequence homology, receptor and ligand sequences were clustered independently, and the resulting clusters were used to construct training, validation, and test sets with no overlap in either receptor or ligand clusters. EvoStruct-GAT represents the target protein as a residue-level graph and integrates ESM-2 protein language model representations, DSSP-derived structural descriptors, and distance-aware graph attention, together with a combined strategy for addressing class imbalance. Using a minimum cross-partner heavy-atom distance of less than 5 Å to define interface residues, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.8081, an AUPRC of 0.4475, and an F1 score of 0.4562 on the independent test set. Alternative labels based on 4.0 Å, 4.5 Å, and ΔSASA definitions produced comparable AUROC values, indicating that the residue-ranking capability was reasonably robust across the tested interface definitions. Ablation experiments identified ESM-2 representations as the principal contributor to performance, with DSSP information and inter-residue message passing providing additional value. Under a common evaluation protocol, EvoStruct-GAT outperformed simplified internal baselines and showed complementary performance characteristics in external comparisons with publicly available models. These results demonstrate that EvoStruct-GAT can effectively rank potential interface residues without requiring information about a known binding partner, thereby supporting candidate-site selection, experimental validation, and downstream structural and functional analyses.

title: Machine Learning in Amyloidogenic Polypeptide Research: From Sequence Prediction to Drug Discovery
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) has established a transformative paradigm for investigating amyloidogenic polypeptides. Characterized by their propensity to form ordered, β-sheet-rich fibrillar aggregates, these polypeptides are centrally implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). This review systematically evaluates the application of ML across critical domains of amyloid investigation: sequence-based amyloidogenicity prediction, structural biology, inhibitor design, and amyloid-related clinical objectives. We further summarize the diverse array of ML architectures currently employed in amyloid research, spanning classical algorithms (e.g., support vector machines and random forests) to advanced deep learning frameworks, such as the transformer framework, protein language models (PLMs), etc. Additionally, we spotlight emerging frontiers, namely, the integration of ML with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the use of generative AI for de novo inhibitor design, etc., while addressing persistent bottlenecks in the field, including data standardization, model interpretability, and rigorous experimental validation for in silico predictions. Ultimately, this review serves as a foundational roadmap for emerging researchers and a definitive reference for established investigators operating at the intersection of artificial intelligence and amyloid biology.

title: DynML-Net: a porcine enteric virus identification network based on protein language models and a dynamic heterogeneous multi-branch architecture
abstract: BACKGROUND: Porcine Enteric Viruses (PEVs) pose a serious threat to the global pig industry, leading to substantial economic losses. However, traditional clinical diagnostic methods are limited by high costs, long turnaround times, and difficulties in rapidly addressing challenges such as co-infections with multiple viruses and the emergence of different viral species. To overcome the limitations of existing approaches in recognizing viruses under complex clinical conditions, poor adaptability to variant strains, and the insufficient extraction of key features, this study proposes a deep learning network integrating the ESM-2 protein language model and a multi-branch heterogeneous architecture, named DynML-Net. RESULTS: The model adaptively integrates decision outputs representing local architectural patterns, global dependencies, and long-sequence evolutionary features through a dynamic gating mechanism, and enhances classification performance via a deep mutual learning (DML) strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that DynML-Net achieves accuracies of 94.52% and 89.16% for binary and multiclass classification tasks, respectively, outperforming current mainstream models, while exhibiting robust performance under conditions of sample imbalance, data reduction, and heterologous viral datasets scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrated the efficacy of DynML-Net in PEVs identification and classification tasks, and based on DynML-Net, a Streamlit-based locally deployable system was developed to facilitate a closed-loop workflow from sequence upload to automated identification, providing an accurate and efficient computational solution for the rapid detection of PEVs.

title: Isocaloric substitution of animal-based protein with plant-based protein and academic performance in Spanish adolescents: The EHDLA study
abstract: Background The source of dietary protein has been linked to cognitive outcomes; however, evidence on the association between isocaloric substitution of protein sources and academic performance in adolescents is limited. This study examined whether replacing animal-based protein with plant-based protein was associated with academic performance in adolescents. Methods This secondary analysis used data from the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study (n = 769; 55.5% girls; 12-17 years). Dietary intake was assessed using the 45-item food-frequency questionnaire. Academic performance was evaluated using grade point average and specific subjects (i.e., language, maths, and foreign language). Isocaloric substitution models were applied to estimate the association of replacing animal-based with plant-based protein, adjusting for relevant sociodemographic, lifestyle, and anthropometric factors. Robust linear regression was used. Results Replacing animal- with plant-based protein was consistently associated with higher academic performance across all outcomes (all p < 0.001). Substituting 5% of total energy intake was associated with higher grade point average and subject-specific scores. These associations were primarily driven by replacing protein from red/processed meat and certain fish with plant-based sources. Conclusions Isocaloric substitution of animal-based protein with plant-based protein was associated with better academic performance in adolescents, highlighting the potential importance of protein source in dietary patterns related to educational outcomes. Impact Replacing animal-based protein with plant-based protein is associated with better overall and subject-specific academic performance in adolescents. This is the first study to apply an isocaloric substitution approach to examine the association between protein source (plant vs. animal) and academic performance in adolescents. Dietary patterns with a higher contribution of red and processed meat protein (relative to plant protein) were associated with less favorable academic outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of protein quality within dietary patterns and may inform nutrition-based strategies to support academic achievement during adolescence.

title: Evaluation of FGFR2, VEGFA, and MMP1 gene variants for ovarian cancer susceptibility among South Indian women: a hospital-based case-control study
abstract: Background Ovarian cancer (OC) is a genetically heterogeneous malignancy characterized by marked molecular and histologic heterogeneity. Genetic variation in pathways involved in angiogenesis and extracellular matrix remodeling may contribute to OC susceptibility. The present study evaluated VEGFA rs833061, FGFR2 rs1219648, and MMP1 rs1799750 polymorphisms in a South Indian cohort and investigated their individual and combined associations with OC risk. Methods This hospital-based pilot case-control study included 240 histopathologically confirmed OC cases and 254 cancer-free controls. Genotyping was performed using PCR-RFLP and allele-specific PCR. Associations with OC susceptibility were assessed using logistic regression with adjustment for age and menopausal status, with the codominant model as the primary genetic model and alternative models as secondary analyses. Exploratory clinicopathological and multifactor dimensionality reduction (MDR) analyses were also performed. Results MMP1 rs1799750 was associated with increased OC susceptibility, with the 2G/2G genotype showing higher odds of OC (aOR = 2.10, 95% CI = 1.12-3.94; p = 0.0179). Similarly, VEGFA rs833061 was also associated with increased susceptibility, with T/C and C/C genotypes showing higher odds (aOR = 2.51, 95% CI = 1.55-4.06; p = < 0.001 and aOR = 1.87, 95% CI = 1.04-3.35; p = 0.021, respectively). However, FGFR2 rs1219648 was not associated with overall OC susceptibility but showed exploratory associations with selected clinicopathological characteristics. The two-locus VEGFA-MMP1 MDR model showed the highest testing balanced accuracy among evaluated models (TBA = 0.5853; CVC = 10/10). Conclusion VEGFA and MMP1 variants showed associations with OC susceptibility in this South Indian cohort. Combined-genotype and MDR findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, independent cohorts.

title: High-intensity interval training modulates the SIRT1–P16 pathway, inflammatory markers, and oxidative stress in the liver of D-galactose-treated male rats
abstract: Purpose Aging contributes to progressive hepatic dysfunction, characterized by increased oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and mitochondrial impairment, which collectively exacerbate metabolic decline. This study examined the effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on the SIRT1-P16 axis, oxidative stress, and inflammatory markers in a D-galactose (D-gal )-induced aging model in male Wistar rats. Methods Twenty-eight rats were assigned to four groups: Control (CTL), HIIT, D-gal, and D-gal+HIIT. Aging model was induced via daily subcutaneous injections of D-galactose (150 mg/kg) for eight weeks, while HIIT was performed on a treadmill five times per week over the same period. Gene expression and protein levels were measured by Real-time PCR and Western blot, respectively. Antioxidant and oxidant, and inflammatory markers were determined via colorimetric and ELISA methods. Results Gene expression analysis showed that D-gal significantly downregulated the expression of AMPK, SIRT1, and PGC-1α, whereas HIIT was associated with increased expression of these markers. Western blot analysis confirmed a reduction and elevation in SIRT1 and P16 protein, respectively, in the D-gal group, which were reversed following HIIT. HIIT also ameliorated the increase in the levels of malondialdehyde, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and the decrease in the SOD and GPx activities. Conclusion Concurrent HIIT attenuated D-galactose-induced hepatic molecular and biochemical alterations associated with aging. These effects were accompanied by changes in SIRT1-P16-related markers, improved redox balance, and reduced inflammatory responses, supporting the potential of HIIT as a non-pharmacological strategy for promoting liver health during aging.

title: De novo design of ligand binding proteins using large language models alone
abstract: Abstract Protein design has rapidly advanced with the advent of sequence- and structure-based machine learning models. However, reasoned design, which applies physicochemical principles and rules derived from sequence-structure-function relationships, has not seen the same benefits from generative machine learning models. Here, we test the ability of common large language models (LLMs; e.g. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini) to consider design principles to generate de novo proteins that bind metals and lipophilic small molecules without copying existing sequences. Common LLMs alone are able to 1) generate protein sequences to adopt a desired fold and bind the target ligand and 2) explain the principles that motivate the design choices. Following structure prediction and filtering, we selected a small set of designs (6 to 12 designs per query) for experimental validation, affording metal binders in one round of LLM-based design (25% hit rate) and perfluorooctanoic acid binders in two rounds (25% hit rate in the second round of design). Importantly, the LLMs produce detailed justification to accompany the de novo designed sequences, providing a conceptual framework on which designs can be evaluated. While the successful designs have some deviations from the prompted parameters and LLM-articulated design rationale, these campaigns provide a case study that highlights the utility of LLMs in making protein design more comprehensible and accessible to users without sophisticated design expertise.

title: The Cytosolic Iron–Sulfur Cluster Assembly Targeting Complex Is Hijacked by Magnaporthe Effector AvrPi9 to Suppress Rice Resistance
abstract: The cytosolic iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster assembly (CIA) targeting complex mediates the maturation of cytosolic and nuclear Fe-S proteins and governs core eukaryotic cellular processes. However, whether this complex contributes to plant disease resistance remains unclear. Here, we show that the Magnaporthe oryzae avirulence effector AvrPi9 targets the host CIA targeting complex to suppress rice blast resistance. AvrPi9 physically interacts with and stabilizes OsAE7, a core subunit of the CIA targeting complex. Using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrate that OsAE7 facilitates Fe-S protein maturation, including the Fe-S protein aconitase OsACO1, and negatively regulates blast resistance in cooperation with another CIA targeting complex subunit, OsCIA1, and the carrier protein OsNAR1 in rice. Furthermore, ectopic expression of AvrPi9 enhances the activity of the CIA complex and the maturation of OsACO1. Knockout of OsACO1 elevates ferrous iron levels, triggers a reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, and activates pathogenesis-related gene transcription, thereby strengthening rice resistance to blast. Our findings reveal a critical role of the CIA targeting complex in plant disease resistance and uncover a novel virulence strategy whereby AvrPi9 hijacks the host CIA pathway to dampen basal resistance and promote infection.

title: Cyclo(Val-Pro), a Potential Plant Immunomodulator, Confers Rice Blast Resistance via Circadian-Clock-Modulated Immune Activation and Metabolic Reprogramming
venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, is a devastating disease threatening global rice production, with current control strategies facing resistance and environmental risks. Small bioactive peptides have emerged as promising eco-friendly plant immunomodulators with low resistance risk for sustainable crop disease control. Here, we identified cyclic dipeptide cyclo(Val-Pro) as a potential plant immunomodulator with no direct fungicidal activity, which effectively conferred robust rice resistance to M. oryzae via promoting host intrinsic defense responses. Pre-treatment with cyclo(Val-Pro) activated salicylic acid (SA)- and jasmonic acid (JA)-mediated innate immunity, triggered reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and callose deposition, and modulated core circadian clock genes in rice leaves. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analysis revealed that optimal blast resistance efficacy by cyclo(Val-Pro) pre-treatment at 14:00 was associated with circadian clock regulation and metabolic reprogramming. Specifically, cyclo(Val-Pro) rewired phenylpropanoid and tryptophan metabolism in rice leaves, and tryptamine was validated as a key functional downstream metabolite.

title: Comparative genome assemblies reveal distinct allelic and structural variation at blast resistance loci in rice CT21375‐F4‐4 and Moroberekan
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, remains a major constraint to rice (Oryza sativa L.) production, and durable resistance will require broader use of genetic diversity beyond commonly studied elite cultivars. We present chromosome-scale genome assemblies of two agronomically significant but genetically divergent rice cultivars: CT21375-F4-4 (hereafter, CT21) and Moroberekan. Despite their genetic divergence, both cultivars show consistently strong resistance to blast under multiyear field conditions. We combined field phenotyping with genome-wide protein-to-genome alignment, predicted proteome comparisons, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) annotation, and locus-specific analyses of cloned blast resistance genes to examine resistance-associated genomic variation in these cultivars. The cultivars contained similar numbers and overall subtype compositions of NLR loci, but differed markedly in their correspondence to characterized blast resistance genes. CT21 contained multiple exact or near-exact matches to cloned blast resistance genes and alleles, whereas Moroberekan contained fewer exact matches and was characterized predominantly by high-identity but divergent homologs, suggesting the presence of divergent alleles or resistance architectures that are not well represented by the cloned gene repertoire. Locus-specific analyses further confirmed that high sequence similarity alone does not reliably predict resistance function, and revealed structural variation, including duplication within the Pish NLR cluster in CT21. These results demonstrate that comparable blast resistance phenotypes can occur in cultivars with distinct allelic and structural architectures at known resistance loci. The assemblies and comparative framework developed here provide resources for identifying resistance diversity that may be overlooked by reference gene or marker-based analyses and for prioritizing candidate loci for functional validation and rice improvement.

title: Synthesis of Bioactive Fluorinated 2-Heterocyclic Pyrrolidines via Copper(I)-Catalyzed Asymmetric 1,3-Dipolar Cycloaddition of Azomethine Ylides
abstract: A copper-catalyzed asymmetric 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of α-N-(heteroaryl-methyl)imines with gem-difluoroalkenes is reported. Using a Cu(I)/Segphos complex, this protocol provides diverse chiral fluorinated 2-heterocyclic pyrrolidines in high yields (up to 99%) with excellent stereoselectivity (up to 98% ee, >20:1 dr). This method is compatible with various heteroaryl groups and complex natural products. Notably, these scaffolds exhibit potent antifungal activity against Magnaporthe oryzae, with the lead compound 4a outperforming the commercial fungicide isoprothiolane by 50% in EC50 values.

title: CentroFinder: a multi-feature framework for de novo prediction of fungal regional centromeres
abstract: Abstract Motivation Centromeres are essential chromosomal loci, yet their computational identification remains challenging due to rapid sequence evolution, high repeat content, and the absence of conserved defining motifs. This challenge is particularly pronounced in fungi, where centromere architectures vary widely in size, sequence composition, and chromatin organization, limiting the effectiveness of single-feature or motif-based prediction approaches. Results We present CentroFinder, a fungal-specific computational framework for de novo centromere prediction from long-read sequencing–based genome assemblies. CentroFinder integrates multiple genomic and long-read–derived features into a weighted scoring model to identify loci where centromere-associated signals converge. Benchmarking against experimentally mapped centromeres in Cryptococcus deuterogattii, Magnaporthe oryzae, and Neurospora crassa showed that 27 of 28 predicted intervals overlapped the corresponding experimental domains, yielding 96.4% chromosome-level detection sensitivity. Application to 11 additional fungal genomes produced one contiguous predicted centromeric region per chromosome, supporting the transferability of the workflow for chromosome-level centromere prediction. Availability and implementation CentroFinder is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/RahnamaLab/CentroFinder. The pipeline is designed for high-performance computing environments and leverages features derived from long-read sequencing data.

title: Harnessing Rare Earth Elements in Proteins and Functional Materials for Advanced Optical, Magnetic, and Mechanical Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT Rare earth‐proteins and their functional materials integrate unique physical properties of rare earth ions (RE 3+ ) with structural programmability of proteins, attracting increasing attention in a wide range of applications. Coordination with RE 3+ can enhance the rigidity and stability of certain proteins, even induce secondary structure transitions, and confer distinct physical properties onto functional materials. The programmability of amino acid sequences regulates coordination chemistry between proteins and RE 3+ , enabling the modulation of their optical and magnetic properties. Moreover, RE 3+ incorporation turns protein structures and aggregation state, leading to enhanced mechanical properties and adhesion strength. However, the development of such materials still faces significant challenges due to lack of molecular mechanism analysis and systematic rational design strategies. This review highlights the chemical structural analysis, rational design and synthesis strategies of rare earth‐protein and their functional materials. In addition, their applications in optics, magnetics, and mechanics are summarized. Finally, their current challenges and future perspectives are discussed.

title: Engineering of Redox‐Active Residues Enhances P450 Peroxygenase Performance
abstract: Cytochrome P450 peroxygenases depend on the high-valent iron-oxo intermediate Compound I (Cpd I) to activate C-H bonds. However, the nonproductive oxidative damage caused by Cpd I compromises enzyme stability and limits catalytic efficiency. Here, we report a rational protein engineering strategy to address this bottleneck by constructing additional "hole traps" on the enzyme surface. Guided by structural analysis, we introduced redox-active tyrosine/tryptophan residues at spatially defined positions on the surface of the P450BM3 F87A mutant. The optimal engineered variant M8 (F87A/L215W/H408W) significantly enhances turnover numbers (TONs) across a range of peroxide-driven hydroxylation reactions of aliphatic and aromatic substrates. Steady-state kinetics, reductant supplementation assays, and half-life measurements consistently indicated that the introduced Trp residues play a crucial protective role, improving both catalytic output and enzyme robustness. The crystal structure of M8 revealed that the mutations facilitate an expanded local network of π-π interactions, forming efficient surface hole traps. This strategy was then demonstrated to efficiently improve the catalytic performance of two engineered CYP199A4 peroxygenase variants (F182A and D251Q/T252E). These findings establish the rational construction of auxiliary hole traps as an effective strategy to enhance P450 peroxygenase performance, with potential applicability to other heme and even broad oxidizing enzymes.

title: Infection history and TCR sequence features shape the breadth of TCR cross-reactivity
abstract: The T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire enables recognition of a vast array of pathogens, despite containing far fewer unique TCRs than the diversity of encountered epitopes. This potential contradiction is resolved by TCR cross-reactivity, whereby individual TCRs recognize multiple distinct epitopes. However, the features defining broadly cross-reactive TCRs remain poorly understood. Here we systematically analyze TCRs from mice sequentially infected with influenza viruses containing naturally occurring single amino acid variants of the D b NP 366 epitope. We identify 967 unique paired TCR sequences across 18 infection histories and test 22 representative TCRs against 172 epitope variants, yielding 3,784 TCR-epitope interaction measurements. These TCRs exhibit a continuum of cross-reactivity, with infection history influencing both TCR sequence similarity and reactivity profiles. We find specific TCR sequence features associated with broader cross-reactivity, highlighting the interplay between epitope exposure, TCR diversity, and function, and providing insights into CD8 + T cell adaptability, immune memory, and vaccine design.

title: Development of Novel Antimicrobial Peptides and Their Engineering into Nanoparticles to Improve Performance
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising alternatives to antibiotics, but discovering potent, low-toxicity candidates and improving their delivery remain challenging. In this study, novel AMPs were identified by constructing and screening a synthetic random peptide library using a bacterial surface display system. Rational design generated derivative peptides, among which WP-4 and WP-6 showed high antimicrobial activity, good biocompatibility, rapid bactericidal effects, and low propensity for resistance development. WP-6 also showed good in vivo therapeutic potency in a murine Escherichia coli systemic infection model. Mechanistic studies indicated that WP-4 and WP-6 target bacterial cell membranes, disrupt the proton motive force, and induce excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation. To further improve their activity and in vivo performance, WP-4 and WP-6 were encapsulated within zeolitic imidazolate framework-8, yielding improved antimicrobial activity and proteolytic resistance. These nanoparticles exhibited superior therapeutic efficacy in a Streptococcus suis-induced arthritis model. Our study identified potent AMPs with promising therapeutic potential.

title: Designing a DeepPCD Strategy for Efficient Engineering Nitrilases toward Industrial Bioconversion
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence with protein engineering has created unprecedented opportunities for enzyme discovery and the enhancement of overall catalytic performance. In this study, a novel nitrilase, BhNIT, was identified from Bradyrhizobiumhuanghuaihaiense through a computationally assisted screening strategy. Using BhNIT as the target protein for engineering, we established DeepPCD as an integrated computationally guided workflow that organizes sequence-design, structure-filtering, stability-assessment, evolutionary-compatibility, and molecular dynamics analyses to prioritize experimentally testable mutations. Compared with approaches that require extensive experimental screening of large mutant libraries, the DeepPCD workflow facilitates efficient enzyme engineering modifications. By modifying only seven candidate residues of BhNIT, we obtained a mutant exhibiting a 1.3 × 105-fold improvement in hydrolytic efficiency. In addition, this mutant showed a 20.4°C increase in melting temperature and a broader operational pH range extending toward more alkaline conditions, substantially enhancing its potential for industrial applications. Molecular dynamics simulations and structural analysis revealed that the enhanced performance stems from effective reshaping of the substrate-binding pocket and access channel, along with a strengthened interaction network. Furthermore, preliminary computational application to additional nitrilases suggested the potential transferability of this workflow within the nitrilase family. Overall, this work provides an experimentally validated case study for computationally guided nitrilase engineering and offers a practical workflow for prioritizing mutations that may improve activity and stability, although broader generalization will require further validation across more diverse enzyme systems.

title: Automated Flow Synthesis of Nature-Derived, Engineered, and De Novo -Designed Functional Luciferases
abstract: Luciferases are widely used bioluminescent reporters, yet access to these enzymes has historically relied on recombinant expression. Using automated fast-flow peptide synthesis (AFPS), we synthesized Gaussia luciferase (GLuc, 18.1 kDa, 168 amino acids), picALuc (13 kDa, 120 amino acids), and LuxSit-i (13.8 kDa, 118 amino acids), representing a nature-derived disulfide-rich luciferase, an engineered luciferase, and a de novo-designed luciferase, respectively. Synthetic GLuc was purified, oxidatively folded, and recovered as a monomeric, enzymatically active enzyme with biophysical properties comparable to its recombinant counterpart. picALuc likewise required oxidative folding, whereas cysteine-free LuxSit-i was folded by denaturant removal using size-exclusion chromatography. Biochemical and biophysical analyses confirmed the structural integrity and activity of the three synthetic enzymes. Notably, LuxSit-i represents, to our knowledge, the original total chemical synthesis of a fully de novo-designed enzyme. Together, these proteins expand the known repertoire of fully synthetic enzymes produced by solid-phase peptide synthesis by approximately 14% and establish the initial examples of fully synthetic luciferases produced by solid-phase peptide synthesis that demonstrate enzymatic activity. These findings position AFPS as a platform for accessing functional enzymes across evolutionary and design spaces and may enable the development of luciferases incorporating noncanonical residues, site-specific modifications, or mirror-image sequences.

title: A Generalized Theory for the Structural and Spatial Mapping of Energy, Entropy, and Free Energy
venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
abstract: Systems in which the free energy density is nonuniform in space are familiar; the surface tension of a water droplet and the surface energy of a solid are good examples. Some such cases can be treated with prior theory, notably inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST), but IST is applicable only to liquids. Despite this limitation, IST has proven useful as a guide to the design of ligands to bind a targeted protein, based on the idea that ligands that displace high free energy water will tend to bind more tightly, other things being equal. Here, we present Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping (GTM) theory, a more general theory that is applicable to the entirety of a biomolecular or other chemical system, and which thus may provide additional guidance for molecular design. For example, it might highlight parts of a ligand whose local free energy rises on binding, thus suggesting where modifications could improve affinity. Starting from classical statistical thermodynamics, we derive structural decompositions that assign energy and entropy to individual atoms or to larger chemical components, such as amino acid residues, and spatial decompositions that define continuously varying thermodynamic densities throughout the system. The potential energy is decomposed via the multibody expansion, and the entropy via the mutual information expansion. The resulting thermodynamic densities satisfy key desiderata: their spatial integrals yield the correct total thermodynamic quantities, the densities vanish where the atomic number density is zero, and all entropy terms above first order go to zero in the absence of correlation. The entropy decomposition in GTM theory is closely related to that of IST, but it is simpler, largely because it expresses the entropy in terms of normalized probability density functions instead of nonnormalized correlation functions. We show that GTM theory is formally exact for any number of particles, N, whereas IST is not. The unified framework presented here enables thermodynamic mapping of solute and solvent alike and is expected to support a range of applications, including in structure-based drug design, protein design, the analysis of allostery, and materials science. The use of GTM theory to gain insight into protein-ligand binding is illustrated here with an initial case study.

title: Programming N-linked glycan composition through de novo protein design
abstract: N-linked glycans are ubiquitous post-translational modifications that mediate diverse biological processes, including cell signaling and adhesion, molecular recognition, and host-pathogen interactions. Despite their importance, N-linked glycans have largely remained beyond the reach of biomolecular design due to a lack of methods capable of jointly modeling glycans and protein structure. Here, we develop a general all-atom computational pipeline for creating de novo glycoproteins in which the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. The method uses three-dimensional protein structure to tune glycan accessibility to processing enzymes in the eukaryotic secretory pathway. Systematic increases in steric restriction progressively reduced processing, shifting glycans from heterogeneous complex-type structures toward increasingly underprocessed oligomannose-type species resembling those found on many viral glycoproteins. Despite this programmed restriction, the resulting oligomannose glycans remained accessible for biological recognition, inhibiting uropathogenic Escherichia coli adhesion to human bladder cells and binding mannose-binding lectin. These results establish steric control of N-glycan processing as a genetically encodable design principle and extend computational protein design to functional glycoproteins with programmed composition.

title: Photobiocatalytic Diastereo- and Enantioselective Synthesis of Non-Canonical Amino Acids Bearing Challenging Stereochemical Dyads and Triads
abstract: Catalyst-controlled stereodivergent synthesis of acyclic molecules bearing multiple stereogenic centers remains a longstanding challenge in asymmetric catalysis, particularly through intermolecular radical C-C coupling. Here, we report the directed evolution of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent biocatalysts for the stereodivergent synthesis of non-canonical amino acids bearing either skipped α,γ-stereo-chemical dyads or contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads. Starting from a thermophilic tryptophan synthase β-subunit, protein engineering generated complementary enzyme variants that selectively construct three of the four possible α,γ-stereoisomers through biocatalyst-controlled reversal of both remote γ-stereochemistry and proximal α-stereochemistry. These engineered enzymes catalyzed intermolecular radical C-C bond formation with a broad range of secondary alkyltrifluoroborates, affording α,γ-disubstituted amino acids in excellent yields and stereose-lectivities. Furthermore, directed evolution enabled efficient β-dehydroxylative radical coupling of the non-native threonine-derived amino-acrylate intermediate, providing amino acids bearing contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads with up to 96:4:<0.1:<0.1 d.r. and >99:1 e.r.. To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this platform, the stereochemically enriched amino acids were transformed into valuable γ-chiral amines through engineered PLP-dependent tryptophan decarboxylases, establishing a dual PLP enzyme-based biocatalytic cascade for the en-antiodivergent synthesis of privileged amine scaffolds. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that enzyme-controlled γ-stereoselectivity originates from active-site remodeling that modulates π-π interactions and steric contacts governing the facial selectivity of the radical addition step. This work expands the synthetic capabilities of radical biocatalysis by enabling catalyst-controlled stereodivergent assembly of complex acyclic stereochemical arrays and establishes engineered PLP enzymes as versatile catalysts for the synthesis of stereochemically complex amino acids and chiral amines.

title: Development and application of bioactivity evaluation methods for melanin synthesis inhibitors in rice blast control
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae , is one of the most important diseases affecting rice production. Melanin synthesis inhibitors (MSIs) are widely used to control this disease, and their bioactivity can be evaluated using in vitro , in planta , and target enzyme assays. However, conventional methods mainly rely on endpoint measurements and provide limited information on MSI activity during the infection process. Recent advances in live-cell imaging and quantitative microscopy enable dynamic monitoring of M. oryzae infection with high spatial and temporal resolution, providing opportunities to connect infection-related functions such as turgor generation and host penetration. In this review, we summarize current approaches for evaluating MSI bioactivity and quantitative methods developed for studying M. oryzae infection biology. We further discuss the potential of live-cell imaging to integrate morphological and functional indicators throughout infection. Based on these approaches, we propose a process-based framework comprising temporal, spatial, and dose-response dimensions, together with a stepwise evaluation strategy from basic in vitro screening to melanin-specific detection, appressorial function, host-pathogen interactions, and plant-level efficacy. This framework may provide a systematic basis for quantitative and mechanistic MSI evaluation and support fungicide discovery and formulation development.

title: Early Life Stage Exposure to Environmentally Relevant Concentrations of TCPP Induces Multigenerational Reproductive Toxicity in Estuarine Fish: A Study Based on Whole-Genome Methylation and Steroidogenesis Pathway
abstract: Abstract Tris (1-chloro-2-propyl) phosphate (TCPP) is ubiquitous in estuarine environments. Parental TCPP exposure impaired reproduction and offspring developmental in zebrafish; yet its multigenerational and transgenerational effects and epigenetic mechanisms in estuarine fish remain unknown. Here, Mugilogobius chulae embryos were exposed to TCPP until 25 days posthatching and reared in clean seawater until F2 hatching. Reproductive and gonadal end points were assessed across generations, while gonadal steroidogenesis and whole-body DNA methylation in larvae were analyzed in F0 and F1 to investigate potential endocrine and epigenetic mechanisms. TCPP induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity that was transmitted to F2 embryos, with F1 and F2 lowest observed effect concentrations 1 order of magnitude lower than that in F0. In F0, 100 μg/L TCPP reduced fecundity and male gonadosomatic index. In F1, 10, and 100 μg/L prolonged spawning latency and affected male gonadal development. In F2, 10 μg/L reduced embryonic hatching. Disruption of steroidogenesis gene expression and hormone levels occurred in F0 and F1 male gonads but only in F1 females. Whole-genome DNA methylation revealed persistent hypermethylation of nerve growth factor receptor (NGFR) and calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit γ 2 (CACNG2) in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway across F0 and F1. Their hypermethylation and reduced expression were associated with decreased steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (STAR) and cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily A member (CYP11A) in male gonads, suggesting NGFR and CACNG2 may represent candidate epigenetically regulated genes associated with TCPP-induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity. This study reveals transgenerational risks of environmental concentrations of TCPP to estuarine fish and provides epigenetic evidence for multigenerational endocrine disruptors.

title: Genetic Diversity of Pyrenophora tritici-repentis Based on Virulence Phenotyping, Effector Gene Profiling, and SSR Markers
abstract: Tan spot is an economically important disease that occurs wherever wheat is grown in Russia. The variability of Pyrenophora tritici-repentis isolates collected in 2025 from common and durum wheat in the Volga region of the Russian Federation—namely Tatarstan, Penza, and Saratov—was characterised for virulence phenotypes, effector genes ToxA, ToxB, and ToxC, and SSR loci. A total of 74 isolates were studied. The ToxA gene was identified in 83.8% of the isolates, while ToxB was not detected; conversely, the ToxC1 allele, one of the genetic determinants of PtrToxC, was present in all isolates. A discordance between phenotypic and molecular assays was noted for PtrToxA detection. Genetic diversity was examined using ten microsatellite (SSR) markers. After clone correction, 55 multilocus haplotypes were resolved. Isolates from common wheat in Tatarstan and Penza showed high similarity, in contrast to the Saratov isolates from durum wheat, which were significantly differentiated. The observed differentiation may be associated with host specialisation to durum wheat, but this hypothesis requires further validation with multi-year and genomic data.

title: Identification of Symptom Clusters and Core Symptoms of Menstrual Distress in Reproductive-Age Women: A Network Analysis
venue: International Journal of Women s Health
abstract: Background: Menstruation is a key indicator of women's health, yet current research often focuses on isolated symptoms or specific syndromes, overlooking how multiple symptoms interrelate. Purpose: This study adopted network analysis to clarify intercorrelations among menstrual distress symptoms, identify core symptoms and symptom clusters, and provide evidence for developing systematic and targeted management strategies for menstrual symptoms. Methods: This cross-sectional study recruited 723 women of reproductive-age through convenience sampling in Yangzhou, China, between July and October 2024. Descriptive analysis (SPSS 26.0) and exploratory factor analysis identified symptom clusters; network analysis (R 4.3.1) constructed the symptom network and identified core symptoms. Results: The study found that reproductive-age women had a menstrual symptom distress score of 20.35±11.01. The most common symptom was lower abdominal pain (75.1%), hypomenorrhea or hypermenorrhea (70.4%), irregular menstrual cycle (70.0%), emotional instability (66.1%),and bloating or breast tenderness (66.0%). Exploratory factor analysis identified five symptom clusters: abnormal menstruation, pain and discomfort, gastrointestinal symptoms, psychological and emotional, and behavioural changes. Network analysis revealed that menstrual insomnia or hypersomnia ranked highest in both strength centrality (2.089) and expected influence (2.177), indicating that this symptom served as a core symptom within the symptom network. Conclusion: Women of reproductive-age experience moderate menstrual symptom distress, with menstrual insomnia or hypersomnia as the core symptoms. Findings from this network analysis suggest that this symptom may be a potential focus for the development of comprehensive symptom management strategies. Future studies could explore whether symptom management strategies that include this core symptom are associated with better outcomes.

title: Genome-Wide Identification of NLR Gene Family and Expression Patterns in Response to Colletotrichum camelliae Infection in Tea Plant (Camellia sinensis)
abstract: Background: Colletotrichum camelliae is an important fungal disease in tea plants (Camellia sinensis), and NLR gene family play a central role in plant disease resistance recognition. Analyzing the expression characteristics and regulatory network of NLR genes in tea plants in response to anthracnose infection can provide a theoretical basis for exploring key genes for tea plant resistance to anthracnose and elucidating the molecular mechanisms of disease resistance. Method: Using the tea tree reference genome Shuchazao 2 as the material, CsNLR genes were identified based on NB-ARC (Pfam ID: PF00931) and LRR (Pfam ID: PF00560) conserved domains; Conduct bioinformatics analysis using TBtools, MEME, and MEGA; Using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) to detect the expression changes of CsNLR in the common variety Sucha 120 and the purple variety Ziying 2 after anthracnose infection, and constructing a protein prediction association network. Result: A total of 158 CsNLR genes were identified, and their physicochemical properties, phylogenetics, gene structure, and cis element analysis revealed differentiation among family members. The promoters generally contain stress and hormone response elements; CsNLR is highly expressed in roots, stems, and mature leaves. After 4 days of inoculation with anthracnose infection, the expression trends of CsNLR in the two tea tree varieties were opposite, with Sucha 120 upregulated and Ziying 2 downregulated; The predicted protein association network shows CsNLR as the central node of the network, with 77 CsNLR proteins were included in the predictive functional association network, and there were differences in the connectivity of different members. Conclusions: The CsNLR identified in this study is a potential NLR resistant gene for anthracnose in tea plants, laying the foundation for subsequent functional verification of disease resistant genes and analysis of resistance mechanisms.

title: RXLR effectors of Phytophthora infestans: delivery, host targets and immune suppression
abstract: Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen responsible for the devastating potato disease known as late blight, poses a significant threat to plant health. A major determinant of its pathogenic success is the deployment of cytoplasmic effector proteins, particularly the RXLR class of effectors, which accumulate within the host cells and manipulate plant immune responses. These effectors function as key virulence factors that interfere with multiple layers of plant defense, including pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) and effector-triggered immunity (ETI). Recent studies have revealed that RXLR effectors target diverse host cellular processes such as transcriptional regulation, post-translational modifications, vesicle trafficking, autophagy, chloroplast-mediated immune signalling, and protein stability. By converging on these critical immune hubs, RXLR effectors reprogram host cellular networks to promote pathogen colonization and disease progression. Advances in genomics, structural biology, and host-interactor screening have significantly expanded our understanding of RXLR effector diversity, their molecular mechanisms, and their interactions with host susceptibility factors. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge on the functional roles of RXLR effectors of P. infestans, highlighting their subcellular localization, host targets, and mechanisms of immune suppression. We also discuss emerging concepts in effector biology and their implications for developing durable resistance strategies against late blight disease.

title: WAK This Way: The Roles of Wall-Associated Kinases in Plant Disease Resistance
abstract: Plant wall-associated kinases (WAKs) and WAK-like kinases (WAKLs) are closely related subfamilies of receptor-like kinases (RLKs) that bridge the plant cell wall and cytoplasm and mediate essential signaling functions. Beyond their developmental roles, accumulating evidence highlights their important contributions to plant immunity. Initially identified in Arabidopsis thaliana, these proteins have emerged as important regulators of plant responses to biotic stresses. This review focuses on the disease-resistance functions of this protein family and their associated signaling pathways across diverse plant species. Notably, recent genetic evidence has challenged the long-held view that Arabidopsis WAKs serve as bona fide receptors for oligogalacturonides (OGs), highlighting unresolved questions about how WAKs and WAKLs perceive pathogen invasion. Based on current knowledge, we propose a working model for pathogen recognition by WAKs and WAKLs and outline potential shared immune signaling pathways mediated by this receptor family.

title: DUFB Promotes Broad-Spectrum Disease Resistance by Stabilizing GS1;1 in Rice
venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Excessive nitrogen (N) fertilization increases rice susceptibility to pathogens, yet the molecular links between N signaling and immunity remain largely unresolved. In this study, we identified three genes encoding DUF-domain-containing proteins, DUFA, DUFB, and DUFC, which were induced by Rhizoctonia solani (R. solani) infection and N treatment. Analyses of dufa/b/c mutant and overexpression lines showed that DUFA/B/C genes have functional redundancy and confer broad-spectrum resistance to sheath blight (ShB), blast, and bacterial blight. DUFA/B/C interacted with glutamine synthetase 1;1 (GS1;1), suggesting that distinct DUF proteins may converge on a shared GS1;1-associated defense pathway. Subsequent analyses demonstrated that DUFs enhance rice ShB resistance by inhibiting ubiquitin-mediated GS1;1 degradation. The GS1;1 protein level was reduced in high-nitrogen (HN) compared to in low-nitrogen (LN) conditions, implying that DUFB-GS1;1 signaling might be involved in N-dependent rice disease resistance. Overall, these findings reveal a mechanism linking the N status to rice immunity through DUFB-mediated stabilization of GS1;1.

title: From genome editing to chromosome engineering in plants
abstract: Engineering large genomic segments is rapidly expanding the scope of plant genome manipulation from individual genes to chromosome-scale redesign. Recent advances in double-strand break-, prime-editing-, recombinase-, and transposase-based technologies now enable programmable deletion, insertion, replacement, duplication, inversion, and translocation of DNA fragments ranging from kilobases to megabases. In this review, we summarize the major strategies for large-fragment genome engineering in plants, compare their strengths and limitations, and discuss their applications in both fundamental plant biology and crop breeding. We further highlight that the integration of artificial intelligence is catalyzing the rapid optimization of large-fragment genome engineering. The ongoing transition from genome editing to chromosome engineering promises to revolutionize crop breeding and plant synthetic biology, ultimately enabling rational design of plant genomes.

title: Type III Effectors of Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Manipulation Networks, and Implications for Plant Disease Resistance
abstract: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000) is a reference system for dissecting how type III-secreted effectors (T3Es) suppress plant immunity and reconfigure host physiology. Here, we reassess the DC3000 effector repertoire through an evidence-graded framework that links experimentally resolved effector–target mechanisms to repertoire-level genetic interactions and, ultimately, to disease-resistance strategies. We distinguish findings demonstrated with Pst DC3000 from mechanistic examples derived from other P. syringae pathovars and from computationally generated hypotheses. At the molecular level, validated DC3000 effectors perturb pattern-recognition receptor signaling, protein turnover, vesicle trafficking, plasmodesmatal communication, organelle function, and hormone-associated processes. At the repertoire level, deletion and reconstruction studies reveal functional redundancy, specialization, conditional suppression, and context-dependent interactions; importantly, convergence on a common host phenotype is not treated as evidence of direct physical cooperation between effectors. We further evaluate how effectoromics, multi-omics, single-cell and spatial approaches, structure prediction, and machine-learning tools can prioritize new hypotheses while emphasizing their need for genetic, biochemical, and infection-based validation. Finally, we consider how conserved effector targets, susceptibility factors, NLR engineering, and CRISPR-based editing may translate mechanistic knowledge into more durable bacterial-disease resistance. This synthesis positions the DC3000 system as a bridge between mechanistic effector biology, quantitative effector-network analysis, and experimentally testable strategies for crop protection.

title: Plant Genetic Improvement for Better Disease Resistance through Biotechnological Tools
abstract: Biotic stress caused by pathogen invasion into plant cells is one of the most detrimental factors in the global agricultural scenario. Among the multitude of rogue pathogens, bacterial and fungal pathogens comprise the majority and are the most challenging opponents for the plants. Although plants have a strong protective army repertoire, at times, they fail to protect their host cells successfully owing to smart resistance-developing pathogens. Hence, the use of the protective system of the plants through present-day biotechnological tools can fortify plants effectively to prevent pathogen attacks. Firstly, plants possess the pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) and nucleotide-binding and leucine–rich repeat (NLR) proteins at the site of pathogen perception to prevent their entry followed by defense signaling members, for example, jasmonate and salicylic acid pathway along with disease–related genes like natriuretic peptide receptor A/guanylate cyclase 202 A ( NPR1 ), WRKY transcription factors, and so forth, which act to protect plant cells from getting harmed. Additionally, another interesting category is the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) in plant cells, which has been utilized massively to build stronger pathogen–resistant plants. Along with the AMPs, many other members of the defense pathway have been cloned, genetically manipulated, and when introgressed in crop plant genomes either singly or in combination, have turned out to be effective in preventing the huge losses incurred in crop quality and yield by pathogen outbreaks.

title: Metabolic hallmarks of regulated cell death
abstract: Regulated cell death (RCD) is characterized by distinct molecular execution mechanisms, but its initiation, progression, and biological consequences are increasingly recognized as being shaped by cellular metabolism. Bioenergetic state, redox homeostasis, nutrient availability, metal ion metabolism, inflammatory metabolism, and organelle function collectively determine cellular susceptibility to death and influence the activation and execution of diverse RCD programs. In this review, we synthesize the metabolic hallmarks of established, independently validated, and recently proposed forms of RCD, highlighting both their mechanistic diversity and their extensive metabolic convergence. We then examine the endogenous mechanisms that maintain metabolic homeostasis and discuss how their disruption reshapes cell death responses in human disease and therapeutic contexts. Together, these insights provide a guide to the metabolic landscape of RCD and reveal metabolism not only as a modifier of cell death, but as a fundamental determinant of when, how, and with what consequences cells die. We conclude by discussing key conceptual and mechanistic challenges and emerging opportunities for therapeutically exploiting the metabolic control of RCD.

title: Identification of an Inhibitory Fraction from Cinnamomum cassia Against Digestive Lipases
abstract: Natural inhibitors of digestive lipases offer promising alternatives to conventional obesity medications. This study screened nine medicinal plant extracts, identifying the ethanolic bark extract of Cinnamomum cassia as the most potent inhibitor for gastric and pancreatic lipases. Using an integrated approach combining bioactivity-guided fractionation and mass spectrometry, we isolated the highly active fraction, F3-1-1, which exhibited dose- and time-dependent inhibitory effects against human and porcine pancreatic lipases, as well as dog gastric lipase (DGL). Further mass spectrometry and peptide mass fingerprint analysis putatively annotated cinncassiol A-19 glucoside as a bioactive constituent. Notably, this compound was likely bound covalently to the catalytic peptide containing the Ser153 residue in DGL, characterized by a mass shift of +553.10 Da. Molecular docking simulations supported these suggestions, demonstrating stable interactions within the catalytic pocket of DGL through hydrogen and hydrophobic bond interactions. These findings highlight C. cassia as a promising source of natural anti-obesity agents.

title: Epilepsy domain adapted large language models enhance epileptogenic zone prediction from seizure semiology
abstract: Seizure semiology provides clinically meaningful clues for localizing the epileptogenic zone (EZ) in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, but its interpretation varies across clinicians and institutions. We aimed to develop and externally validate a domain-adapted large language model for EZ localization from narrative seizure descriptions. We developed EpiSemoLLM using 1,372 surgically verified semiology–EZ pairs collected from 392 published studies and a retrospective cohort from Far Eastern Memorial Hospital. Of these cases, 1,272 were used for model development and 100 were reserved for evaluation. The model combined parameter-efficient fine-tuning with structured epilepsy knowledge and literature-based evidence retrieval. We compared its performance with general-purpose and biomedical language models and with five epileptologists. External validation was conducted in an independent cohort of 83 cases from Taipei Veterans General Hospital evaluated by six epileptologists. Performance was assessed using case-level and region-level localization measures, with uncertainty estimated by paired bootstrap resampling. Here we show that EpiSemoLLM achieves the strongest overall localization performance among the evaluated language models and performs better than the median epileptologist in the held-out cohort. Similar findings are observed in the independent external cohort. The model shows relative strengths in temporal, parietal, occipital, and cingulate localization, whereas clinicians perform better in frontal and insular localization. These findings support the use of domain adaptation and literature-based evidence retrieval for interpreting seizure semiology. EpiSemoLLM may complement clinical reasoning during early presurgical evaluation and help improve the consistency of EZ localization across clinical settings. Prospective validation is needed before routine clinical use. People with epilepsy that does not improve with medicine may be considered for brain surgery. Before surgery, doctors need to identify the part of the brain that is responsible for the seizures and should be targeted during treatment. Signs and symptoms during a seizure can help, but different doctors may interpret them differently. We trained a language model using published reports and hospital records from patients whose seizure-related brain regions had been confirmed by surgery and follow-up. We compared its answers with those of epileptologists and tested it on cases from another hospital. Our model outperformed all baselines and was as accurate as or more accurate than the epileptologists. It is designed to complement clinical expertise and standard presurgical tests, supporting more consistent early assessments. ED SUM: Yang et al. develop and externally validate EpiSemoLLM, a domain-adapted language model that localizes epileptogenic zones from seizure semiology. The model outperforms evaluated language models and performs comparably to or better than epileptologists across internal and external cohorts.

title: Rhizobial type III effectors as regulators of root-nodule symbiosis in legumes
abstract: The rhizobia-legume nitrogen-fixing symbiosis begins when plants perceive rhizobial Nod factors (NF), activating the Common Symbiosis Signalling Pathway (CSSP) that drives nodule organogenesis. Rhizobia also inject Type III effectors (T3E) into host cells through a Type III Secretion System (T3SS) related to those of pathogenic bacteria. These effectors were long viewed only as suppressors of plant immunity and determinants of host compatibility, but this picture has changed. Recent studies revealed that rhizobial effectors (known as Nodulation Outer Proteins, Nops) such as NopT, NopM, NopL, NopP and NopZ directly target NF receptors or associated kinases, thereby regulating CSSP activation. The effector-triggering nodulation proteins (ET-Nods), a separate class of T3Es found in various Bradyrhizobium species, can activate nodule organogenesis independently of NF perception by rewiring host transcriptional and SUMOylation-based signalling. We trace the evolutionary origins of these activities, which may derive either from redirection of ancestral immune-targeting effectors toward symbiotic functions or from rhizobium-specific innovations. We ask whether the T3SS contributed to nodulation. We then consider what this interference means for the host, ranging from reinforced partner choice to partial loss of host control, and argue that rhizobial effectors have evolved as specialised modulators that converge on the signalling hubs governing symbiosis.

title: Aerosol Optical Properties in the Community Radiative Transfer Model for Data Assimilation
abstract: Abstract Aerosol particles have significant impacts across the Earth System, yet quantifying these impacts remains challenging. An effective technique to predict aerosol distribution and study their impact is data assimilation (DA), for which the aerosol optical properties (AOPs) are critical. AOPs govern the interaction of light with aerosols, serve as the fundamental parameters in aerosol retrieval algorithms, and link the modeled aerosol concentration to retrieval products, such as aerosol optical depth (AOD). Ensuring consistent and scientifically accurate AOPs across aerosol models, observation, and observation operators is therefore essential for aerosol DA. To support this need, on top of the default aerosol scheme developed and adopted by NOAA, the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) team has implemented and released three optional aerosol schemes in recent years to facilitate aerosol DA with the Community Multiscale Air Quality, NAAPS, and GOCART‐GEOS5 models. In this paper, we present updates to the CRTM aerosol component, examine the impacts of different aerosol schemes on simulated AOD and brightness temperature, and compare the AOPs used in the selected chemical transport model and satellite retrieval algorithms, including Dark Target and Deep Blue. This work aims to better constrain AOPs across selected DA systems and discusses the recent progress as well as remaining challenges.

title: Recognition-dependent activation of the Arabidopsis RRS1-R/RPS4 TIR-NLR immune receptor pair
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Plant TIR domain-containing proteins exhibit NADase activity upon pathogen effector recognition, creating small molecules that activate defense via EDS1 and its associated proteins. Arabidopsis RPS4 and RRS1 comprise a TIR-NLR immune receptor pair that recognizes multiple effector proteins including AvrRps4 and PopP2. We show here that RPS4 and RRS1 acquire NADase activity upon recognition of a cognate effector. However, both in the presence and absence of effector, RPS4 and RRS1 form an oligomer that does not change in size upon effector provision. Effector-dependent defense activation by RPS4 and RRS1 requires the catalytic glutamate residue and the BB-loop motif of RPS4, which is absent in RRS1 and other RRS1-like TIR domains in Arabidopsis . Oligomerization of RPS4 and RRS1 occurs through multiple domains, but oligomerization does not require enzymatic activity. We propose that conformational changes or reconfiguration within the RPS4/RRS1 oligomer upon effector recognition derepresses the complex for immune activation.

title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. METHODS: We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. RESULTS: In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). DISCUSSION: Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

title: Effects of resveratrol supplementation on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in metabolic disorders: a systematic review and dose–response meta‑analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Background Chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress are hallmarks of metabolic disorders. A naturally occurring polyphenol, resveratrol (RSV), has shown promise in modulating these pathways, however clinical evidence is mixed. To systematically review and perform a dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to assess the effects of RSV supplementation on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in patients with these disorders. Methods A systematic search up to August 2026 following PRISMA guidelines was conducted to identify RCTs that examined the effect of RSV on inflammatory (including C-reactive protein (CRP), Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-6 (IL-6)) and oxidative stress (malondialdehyde (MDA), superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and total antioxidant capacity (TAC)) biomarkers in populations with metabolic disorders. Random effects models were used to combine the data. Dose-response relationships were evaluated using linear and non-linear modelling. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was performed to adjust for repetitive testing, calculate the required information size (RIS), and assess the robustness of the cumulative evidence. Results Meta-analysis of 25 RCTs for CRP showed a statistically significant reduction (SMD = -0.18, 95% CI: -0.33 to -0.03, p = 0.0202, I 2 = 20%), while IL-6 and TNF-α showed non-significant changes with high heterogeneity. Regarding oxidative stress markers, no significant overall effects were observed for CAT, MDA, or SOD. Analysis of TAC showed a non-significant trend (SMD = 0.63, 95% CI: -0.08 to 1.33, p = 0.0668, I 2 = 58.5%), which became statistically significant only after the exclusion of one influential outlier trial (SMD = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.23 to 1.44, p = 0.0273, I 2 = 0%). TSA crossed the monitoring boundary for CRP, supporting an anti-inflammatory effect, while evidence for other biomarkers remained inconclusive. Dose-response meta-analyses identified no significant linear or non-linear associations between daily RSV dosage and inflammatory outcomes. Conclusion RSV supplementation is associated with a modest reduction in CRP, supported by TSA; however, effects on other inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers were null or inconclusive. The absence of a clear dose-response relationship and the surrogate status of CRP limit the clinical interpretability of these findings.
