title: Nutrient Calculation Accuracy, Expert-Rated Clinical Appropriateness and Safety Indicators, and Reproducibility of Large Language Model-Generated Diet Plans for Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome: A Real-Case-Based Evaluation
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluated the nutrient calculation accuracy, reproducibility, and expert-rated clinical appropriateness and safety indicators of three-day diet plans generated for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently proposed to be termed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Methods: Anonymized data from six women with heterogeneous PMOS profiles, purposively selected from a single clinic, were converted into standardized Turkish prompts and submitted to ChatGPT-4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Mistral 2.0 through free web interfaces. Three independent generations per case–model combination yielded 216 daily menus. LLM-reported nutrient values were compared with BeBiS 9.0 calculations. Reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Two experts independently evaluated the first generated plan for each case–model combination using a study-specific clinical appropriateness rubric and red-flag checklist. Results: No model achieved consistently low error across nutrients. Claude Sonnet 4.6 showed the lowest percentage errors for energy, carbohydrate, and fiber; ChatGPT-4 for protein; and Mistral 2.0 for fat. Gemini 2.5 Flash showed the largest percentage errors across all nutrients and a mean energy bias of +531.1 kcal. ChatGPT-4 showed comparatively higher plan-level reproducibility, while the remaining models generally showed poor reproducibility. Claude Sonnet 4.6 had the highest descriptive clinical appropriateness scores and Gemini 2.5 Flash the lowest, but no pairwise differences remained significant after Holm correction. Gemini 2.5 Flash generated the most confirmed study-specific red flags (n = 28), with all six cases meeting the criterion for the “masked low-energy” indicator. Conclusions: LLM-generated diet plans showed model-dependent calculation errors and limited reproducibility, and the present findings do not support their independent or unsupervised use as individualized clinical nutrition recommendations.

title: Magnetic boronate–Ti(IV) dual-affinity nanoparticles for simultaneous enrichment and sequential elution of glycopeptides and phosphopeptides
abstract: The simultaneous enrichment of glycopeptides and phosphopeptides from complex peptide mixtures remains challenging because boronate affinity and immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) typically require different pH conditions for efficient binding. We evaluated the previously reported dual boronate-Ti(IV) magnetic nanomaterial, Mag@DBA-Ti(IV), as a sample-preparation platform for the single-sorbent, single-loading-condition enrichment and sequential elution of glycopeptides and phosphopeptides. The material, prepared by co-immobilizing a low-pKₐ boronic acid ligand and alendronate on magnetic nanoparticles, followed by Ti(IV) chelation, was originally developed for small-molecule enrichment; its translation to peptide-level proteomics is established here. The integrated boronate and Ti(IV)-IMAC sites enabled concurrent binding of glycopeptides and phosphopeptides under neutral loading conditions, with selective release achieved using acidic and alkaline eluents, respectively. This translation required redesigning the elution chemistry for MS compatibility, replacing the high-pH sodium phosphate eluent used for small molecules with 0.4 mol L⁻¹ NH₃·H₂O, and establishing that the dual-affinity sites retain selectivity when glycopeptides and phosphopeptides are low-abundance species competing with a large excess of unmodified peptides. Mag@DBA-Ti(IV) exhibited high adsorption capacities toward model protein digests, reaching 71.4 mg g⁻¹ for IgG digest and 125 mg g⁻¹ for α-casein digest. The material also showed high selectivity for both glycopeptides and phosphopeptides in the presence of a 500-fold excess of bovine serum albumin digest, allowing detection at concentrations as low as 10⁻¹⁰ mol L⁻¹. When applied to U251 cell lysate digests, Mag@DBA-Ti(IV) enabled the identification of 1,945 glycopeptides from 752 glycoproteins and 7,498 phosphopeptides from 2,410 phosphoproteins in a single experiment. These results demonstrate that the dual boronate-Ti(IV) affinity concept, originally established for small molecules, can be translated to peptide-level bottom-up proteomics, providing a single-sorbent route to integrated glycoproteomic and phosphoproteomic determination.

title: Electroacupuncture Ameliorating Cerebral I/R-Induced Inflammatory Response through the TLR/TRAF6/NF-κB Pathway
abstract: Background The inflammatory response plays a crucial role in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury and may offer a new therapeutic approach for stroke. Electroacupuncture has shown potential in treating cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury. Methodology Male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to four groups: the sham group, middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) group, sham electroacupuncture (SEA) group, and electroacupuncture (EA) group. The SEA and EA groups received 30 min of treatment after 60 min of ischemia. Body weight was measured before and 24 h after the MCAO/R procedure. Neurological function and infarct volume were assessed 24 h after the MCAO/R procedure. Protein and messenger RNA (mRNA) expression levels of TLR4, TLR9, TRAF6, and NF-κB were evaluated using western blot and reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The mRNA and protein expression of inflammatory markers was assessed using RT-PCR and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results Compared with the MCAO/R group, the EA group exhibited improved neurological function, reduced infarct volume, and down-regulated expression of TLR4, TLR9, TRAF6, and NF-κB. Additionally, in the EA group, the mRNA and protein expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) were decreased, while the expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine (IL-10) was increased. Conclusions Electroacupuncture exerts a neuroprotective effect on MCAO/R, potentially through the modulation of the TLR4, TLR9, TRAF6, and NF-κB pathways. This treatment may reduce the cerebral I/R-induced inflammatory response by influencing the TLR/TRAF/NF-κB signaling pathway.

title: Switching from Intravenous to Subcutaneous Infliximab in Children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Purpose of review Subcutaneous infliximab (IFX-SC; CT-P13 SC/infliximab-dyyb/Remsima-SC/Zymfentra) is an approved maintenance option after intravenous (IV) induction in adults with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but it is not approved for patients < 18 years, and the pediatric evidence remains dispersed across small, largely observational cohorts. This review synthesizes the published pediatric experience of transitioning from IV to SC infliximab, examining maintenance of remission, drug concentrations, safety, and acceptability, and situates it within the adult evidence base and the distinctly pediatric concerns of access and dosing. Recent findings A systematic search (PROSPERO: CRD420261465026) identified six independent, non-overlapping pediatric switch cohorts (n = 173). Random-effects proportional meta-analysis yielded pooled treatment persistence of 92% (95%CI 84-98), maintained clinical remission of 93% (95%CI 84-99), and any-cause discontinuation of 8% (95%CI 2-16), most often for injection-site intolerance, disease relapse, or paradoxical dermatitis. New anti-drug antibody formation was rare among the 129 children in cohorts measuring immunogenicity (four children, none sustained) while previously positive antibodies frequently resolved after switching. Steady-state SC concentrations ran roughly 2-fold above prior IV troughs, an expected step-up reflecting sustained subcutaneous exposure. Patient and caregiver satisfaction was high due to decreased school absence and travel, and cost analyses signaled net savings from avoided infusion-center use. The principal barrier was administrative: age-based denial. In appropriately selected children, transition to IFX-SC sustains remission with predictable pharmacokinetics, a reassuring immunogenicity profile, and excellent tolerability, mirroring the adult experience. These observations constitute a well-supported real-world signal and warrant prospective validation and pursuit of pediatric labeling.

title: Aspirin dose and coronary artery lesions in Kawasaki disease: a two-center retrospective comparative effectiveness study
abstract: Coronary artery lesions (CAL) are the most common complication of Kawasaki disease (KD). Chinese guidelines recommend aspirin at 30-50 mg/kg/day during the acute phase, yet whether the dose within this range affects coronary outcome remains unclear. We retrospectively analyzed 997 children with complete or incomplete KD who received IVIG plus aspirin at two tertiary hospitals in Sichuan, China, from January 2017 to December 2025. Low-dose aspirin (30 to < 40 mg/kg/day; n = 630) was compared with high-dose (40 to 50 mg/kg/day; n = 367). Confounders were selected by intersecting a directed acyclic graph (Supplementary Fig. S1) with univariate screening at P < 0.10, yielding a final multivariable model of 7 predictors (136 CAL events; events-per-variable ratio of 19.4). Linearity of the continuous covariates and the absence of multicollinearity were verified (Supplementary Tables S1-S2). The dose-response relation was examined with restricted cubic splines, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was added as a sensitivity analysis. CAL at 4 weeks occurred in 13.5% of the low-dose group and 14.7% of the high-dose group (P = 0.658), with an adjusted OR of 0.94 (95% CI 0.64-1.38; P = 0.752). IVIG non-response was similar (4.1% vs 3.8%; P = 0.940), whereas aspirin-related adverse drug reactions were twice as frequent with high-dose aspirin (3.0% vs 6.3%; P = 0.021). The spline showed no significant linear (P = 0.253) or non-linear (P = 0.547) dose-response trend. IPTW yielded an OR of 0.95 (95% CI 0.65-1.38), and the doubly robust estimate was 0.95 (95% CI 0.65-1.40). Conclusions Within the guideline-recommended 30-50 mg/kg/day window, no significant differences were detected between low- and high-dose aspirin in coronary or IVIG non-response outcomes, while the lower dose halved adverse drug reactions. Although equivalence cannot be formally demonstrated in an observational study, these data suggest that 30 to < 40 mg/kg/day may be the preferable choice during the acute phase of KD in Chinese children. What is known • Chinese guidelines recommend aspirin at 30-50 mg/kg/day during the acute phase of KD, yet comparative coronary outcome data within this dose range remain limited. What is new • In a two-center cohort of 997 children, low-dose (30 to < 40 mg/kg/day) and high-dose (40 to 50 mg/kg/day) aspirin produced similar coronary artery lesion rates and IVIG non-response rates, whereas the lower dose halved the rate of adverse drug reactions.

title: Complete blood count-derived inflammatory indices versus C-reactive protein for identifying complicated appendicitis in children: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) are increasingly proposed for identifying complicated appendicitis in children, yet reported cut-offs vary widely and are seldom externally validated. We aimed to test the limits of these indices for identifying complicated appendicitis in a large pediatric cohort, using C-reactive protein (CRP) as the benchmark. This study evaluates the laboratory ceiling of these indices rather than complete diagnostic risk stratification. We retrospectively studied 422 children with histopathologically confirmed appendicitis (2012-2026), of whom 158 (37.4%) had complicated disease defined by intraoperative findings. Discrimination for complicated appendicitis was assessed by the area under the ROC curve (AUC) and compared with CRP (DeLong test). We additionally applied previously published pediatric cut-offs to our cohort, examined discrimination across developmental age strata and after age-normalization, assessed added value over CRP, and tested temporal stability across two consecutive periods. CRP discriminated complicated appendicitis better (AUC 0.812) than NLR (0.641), SII (0.641), or PLR (0.604; all p < 0.001 versus CRP), and the white cell count alone performed as well as the indices. None of five published cut-offs transported to a clinically useful accuracy (45.7-63.5%). In children aged 2-7 years-those with the highest proportion of complicated disease (52.7%)-the indices showed no evidence of discrimination (AUC 0.475-0.495), whereas CRP retained its highest discrimination (0.863); age-normalization did not help. Added to a CRP-based model, NLR and SII contributed statistically but slightly (ΔAUC + 0.018 and + 0.016), while PLR did not. Between the two periods, index values fell significantly despite an unchanged proportion of complicated disease, and an earlier-derived threshold lost approximately ten points of sensitivity in the later period; the CRP threshold instead lost specificity while retaining sensitivity, so no marker was fully stable, although discrimination was preserved for all and the median CRP was unchanged. Conclusion: NLR, PLR, and SII offer limited and unstable value for identifying complicated appendicitis in children. They are consistently outperformed by CRP, discriminate poorly in the youngest children in whom the distinction matters most, and depend on thresholds that transport poorly between settings and over time. These indices are best regarded as continuous adjuncts to CRP rather than standalone tests.

title: Circuit-constrained molecular neuroethology in the medicinal leech Hirudo verbana
abstract: Medicinal leeches have long served as classic systems in comparative neuroethology because individual neurons can be identified across animals and linked to well-defined behaviors. This review argues that Hirudo verbana is now positioned for a new phase in which this identified-cell framework can be connected directly to molecular mechanisms. We first outline the organization and experimental accessibility of the leech nervous system, then evaluate genomic and transcriptomic resources as tools for testing physiologically constrained hypotheses rather than as endpoints in themselves. We focus on selected problems in which behavior, identified neurons, and molecular candidates can be brought into close alignment: sensory encoding, serotonergic state-dependent gating, multifunctional behavioral circuits, heartbeat rhythm generation, and endocannabinoid-dependent plasticity. Across these examples, the comparative value of Hirudo verbana lies not in nervous-system simplicity alone, but in interpretability: receptors, ion channels, pumps, peptides, gap-junction proteins, and metabolic enzymes can be examined in relation to cellular and circuit operations already defined by physiology. Future progress will require tighter integration of circuit-defined phenotypes with cell-resolved transcriptomics, spatial localization, targeted perturbation, and quantitative modeling. This circuit-constrained strategy positions Hirudo verbana as a valuable bridge between classical identified-cell neuroethology and molecular tests of circuit physiology.

title: Hos2-mediated KatG1 decrotonylation orchestrates ROS scavenging in rice blast infection
abstract: In plant–pathogen interaction, plants trigger reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts to defend against pathogen invasion, while pathogens evolved antioxidant systems to scavenge ROS for infection. Our study reveals a regulatory mechanism of ROS adaptation and scavenging in the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae. We found that KatG1, a bifunctional catalase-peroxidase, acts as a ROS-responsive regulatory enzyme. During infection, the deacetylase Hos2 mediates the decrotonylation of KatG1 at K422, initiating the ROS clearance process. Decrotonylated KatG1 depolymerizes into monomers, interacts with the Hsp70 protein Ssb1, and translocates to the nucleus. Nuclear KatG1 promotes the dissociation of the Atf1-Tup1 complex, activating the expression of Atf1-mediated oxidoreductase genes and enhancing fungal infection. Moreover, we identified a small molecule, orcinol gentiobioside (OGB), that targets KatG1, inhibiting M. oryzae invasion. This study elucidates a regulatory mechanism of ROS metabolism and stress adaptation in plant fungal infections and provides a potential target for fungicide development to control rice blast disease. Plants trigger reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts to defend against pathogens. Here the authors report that decrotonylation and relocalization of the rice blast fungus KatG1 protein can activate fungal ROS responses and propose targeting of this pathway in fungicide development.

title: Structure-based targeting of Atg8 uncovers its essential role in autophagy-mediated detoxification
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Autophagy degrades and recycles intracellular material, allowing cells to maintain homeostasis and adapt to environmental stress. In the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae , the core autophagy protein MoAtg8 is required for autophagosome formation and host infection. Here, we determined the crystal structure of MoAtg8 and used it for structure-guided virtual screening of a focused compound library enriched for natural products and autophagy-related molecules. This screen identified nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA), a naturally occurring lignan, as a MoAtg8-binding compound. NDGA suppressed conidial germination and appressorium formation, disrupted membrane integrity, and reduced pathogenicity in M. oryzae , with no detectable phytotoxicity to rice under the conditions tested. Mechanistically, the 5-lipoxygenase Mo5Lox, a target of NDGA, bound NDGA with lower affinity than MoAtg8. MoAtg8 associated with NDGA through Gln81 and promoted its autophagy-dependent delivery to vacuoles, thereby reducing compound availability to toxicity-associated targets. Disruption of autophagy or mutation of Gln81 in MoAtg8 increased fungal sensitivity to NDGA. These findings identify an autophagy-mediated detoxification route for an exogenous antifungal compound and reveal how MoAtg8-dependent trafficking modulates NDGA efficacy in a plant-pathogenic fungus.

title: Avirulence genes of Magnaporthe oryzae are a pathogen defense arsenal shaped by cognate rice resistance genes in the field
abstract: We examined the frequency of and variation in eight avirulence (AVR) genes from 840 Magnaporthe oryzae field isolates collected from the Southern United States relative to rice resistance (R) genes deployed from 1959 to 2017. Little coding or noncoding variation was detected in AVR-Pi9, AVR-Pib, ACE1 and AVR-Pizt, which correspond to R genes not used in the United States. In the United States, AVR-Pik, corresponding to rice R gene Pi-k alleles deployed at varying levels since the late 1960s, was present in 37% of the isolates over six decades. AVR-Pita1, corresponding to Pi-ta deployed in the late 1990s, reached a low point in the 5-yr period following Pi-ta deployment and then recovered to 99% in recent years. Our results suggest a fitness penalty for M. oryzae isolates carrying nonfunctional AVR variants and provide concrete data on how changes in plant R gene composition can impact pathogen populations. These findings will inform localized strategies for R gene usage and durable control of blast disease. AVR frequencies differ over time between United States and global samples for AVR-Pik, AVR-Pi9, AVR-Pii and AVR-Pita1. Further whole genome analysis including additional US samples is necessary to confirm whether the United States is a geographically isolated population.

title: OsWHY1 Negatively Modulates Rice Immunity Against Magnaporthe oryzae
abstract: WHIRLY proteins, known for their DNA/RNA-binding capabilities conferred by a highly conserved WHIRLY domain, are integral to plant defense mechanisms. However, the role of OsWHY1 in rice immunity remains to be clarified. We examined OsWHY1 expression after treatment with exogenous hormones, PAMPs, and Magnaporthe oryzae. We generated OsWHY1-overexpressing rice plants and performed yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), transcriptome, and RT-qPCR analyses. OsWHY1 expression was upregulated by exogenous hormones and PAMPs, with a significant increase at 24 h post-inoculation with M. oryzae. Overexpression of OsWHY1 correlated with reduced resistance to M. oryzae. Y2H and BiFC assays demonstrated that OsWHY1 could form homomeric complexes within the chloroplast, and OsWHY1 did not possess transcriptional activation activity. Transcriptome profiling of OsWHY1-overexpressing plants revealed significant downregulation of genes associated with glutathione transferase activity. Chitin-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation was diminished in OsWHY1-overexpressing plants compared with the Nipponbare (NPB) control. The transcriptional levels of key stress- and defense-related genes, including OsWAK1, OsWRKY53, OsPR2, OsSAG12, OsHSP58.7, OsCATB and OsMYB1R, were markedly downregulated in OsWHY1-overexpressing plants. Collectively, these findings indicate that OsWHY1 functions as a negative regulator of rice immunity against M. oryzae by suppressing the expression of defense-related genes. Thus, our study identifies OsWHY1 as a negative immune regulator and suggests that its manipulation could be a strategy for breeding blast-resistant rice varieties.

title: Green Foxtail-Derived Endophytic Fungus Chaetomium novozelandicum SV7 Produced Orsellinic Acid Ester Glycosides Active Against Rice Blast Pathogen
abstract: Plants encounter various fungi during their life history, with some of them pathogenic, some beneficial, and some neither, forming complex plant–fungi interactions. Endophytic fungi are a type of fungi that live inside the plant, and are often beneficial to the host. In this study, the endophytic fungi of green foxtail (Setaria viridis) were explored for their defensive role against the pathogenic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, which causes rice blast, one of the most devastating crop diseases. The endophytic fungi were isolated, taxonomically identified, fermented, and chemically extracted. The fungal extracts were screened for their inhibition against M. oryzae using mycelial growth rate assay, of these, Chaetomium novozelandicum SV7 displayed the most inhibition. A scale-up fermentation of this fungus, followed by extraction and chromatographic purification, led to the isolation and identification of eleven orsellinate-types of metabolites (1–11), including four new compounds (1, 2, 6, 8), named chaetorsellide A-D. The structures of the new compounds were elucidated by means of NMR, HRMS, and quantum chemical calculations. All these metabolites were reported from C. novozelandicum for the first time, with five of them being orsellinic acid ester glycosides (1–5). Plant infection assay was carried out for the isolated compounds, among which compounds 8 and 3 displayed significant activities, with 8 being the most potent. These results not only reveal that these compounds have potential to be developed as natural fungicides against the rice blast pathogen, but also add one more example for exploring new antimicrobial substances from plant–microbe interactions.

title: Exogenous anti-MoPMK1 microRNA and precursor formats reduce Magnaporthe oryzae infection in rice
abstract: Exogenous RNA application is emerging as a useful strategy to investigate plant-pathogen interactions. Most studies against fungal pathogens have focused on long double-stranded RNAs, whereas the potential of artificial miRNA and miRNA-precursor formats remains less explored. Here, we targeted the Magnaporthe oryzae MAP kinase gene MoPMK1, a central regulator of appressorium-mediated penetration, invasive growth and host tissue colonization, using three exogenous RNA formats: chemically synthesized mature miRNA duplexes, in planta-produced anti-MoPMK1-containing small RNA fractions and in vitro-synthesized miRNA precursors. All three anti-MoPMK1 formats reduced blast symptoms in rice leaves and were accompanied by lower accumulation of fungal MoPMK1 transcripts. Under the mass-based doses and assay conditions tested, the in vitro-synthesized precursor was associated with a marked reduction in lesion development despite being applied at a lower molar concentration than the mature duplex. Leaf sheath infection assays further showed altered fungal development after anti-MoPMK1 precursor treatment, whereas appressorium formation was reduced most clearly at the highest precursor concentration tested. In addition, application of the precursor through the leaf base reduced disease symptoms at a distal infection site in detached leaves. Direct incubation of fungal spores with the precursor in liquid culture did not reveal a clear inhibitory effect, suggesting that the infection context in plant tissue contributes to precursor activity. Together, these results identify mature and precursor anti-MoPMK1 microRNA formats as sequence-defined RNA tools with biological activity in the rice-M. oryzae interaction, while highlighting RNA format and plant tissue context as important determinants of exogenous RNA activity.

title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
abstract: Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis 1 . Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction (k cat /k uncat ) of up to 3 × 10 7 . The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications.

title: Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3
abstract: The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. Here, we describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which employs free atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active site architecture incorporating a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases we obtain active catalysts in zero shot 96 construct design campaigns.

title: Programming biological behavior with AI-guided de novo protein design
abstract: Driven by advances in artificial intelligence, de novo protein design can now generate diverse molecular functions from the ground up, achieving remarkable success in engineering binders against many macromolecular targets. Here, we provide a perspective on how de novo design can progress beyond bimolecular interactions toward the bottom-up construction of protein reaction networks. We highlight how programmable, modular, and controllable de novo components can drive complex, emergent biological behaviors. Overcoming current challenges-including designable protein dynamics, multi-step functionalities, and non-equilibrium systems-is essential for this transition. With continued foundational method improvements, the field is poised to pioneer precise protein perturbations for systems-level insight and to engineer emergent cellular behaviors like signal amplification, decision-making, and error correction de novo to fundamentally advance synthetic biology, biotechnology, and medicine.

title: A Fluorogenic Cysteine‐Tetrapeptide Tagging Strategy for Nonperturbative Protein Labeling and Protein–Ligand Interaction Tracking
abstract: Fluorescent labeling approaches are essential for visualizing protein dynamics and dissecting biological processes in living systems. However, existing strategies may cause structural perturbations or require extensive protein engineering. Here, we report a fast, site-selective, and fluorogenic labeling strategy based on a compact four-residue peptide tag, Phe-Cys-Pro-Phe (FCPF), and an environmentally sensitive sulfonyl benzoxadiazole chloride (SBD-Cl) derivative. By screening peptide microenvironments and SBD substituents, we identified FCPF-A15 as a sequence-dependent reaction pair that produces strong fluorogenic activation in vitro and can be genetically inserted at terminal or loop-exposed positions. NMR analysis suggests that A15 conjugation promotes a half-clamp arrangement in which the benzoxadiazole fluorophore is locally confined by the Phe-rich motif, providing a structural basis for enhanced fluorogenic output. The synergy enabled wash-free imaging of proteins in various subcellular locations of living cells. Implementation of a fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) design improved signal-to-noise ratios by up to 20-fold and allowed monitoring of ligand-induced GPCR conformational changes and selected protein-ligand interactions after single-site mutagenesis of native FXPF motifs. In summary, this study positions the FCPF-A15 pair as a compact, genetically encodable fluorogenic reporter chemistry for low-perturbation insertion and FRET-assisted quantitative dynamic readouts, providing a facile approach for wash-free visualization of protein dynamics.

title: DESIGN: a framework for generative AI-enabled crop molecular design-driven breeding
abstract: Crop breeding is shifting from selecting naturally occurring variants to actively designing genetic features. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides a computational foundation for this transition; however, its application in crop systems remains limited. This review bridges this gap by systematically evaluating the translational potential of GenAI for crop molecular design breeding. We examine four major computational architectures and their applications across six key areas relevant to crop breeding: gene regulatory element design, protein engineering, small-molecule generation, gene-editing tool optimization, single-cell modeling, and cross-domain knowledge integration. Building on these advances, we propose the DESIGN framework, which organizes GenAI-enabled breeding into six synergistic capabilities: Discover, Engineer, Simulate, Integrate, Generate, and Navigate, thereby forming a closed-loop system spanning molecular design to field deployment. Finally, we discuss key bottlenecks in data, models, and validation, and outline a roadmap for translating GenAI into breeding practice. This review provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for the emerging paradigm of design-driven crop breeding.

title: A “knob-in-hole” gate in the antibody C H 1 domain underlies subclass-independent IgA hinge cleavage by the commensal metallopeptidase IgAse
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Human immunoglobulin (Ig) A (IgA) protects ≈400 m 2 of mucosae from microbes. Bacterial IgA-peptidases subvert this defense by cleaving the F ab –F c hinge of subclass IgA1 while sparing the hinge-divergent, colon-dominant IgA2 subclass. The exception is IgAse, a ≈140-kDa, seven-domain, membrane-bound metallopeptidase from the colonic commensal Thomasclavelia ramosa that targets both subclasses but no other protein. We previously narrowed the minimal functional assembly down to the IgAse catalytic and wrapping domains (CD and WD) plus the IgA1/2 F ab ′, i.e., the hinge and a F ab of light and heavy chains (LC, HC), each with a variable and a constant Ig domain (V L + C L , V H + C H 1). The transient interaction culminates in cleavage of a proline–valine bond within the first two hinge residues, downstream of a conserved C-terminal C H 1 disulfide (SS2). Here, single-particle cryoelectron microscopy of a disulfide-stabilized minimal IgAse:IgA2 F ab ′ complex yielded high-quality density strongly supporting two states along the cleavage reaction coordinate, a “recognition complex” and a subsequent “precatalytic complex,” in which F ab ′ binds frontally to the IgAse CD via a C H 1 β-sheet and overhang loop LβEβF. This loop binds like a knob to a preformed hole in the active-site cleft. Binding rearranges the knob and rotates SS2 ≈ 180°, enabling access of the hinge into the cleft of the otherwise unaffected precatalytic complex. Together, this work defines a unique, C H 1-mediated hinge-delivering “gate” mechanism, validated by a crystal structure of unbound IgA2 F ab , point mutations disrupting the C H 1:CD interface, and molecular dynamics calculations, which provide the structural framework for subclass-independent IgA cleavage.

title: Enzymatic PET depolymerization: a review of engineering biocatalysts and systems for efficient plastic deconstruction
abstract: The ever-increasing accumulation of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste poses a severe threat to global ecosystems and human health. Biological upcycling (integrating enzymatic depolymerization with microbial conversion of the resulting monomers) has emerged as a promising approach to overcome the limitations of traditional mechanical and chemical recycling. This review provides a systematic and critical synthesis of recent advances in PET bio-upcycling, covering the period from 2016 to 2026. We first discuss the discovery, classification, structural features, and catalytic mechanisms of PET-hydrolyzing enzymes, highlighting the rate-limiting constraints imposed by glass transition temperature, substrate crystallinity, interfacial interactions, and product inhibition. We then evaluate protein engineering strategies that have dramatically enhanced thermostability, substrate binding, and multi-enzyme synergy, yielding benchmark variants capable of near-complete depolymerization of post-consumer PET within hours to days. Concurrent innovations in whole-cell biocatalysis, enzyme immobilization, surface display, and microbial consortia are examined, with emphasis on how metabolic division of labor and substrate channeling can alleviate product inhibition and process mixed plastic waste. We also summarize metabolic engineering efforts that have enabled conversion of PET-derived terephthalic acid (TPA) and ethylene glycol (EG) into more than 25 value-added products, including biopolymers, platform chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and specialty compounds. Finally, we discuss remaining technological barriers, economic feasibility, and future frontiers (including computational enzyme design, synthetic consortia, tandem chemo-biological processes, and industrial-scale demonstration) and propose a phased roadmap for industrial translation. This review aims to provide a comprehensive resource for advancing PET bio-upcycling from laboratory innovation toward practical implementation in a circular plastics economy.

title: Production of recombinant human proteins in Komagataella phaffii using a sucrose-utilization-based selection marker without antibiotic resistance
abstract: Komagataella phaffii (K. phaffii) is one of the most widely used eukaryotic expression systems for recombinant protein production. However, its industrial application is constrained by reliance on traditional antibiotic-based selection and the inability to utilize sucrose. Based on the heterologous expression of the sucrose hydrolase SucF from Aspergillus flavus in K. phaffii, the strain acquired the ability to utilize sucrose. It was verified that this trait can serve as a dominant selection marker under sucrose-selective conditions, making SucF a selection marker for antibiotic-free strain construction. Under a selection pressure of 40 g/L sucrose, the gene integration efficiency reached 100 %, comparable to that of traditional antibiotic selection. Notably, this system enables the substitution of the original glycerol carbon source with sucrose for fermentation. To improve the selection efficiency of SucF, a triple mutant (T65A/R322Q/S323G) was identified through computer-aided protein engineering, exhibiting a 57 % increase in sucrose hydrolysis rate compared to the wild type. Structural analysis revealed that this mutation remodels the sucrose-binding pocket. Ultimately, the SucF mutant was used as a selection marker in combination with the histidine auxotrophic marker (HIS4) to achieve secretory expression of human lactoferrin (hLF) and human osteopontin (hOPN) in the GS115, and the resulting recombinant strain was free of antibiotic gene residues. This sucrose-based antibiotic-free platform in K. phaffii provides a promising strategy for green biomanufacturing and industrial production of recombinant proteins devoid of antibiotic resistance genes.

title: Designer Enzymes: Food-System-Oriented Biocatalysts for Mitigating Mycotoxin Contamination and Reducing Postharvest Grain Loss
abstract: Mycotoxin contamination remains a major challenge to food and feed safety, agricultural productivity, and postharvest resource utilization. Although numerous mycotoxin-transforming enzymes have been discovered and increasingly improved through protein engineering, only a limited number have progressed from laboratory characterization to practical food or feed applications. This translational gap arises because catalytic efficiency alone does not address matrix interference, processing stress, scalable production, formulation, degradation-product safety, and application-specific regulatory requirements. This review critically examines the development of enzyme-based detoxification across major mycotoxin classes, including aflatoxins, deoxynivalenol and related trichothecenes, zearalenone, ochratoxin A, and fumonisins, while explicitly distinguishing the deployment requirements of food and feed systems. Building on evidence from natural enzymes, engineered variants, matrix studies, animal evaluations, and commercially advanced systems, we use the term "Designer Enzymes" to describe a literature-derived, deployment-oriented engineering concept in which intended-use conditions are defined before optimization and used to guide molecular, manufacturing, formulation, safety, and regulatory decisions. A five-dimensional framework encompassing Mechanistic Understanding, Predictive Design Integration, Multi-Objective Optimization, Deployment Readiness, and Safety and Regulatory Preparedness is used as a qualitative diagnostic tool to identify translational bottlenecks rather than as a formally validated numerical scoring system. Representative systems targeting ZEN, DON, AFB1, OTA, and fumonisins are compared to illustrate their contrasting trajectories from mechanistic discovery to practical deployment. Structure-guided engineering, AI-assisted mutation prioritization, stability optimization, Design-Build-Test-Learn workflows, synthetic biology, multi-enzyme systems, scalable production, formulation, and existing pilot-scale or commercial translation are further evaluated according to the specific bottlenecks they are intended to address. Overall, this review argues that the future of enzymatic mycotoxin detoxification depends less on maximizing technological complexity than on integrating mechanistic evidence, application-specific performance, manufacturability, degradation-product safety, and regulatory readiness. The Designer Enzyme concept therefore provides a structured roadmap for directing promising detoxification enzymes toward credible, safe, and scalable food and feed applications.

title: In silico approach to Helicobacter pylori vaccine design
venue: Berichte aus der medizinischen Informatik und Bioinformatik/Journal of integrative bioinformatics
abstract: Abstract Helicobacter pylori , a Gram-negative microorganism, infects over half of the human population worldwide. Its extensive genetic variability and capacity to bypass host immune defences continue to impede the creation of an effective vaccine. Nonetheless, contemporary progress in computational biology and immunoinformatics has introduced innovative methodologies that can substantially support and accelerate vaccine design against this pathogen. In the present work, an in silico strategy was employed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine targeting H. pylori . The FlaA, UreB and PSA D15 proteins were chosen as primary antigens due to their strong immunogenic potential, critical roles in bacterial physiology, and comparatively low sequence variability among strains. Using advanced bioinformatics and immunoinformatics pipelines, potential epitopes for both B-cell and T-cell were identified and assembled through rational protein engineering approaches to generate the final vaccine construct. Before computational validation, the safety of the selected epitopes was predicted through toxicity, allergenticity, and non-homology to human analyses, which resulted on positive results. Furthermore, the construct’s physicochemical parameters were under acceptable values, as for the population coverage. This construct was subsequently analysed through molecular docking simulations to evaluate its interaction with host immune receptors. The obtained results demonstrated that the designed molecule could accomplish stable interactions with high affinity with the immune components, supporting its potential as a viable candidate for experimental validation and subsequent development.

title: A broad-host-range Rhizobium rhizogenes strain enables transient expression across diverse crop species
abstract: Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered Rhizobium rhizogenes strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean (Vicia faba), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. We further demonstrate that both singleton NLRs and sensor-helper NLR pairs from Solanaceae retain effector recognition and cell death activity when transferred into faba bean, establishing a rapid platform for evaluating cross-family transferability of disease-resistance genes. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.

title: Calcium-dependent protein kinase signalling in plant immune responses: current status and future prospects
abstract: Main conclusion This review focuses on the critical role of CDPKs in advancing plant immunity research, highlighting how their functions can uncover key defence mechanisms and bridge critical knowledge gaps in the field. Calcium serves as the cornerstone of immune signalling, propagating pathogen-induced signals through specific sensors and decoders. Among these, calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) stand out as plant-specific signal transducers, directly converting calcium fluxes into defence activation. By modulating key immune components, CDPKs act as key hubs in plant immunity. Deciphering their role and crosstalks with other signalling networks is crucial for understanding the complexities of plant defence mechanisms. Although functional redundancy and extensive crosstalk among CDPK family members have historically hindered precise functional characterization, these features also highlight the robustness and adaptability of plant immune systems. Recent advances including high-throughput transcriptomics, comprehensive CDPK family-wide analyses, and multiplex genome-editing approaches such as CRISPR-Cas-based multi-gene targeting are now enabling finer functional resolution of CDPK members within complex multigene families. This review synthesizes current insights into CDPK-mediated signal transduction, with particular emphasis on their roles in coordinating defence responses and integrating with major signalling pathways, including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades, reactive oxygen species (ROS) signalling, and WRKY transcription factor-mediated gene regulation. Importantly, the continued development of integrative and high-resolution approaches is poised to overcome longstanding limitations in the field, facilitating deeper dissection of CDPK-specific functions. Collectively, these advances position CDPK research at the forefront of plant immunity studies, with strong potential to reveal novel regulatory mechanisms.

title: Homosalate and UVB co-exposure triggers metabolic disruption and impairs energy homeostasis and antioxidant defenses in early life stages of yellowstripe goby (Mugilogobius chulae)
abstract: Homosalate (HMS), an organic UV filter, is a widespread aquatic contaminant that bioaccumulates in marine organisms, but its combined toxicity with UVB radiation remains unclear. In this study, we investigated the embryonic responses of the marine fish Mugilogobius chulae to HMS and UVB-HMS co-exposure across an environmentally relevant (3 μg L -1 ) and a sub-lethal threshold concentration (300 μg L -1 ). Multi-scale toxicity endpoints-spanning molecular (ATP levels and ATPase activity), physiological indices (oxidative stress and lipid metabolism markers), and organismal phenotypes (hatching and early-life phenotypes)-were integrated with untargeted metabolomics to evaluate the ecological risks of HMS. The results showed that single HMS exposure altered energy balance and induced endocrine disruption. UVB radiation markedly enhanced HMS-induced developmental toxicity, leading to impaired hatching. Significant interaction terms confirmed the potentiation by UVB of elevated heart rate, altered spontaneous movement, and phenotypic lipid accumulation under HMS exposure. Physiological responses exhibited divergent patterns across exposure levels, with low-dose co-exposure inducing prominent energy disruption and oxidative stress. Under environmentally relevant exposure, metabolomic analyses showed that combined UVB-HMS exposure triggered broader metabolic rewiring and pronounced oxidative responses, including altered TCA cycle intermediates, enhanced antioxidant defense, and disturbed lipid metabolism, which corresponded to observable lipid accumulation in larvae. Compared with HMS single exposure, UVB exacerbated disruptions in energy metabolism and further impaired neural signaling. Overall, these findings demonstrate that UVB radiation can potentiate HMS toxicity, providing a scientific foundation for ecological risk assessment under multi-stressor scenarios.

title: Magnaporthe oryzae chrysovirus 1-A confers QoI fungicide tolerance in host conidial development
abstract: Rice blast caused by Pyricularia oryzae (syn. Magnaporthe oryzae) is a major fungal disease of rice, and QoI fungicides are widely used for its control. Here, we established a conidium-based assay for evaluating mycovirus-associated fungicide responses using Magnaporthe oryzae chrysovirus 1-A (MoCV1-A)-infected and virus-free isogenic isolates. The conidial development of the two isolates was compared in the presence of azoxystrobin (AZ). MoCV1-A infection significantly reduced sensitivity to AZ at the conidial stage, although infected isolates remained susceptible at higher AZ concentrations. Quantitative RT-PCR showed that transcript levels of genes associated with mitochondrial respiration, cAMP–PKA signaling, and melanin biosynthesis were maintained in MoCV1-A-infected conidia following AZ treatment. The ATP levels of MoCV1-A-infected conidia also were consistently higher than those of virus-free conidia before and after AZ treatment. These results suggest that MoCV1-A infection reduces QoI sensitivity by maintaining cellular energy homeostasis under fungicide stress through a mechanism distinct from target-site mutations.

title: Novel Modifications ΔI127/L85R in FsSdhD Are Involved in Differential Resistance to Pydiflumetofen in Fusarium solani
venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Lentil root rot (LRR), caused by the soil-borne fungal pathogen Fusarium solani, severely threatens lentil production. Pydiflumetofen (Pyd), a succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor (SDHI) fungicide, is applied to manage diseases caused by Fusarium spp. In this study, the frequency distribution of 50% inhibitory concentration (EC50) of F. solani to Pyd was established, and the mean EC50 value was 0.089 ± 0.0080 μg/mL. A total of 12 Pyd-resistant (PydR) mutants were generated through Pyd-taming, and the resistance frequency was 0.6%. Sequence analysis identified that distinct amino acid substitutions, A85 V in FsSdhC2 or L85R, ΔI127, and D128N in FsSdhD, were associated with moderate to high levels of Pyd resistance. Molecular docking indicated that all mutations significantly reduced the binding affinity between Pyd and the FsSdh complex. These findings advance our mechanistic understanding of SDHI resistance and provide scientific directions for controlling LRR using Pyd.

title: A North American mycorrhizal fungus displays zinc tolerance intraspecific variation and protects pines from zinc toxicity
abstract: Soil zinc (Zn) pollution, largely caused by anthropogenic activities such as mining and metal processing, can disrupt metabolism and reproduction, often leading to death. Some fungi can tolerate elevated Zn concentrations, but the mechanisms of Zn tolerance and if and how they affect symbionts are still unclear. To fill these gaps in knowledge, we investigated Zn tolerance in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Suillus tomentosus and its host pine Pinus contorta, two widespread symbiotic partners in American Western forests. Using a combination of whole-genome resequencing, in vitro Zn fungal assays, fungal-pine partner bioassays, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, we found an absence of S. tomentosus population structure based on Zn tolerance, and that the trait is highly polygenic, constitutive, and associated with Zn exclusion and antioxidant responses to mitigate toxicity. We also found that S. tomentosus protects P. contorta from Zn toxicity by increasing seedling performance under Zn stress, with Zn-tolerant S. tomentosus providing slightly more benefit compared with Zn-sensitive S. tomentosus. Our results illustrate that fungal metal tolerance is a complex trait, and that intraspecific variation should be considered for understanding the impacts of environmental stress on biodiversity, as well as for designing effective biotechnological tools and conservation/reforestation strategies.

title: Genotypic Distribution, Resistance Effects, and Breeding Implications of Rice Blast Resistance Genes in 120 Cultivars Released Over the Past Five Decades
abstract: Abstract Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae , is a destructive disease worldwide. Deployment of broad-spectrum resistance ( R ) genes is an effective strategy for sustainable disease control, but the actual resistance effects of individual genes and their combinations in commercial rice cultivars remain largely unknown. In this study, we evaluated 120 main cultivated rice varieties grown over the past five decades in Chadi, a national rice blast resistance identification nursery, Fujian Province, Southeast China. Fifteen well-known R genes ( Pi5/i , Pib , Pid3/25 , Bsr-d1 , Pi9 , Pi2 , Piz‑t , Pigm , Pi1 , Pik‑p , Pik‑m , Pik , Pid2 , Pit , and Pi‑ta ) were screened using molecular markers. Seedling, leaf, and panicle blast resistance were evaluated under natural field conditions. The average number of detected R genes per variety was 1.00 in period A (≤ 1980, n = 24), 1.57 in period B (1981–1999, n = 42), and 1.48 in period C (≥ 2000, n = 54), with the highest value observed in period B. Genes including Pigm , Pi1 , Pid2 , Pid3/25 , and Bsr-d1 exhibited significant negative correlations with seedling blast, tillering blast, mature-stage blast, and the comprehensive resistance index ( P < 0.01), indicating that their presence is associated with enhanced resistance. These findings demonstrate that pyramiding effective broad-spectrum R genes has significantly enhanced blast resistance in modern rice cultivars and provide practical guidance for gene deployment and breeding programs targeting durable and broad-spectrum resistance.

title: Chlorella sorokiniana aqueous extract suppresses Magnaporthe oryzae and rice blast disease
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae , is among the most destructive rice diseases worldwide and remains a major constraint to sustainable rice production. Its importance extends to Europe, including Portugal, the fourth-largest rice-producing country in the European Union, where rice blast remains a major disease threat. Developing effective biobased alternatives to conventional fungicides is therefore relevant for more sustainable management of this disease. This study evaluated the biocontrol potential of an aqueous extract derived from Chlorella sorokiniana biomass against M. oryzae using complementary in vitro , ex vivo , and in planta assays. The extract inhibited mycelial growth in vitro , reaching 66–79% inhibition at 0.1 g L⁻¹, whereas inhibition decreased to 38–45% at the highest concentration tested (1.5 g L⁻¹). At 0.2 g L⁻¹, the extract reduced appressorium formation from 75–96%, indicating an effect on a key infection-related process. This concentration also reduced lesion development on detached rice leaves by more than 75% and decreased rice blast severity by 64.4% following preventive foliar application. Overall, the results show that a C. sorokiniana -derived aqueous extract can suppress M. oryzae at multiple stages of disease development, with direct effects on fungal growth and appressorium formation associated with reduced disease severity. These findings provide proof of concept for using microalgae biomass-derived products as biobased tools for rice blast management. Further studies should identify the compounds responsible for the observed activity, elucidate their modes of action, and evaluate efficacy and formulation under field conditions.

title: Targeting the Erv29 cargo receptor disrupts effector secretion and confers broad-spectrum resistance against fungal pathogens
abstract: Abstract Plant diseases pose threat to global agricultural productivity and food security. Targeting conserved pathogenicity mechanisms offers a sustainable strategy for antifungal development. In plant pathogenic fungi, effectors suppress host immunity to facilitate infection. Given the precise regulation of effector delivery, key components of this secretion pathway emerge as attractive targets for the antifungal agents. Previously, we identified the cargo receptor MoErv29 in Magnaporthe oryzae as a key regulator of effector secretion. Here, in this study, we define MoErv29 cargo recognition mechanism and reveals a critical binding pocket essential for the pathogenicity of M. oryzae . Based on the predicted structure, we discover a small-molecule compound 0442, which inhibits MoErv29 function and reduces the severity of rice blast. The evolutionary conservation of this pocket allowed 0442 to exhibit broad-spectrum activity against a wide range of plant fungal pathogens. Together, these findings establish Erv29 as a validated molecular target and provide a framework for the development of a new class of broad-spectrum antifungal agents.

title: MTC-TCN-Attn: A TCN-Attention-Based Multi-Task Collaborative Prediction Method for Wheat Soil Moisture
abstract: Wheat is one of the most important staple crops worldwide, and soil moisture plays a critical role in regulating crop growth, irrigation management, and agricultural water-use efficiency. Accurate soil moisture prediction is therefore essential for precision agriculture and intelligent irrigation scheduling. However, soil moisture variations are driven by complex interactions among meteorological conditions, soil layers, and temporal dynamics, resulting in strong nonlinear characteristics and long-term dependencies that remain challenging for conventional prediction approaches. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Multi-Task Collaborative Temporal Convolutional Network with Attention (MTC-TCN-Attn) model for multi-variable wheat soil moisture prediction. The proposed framework integrates a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with a multi-head self-attention mechanism, where causal and dilated convolutions are employed to capture multi-scale temporal dependencies, while the attention module adaptively identifies informative time steps and enhances global temporal feature representation. Furthermore, a multi-task collaborative learning strategy based on shared feature representations is developed to exploit the intrinsic correlations among multiple soil-moisture-related variables and improve model generalization. Experiments conducted on wheat field data demonstrate that the proposed MTC-TCN-Attn model outperforms representative benchmark models, including SVR, LSTM, Transformer, and Multi-Task Long Short-Term Memory (MT-LSTM), across all five prediction targets in terms of R2, RMSE, and MAE. For the three principal soil-moisture-state variables, the proposed model achieved R2 values of 0.9147, 0.9651, and 0.9622 for surface soil moisture (SSM), subsurface soil moisture (SUSM), and soil moisture profile (SMP), respectively. Compared with single-task and multi-task TCN baselines, the proposed MTC-TCN-Attn model consistently reduces prediction errors and improves robustness by effectively integrating temporal dependency modeling and cross-task information sharing. The results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective approach for multi-variable soil moisture forecasting and has promising potential for intelligent irrigation management and precision agricultural applications.

title: Enhanced disease resistance in chickpea and canola via MAGPIE: Major‐Effect Allele and Genomic Polygenic Integration for Enhancement
abstract: The global agricultural industry suffers major economic losses due to fungal diseases. Though selective breeding and introgression of resistance genes with major effects have helped to reduce the impact of these diseases, resistance breakdown occurs within a few generations. Quantitative resistance that relies on multiple small effect genes has proven to be more durable than relying on major effect genes. In this study, we present MAGPIE (Major-Effect Allele and Genomic Polygenic Integration for Enhancement), a computational framework that integrates genomic data, predictive breeding approaches, and cross selection to accumulate favorable major-effect alleles and polygenic resistance. MAGPIE was implemented to improve fungal resistance in chickpea and canola. Seven cycles of selection resulted in 76% genetic gain for resistance to Ascochyta blight in chickpea, and 15% genetic gain for blackleg resistance in canola. For both diseases, more than 90% of genetic gain could be attributed to polygenic resistance rather than major effect genes. Progenies from both breeding programs were field validated, with stem breakage being reduced by 9.7% in chickpea, and survival percentage improved by 10% compared to the founder parents in canola. These results highlight the power of integrating genomic data and predictive breeding approaches to deliver durable, polygenic resistance. This work demonstrates a scalable framework for accelerating resistance improvement in crops vulnerable to rapidly evolving fungal pathogens.

title: The Development of Genetically Encoded Tools to Modulate Phosphatidic Acid Level at the Plasma Membrane in planta
abstract: Plants are confronted with a very dynamic climate throughout their whole life. These changes challenge the plants each and every day and put them, and especially crops, under high stress. To gain further insides on how plants react upon stress is there for an important task to for plant scientists, but also for agriculture economy, the bases of our modern living. Phosphatidic acid (PA) was shown to be a very important second messenger in plants to response to stress. PA is a glycerophospholipid that acts as a signaling molecule, but is also the precursor for the synthesis of all other glycerophospholipids, underlining its importance for plants. Past studies showed that elevating PA level, especially at the plasma membrane, is a key mechanism to regulate protein function in response to stress. To better understand how PA regulates stress response is there for an important challenge. The development of new and optimized already existing techniques could help to gain further insides on how PA regulates stress response. Phosphatidic Acid Phosphatases (PAPs) are important regulators of PA level in all eukaryotes, that dephosphorylate PA to diacylglycerol. The protein structure of yeast and mammalian PAPs was well described in the past. Today we know that PAPs generally consist of a N-LIP, C-LIP and Tryptophan domain, as well as of a N-terminal helix and a M-LIP domain, both important for proper protein localization. The presence or absence of the N-terminal helix and the M-LIP domain in the Arabidopsis PAP PAH1 remained elusive. Our bioinformatical analysis suggests the presence of both, a N-terminal helix as well as a M-LIP domain for Arabidopsis PAH1. Transient expression in tobacco leaves showed that full length PAH1 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, plasma membrane and the cytosol, even though these results need to be verified with other approaches. If the N-terminal helix and the M-LIP domain contribute in regulating PAH1 localization still needs to be shown, while our phenotypic studies in transgenic Arabidopsis plants showed that both domains are important for proper PAH1 function. Deleting the N-terminal helix led to more roundish leaves, comparable to the pah1/2 double knock out mutant. PAH1 without the M-LIP domain had no developmental defects, but seedlings treated with salt showed to be less sensitive compared to the controls. Based on recent paper and experiments done in this work, we tried to develop two genetically encoded tools to modify PA level at the plasma membrane in planta. To target both PA modifying tools to the plasma membrane we used the twelve very N-terminal amino acids of CBL1. This amino acid sequence was shown to mediate plasma membrane localization in the past. For protein detection we chose a triple mCherry fusion protein, were the single fluorophores are separated by small linker consisting of eight serine and seven glycine residues. Tei and Baskin introduced in 2020 a tool to upregulate PA level at different membranes in mammalian cells using the Streptomyces sp. strain PMF Phospholipase D (PLD). We tried to use this particular PLD to modify PA level at the plasma membrane in planta. Protein sequence alignments of the PLD against the twelve Arabidopsis thaliana PLDs revealed an amino acid sequence homology of less than 1%, making unwanted protein-protein interactions that regulate the Arabidopsis PLDs unlikely. Transient PLD expression in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves led to a strong cell death response 62 hours after the infiltration. The negative control, the catalytically inactive dPLD, did not lead to this response. Additionally, we tried to develop a tool to downregulate PA level at the plasma membrane called PAP. We used Arabidopsis thaliana PAH1 and modified the protein, based on recent studies and experiments that were done in this work, to minimize the protein in size and avoid unwanted protein-protein interactions. We used different approaches to verify the activity of both, the PLD and the PAP. We co-infiltrated the PLD and the PAP in tobacco leaves with PA specific biosensors and proteins that were shown to be recruited or activated by PA at the plasma membrane. Also, we used thin-layer and gas chromatography to analyze the activity. Unfortunately, all result lead to the conclusion, that both, PLD and PAP, did not modify PA level at the plasma membrane and need further modifications. Taken together this thesis gave novel insides in the structure of Arabidopsis thaliana PAH1 and set the bases for the development of genetically encoded tools to modify PA level at the plasma membrane in planta.

title: Coordinating structure-guided design and cis-regulatory optimization to engineer elite herbicide-tolerance alleles in crops
abstract: Genome editing facilitates the rapid creation of elite alleles, yet identifying editable sites for durable trait improvement without functional trade-offs remains challenging. Most current strategies modify a single genetic axis, limiting their effectiveness and stability. Here we developed a dual-layer allele engineering framework integrating structure-guided protein design with precise cis-regulatory tuning to overcome such constraints. Using rice 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (OsHPPD) as a model, structural analysis enabled the rational design of coding variants that retain enzymatic activity while conferring herbicide resistance. To further enhance resistance, we introduced a highly efficient 22-bp expression-modulating element into the engineered alleles, generating combinatorial coding and regulatory variants with significantly improved resistance, up to four times the recommended field application rate. Importantly, the dual-layer strategy was successfully applied in polyploid wheat, demonstrating its robustness and cross-species applicability. Our work establishes a versatile framework for functional allele engineering, offering a precise and broadly applicable route for crop improvement.
