title: Long-term exposure to laboratory conditions: can adaptation reshape the biology of pathogens?
abstract: Experimental plant pathology relies heavily on in vitro subculturing of bacteria and filamentous pathogens to study their biology and interactions with host plants (Judelson et al., 2009;Kim et al., 2017). Strains are frequently exchanged between research groups and extension services worldwide, and many pathogens of experimental importance are maintained through repeated propagation on artificial media. Although long-term storage at -70°C or lower can reduce the need for subculturing in some species, cryopreservation is not feasible or reliably effective for all pathogens, leaving continued maintenance in culture as the only practical option in some cases. Among 414 oomycete strains evaluated in one preservation study, 264 (64%) remained viable after one year of storage in liquid nitrogen vapor (Nagai et al., 2005). This indicates that cryopreservation may not provide reliable long-term recovery for all strains. Preservation methods that minimize storage-associated alterations have been developed. However, many microbes still lack efficient long-term preservation methods (Prakash et al., 2020). Importantly, maintaining viability alone is insufficient; preserving wild-type biological functionality is equally critical.In this Opinion article, we argue that extended cultivation on synthetic media under controlled conditions may act as an overlooked selective environment that reshapes pathogen biology. We focus on how successive subculturing on artificial media can alter infection-related phenotypes and gene expression. Throughout, we distinguish reversible responses to the current culture environment, persistent regulatory states, and heritable genomic changes because these processes are frequently conflated. Examples spanning several taxonomically diverse pathogen groups are summarized in Table 1. We further discuss how nutrient sensing and cell wall plasticity might mechanistically link laboratory conditions to infection biology and propose that strain history and subculturing practices should be reported as standard experimental variables. We conclude with recommendations for the pathology research community to improve reproducibility and interpretation of infection assays.Repeated subculturing is known to alter pathogenic traits, including virulence-associated phenotypes, in fungal and bacterial pathogens (Chang et al., 2020;Bag et al., 2025). The effects are not always consistent across assays; successive subculture of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum generated degenerate variants with reduced cell-wall-degrading enzyme activity and attenuated virulence in a soil-infestation assay, yet the same variants were indistinguishable from the parental strain using a root-dipping assay (Chang et al., 2020). Oomycetes are no exception: in the fish pathogen Saprolegnia parasitica, successive subculturing reduced virulence in a strain-dependent manner, with virulence restored after passage through the host (Songe et al., 2014). Those authors noted that attenuation had not previously been documented in oomycetes, including plant pathogens. Phytophthora infestans, the causal agent of late blight disease on potato and tomato, is one of the most studied oomycetes (Nowicki et al., 2012). Sporangia of P. infestans produced on artificial media can differ from those produced on host lesions in germination, aggressiveness, and transcriptional profiles, with more extensive transcriptional differences in the isolate with the longer history on agar media (Fry et al., 2019).Transcriptomic comparisons further revealed that culture conditions can alter metabolic and regulatory programs relevant to infection, including elevated levels of stress-response genes and reduced activation of flagellar genes (Fry et al., 2019). Such differences are not universal; when sporangial maturity was standardized, media-and lesion-derived sporangia showed equivalent infection potential and aggressiveness despite subtle transcriptional divergence (Leesutthiphonchai and Judelson, 2019). Experiments using other pathogens demonstrate that repeated cultivation can produce diverse phenotypic and molecular changes. Serial passage of a clonal Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici isolate on axenic media increased fitness under the same culture conditions and generated abundant transposable-element insertions. Most plate-adapted lines showed reduced virulence, although some showed the opposite pattern (López-Díaz et al., 2025). In the bacterial plant pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum, 50 consecutive subcultures rendered both a virulent and an intermediate strain avirulent on tomato, whereas an initially avirulent strain was unaffected; the reduction in virulence was accompanied by increased genomic DNA methylation (Zheng et al., 2024). Comparable changes are documented across oomycetes, fungi, bacteria, viruses and protozoa (Table 1).These observations raise a broader concern. Are we studying pathogens as they exist in nature, or pathogens whose behavior and phenotypes have been shaped in part by their laboratory history?Microbes preferentially assimilate favorable sugars before utilizing other available carbon sources, a phenomenon known as carbon catabolite repression (CCR), first characterized in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and, among filamentous fungi, studied most extensively in Aspergillus nidulans (Adnan et al., 2018). CCR influences numerous functions, including growth and virulence, and in filamentous pathogens this system often involves regulation of cell wall-degrading enzymes. Direct evidence comes from filamentous plant pathogens themselves. For example, in Fusarium oxysporum, disruption of FoSNF1 reduced the expression of cell-wall-degrading enzyme genes and attenuated virulence on Arabidopsis and cabbage (Ospina-Giraldo et al., 2003). Similarly, disruption of MoCreC in Magnaporthe oryzae affected vegetative growth, conidiation, appressorium formation and virulence. It also activated cell-wall-degrading enzyme genes and compromised cell wall integrity (Matar et al., 2017).Deletion of VdCreA or VdCreC in Verticillium dahliae altered growth, microsclerotium formation, virulence and the expression of plant cell-wall-degrading enzymes (Wang et al., 2024). Nutrient sensing at the fungal plasma membrane is crucial for adaptation to changing environments, and multiple receptors are involved in these complex processes (Van Dijck et al., 2017). In Candida albicans, the choice of carbon source affects cell wall structure and consequently influences virulence (Ene et al., 2012). Whether such culture-induced responses remain reversible or become more persistent during repeated media passages is unknown, but either could leave molecular or phenotypic signatures in strains maintained continuously in culture. Although many mechanistic studies have been performed in fungi, oomycetes also respond strongly to environmental nutrient cues, and similar principles may apply (Judelson et al., 2009). Phytophthora species are routinely cultivated on nutrient-rich media such as ryesucrose agar (Judelson et al., 2009), and they utilize glucose, sucrose and maltose as carbon sources (Khalil and Alsanius, 2009). Whether prolonged growth under such conditions affects pathogen cell-wall composition has received little attention.Cell walls of filamentous plant pathogens are in intimate contact with their host plants and contribute to structural integrity, secretion processes, and the formation of infection structures required for host penetration. The cell wall composition of oomycetes differs fundamentally from that of fungi: P. infestans synthesizes walls composed primarily of cellulose and β-glucans rather than the chitin-rich structures characteristic of true fungi (Mélida et al., 2013). The cell wall also has a direct developmental role, since silencing of cellulose synthase genes leaves P. infestans unable to generate functional infection structures, indicating that cellulose is required for the developmental program underlying pathogenesis (Grenville-Briggs et al., 2008). These two observations frame our central hypothesis. Cell walls respond dynamically to nutrient and stress signals. Prolonged growth on carbohydrate-rich media may therefore alter wall composition or remodeling, influencing the infection structures formed by the pathogen. This remains untested, since cellulose and β-glucan content has not been compared between freshly isolated and long-term subcultured Phytophthora strains. We present this as a potential explanation that remains to be experimentally validated, as no study has yet shown that prolonged cultivation alters cellulose or β-glucan abundance in P. infestans. This hypothesis could be tested directly by comparing freshly recovered and serially subcultured isolates using biochemical fractionation and quantitative determination of cellulose and β-glucan content, together with expression analysis of genes involved in cell-wall biosynthesis and remodeling across defined intervals. The question concerns pathogens that can be maintained in culture, whereas obligate biotrophs depend on living host tissue and generally cannot be maintained on artificial media (Kemen and Jones, 2012).Atypical infection phenotypes observed in widely used laboratory strains provide concrete examples of how culture history may influence interpretation of experimental results. The P. infestans isolate 88069 was collected from tomato in the Netherlands in 1988 (Knapova and Gisi, 2002), is thought to have been maintained in culture ever since, and is now central to many molecular studies. Confocal images of this strain in our recent study show germ tubes with swollen apical tips, a morphology that differs from descriptions of field material, although the infection proceeded as expected (Singh et al., 2026). The origin of this phenotype is unresolved. It could reflect prolonged maintenance in culture, the strain background, or the assay conditions, and we present it as an observation requiring investigation rather than as evidence that laboratory adaptation caused it. Natural populations of P. infestans are in any case genetically and phenotypically variable (Wang et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026), and unreported differences in maintenance practice add a further level of variation. These strainto-strain differences do not imply that laboratory strains are "abnormal" or unsuitable for molecular studies. Rather, they highlight the need to consider strain history and experimental context when interpreting infection-associated phenotypes.The central challenge is not whether laboratory strains are useful, since they are indispensable, but whether their biological history is considered when experimental results are interpreted.Repeated propagation keeps a strain alive, but it also exposes it to an artificial environment where selection can favor adaptation to culture. Traits that improve growth, sporulation, or survival in culture may then become enriched, even when they give no advantage during infection of the host.These culture-associated changes can occur at three levels. The first is a reversible physiological or transcriptional response to the current culture environment. The second is a persistent regulatory state, including an epigenetic state, that may survive transfer to a new environment or host. The third is a heritable genomic change, such as a mutation, structural variation, or a transposable-element insertion, that can persist across generations and is harder to reverse. Observations across several pathogens illustrate these levels. In Magnaporthe oryzae, mutations accumulated during subculture prior to any visible change in phenotype (Jeon et al., 2013). In Fusarium graminearum, subculturing lowered virulence and host passage restored it, and the change was accompanied by differences in DNA methylation (Tini et al., 2021). In Botrytis cinerea, eight months of culture reduced virulence, which recovered after host passage; the change was accompanied by substantial changes in DNA methylation, and the authors identified no mutations they considered sufficient to explain it (Breen et al., 2022).No minimally passaged field strain of isolate 88069 is currently available, which limits how directly these questions can be addressed in P. infestans.Laboratory-maintained strains are also often preferred for transformation and other molecular work, because established protocols exist for them. Taken together, the cases in Table 1 do not point to a single mechanism of laboratory adaptation, and the outcomes are not always a loss of virulence, but they do show that culture history deserves consideration as an experimental variable. Addressing this question in P. infestans would require a dedicated experiment. A minimally passaged or freshly recovered isolate would be propagated independently in separate cultures, with defined intervals and material archived throughout. Phenotypes, virulence, transcriptomes, genomes, methylomes and small-RNA profiles could then be assessed over time, and host passage used to test reversibility. Transcriptome data alone cannot determine whether changes in gene expression are associated with DNA methylation or small RNAs, making methylome and small-RNA profiling important complements. Such a design would help distinguish the three levels of change and identify when divergence first becomes detectable.Reproducibility is a persistent concern in experimental plant pathology. We therefore propose that authors report key aspects of a pathogen's maintenance history, including strain origin, year of isolation where known, history on artificial media, storage conditions, and the propagation regime used immediately before experiments. Such reporting requires minimal additional effort but could improve interpretation of infection assays, resistance screens, and comparisons between laboratory-maintained and field isolates. In parallel, improved long-term storage strategies are needed to preserve pathogens while maintaining both viability and wildtype functionality. study of Gram-positive and Gram-negative fish pathogens. title: Screening Central Asian Wheat Germplasm for Powdery Mildew Resistance and Molecular Characterization of Disease Resistance Genes
abstract: Powdery mildew, caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Bgt), is a widespread and destructive wheat disease. Employing host powdery mildew (Pm) resistance genes is the most cost-effective and environmentally sustainable approach to managing this disease. In this study, we evaluated seedling resistance in 192 wheat germplasm accessions from three Central Asian countries, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan, and identified five accessions with high resistance against Bgt isolate E09. Testing with 12 additional Bgt isolates demonstrated that these five accessions may contain broad-spectrum resistance. Molecular analysis using functional Pm resistance gene markers revealed that two durum wheat accessions, ZY110 and ZY117, may carry Pm68, and one common wheat accession, ZY1, may carry a candidate Pm26 allelic variant. Notably, none of the tested known Pm gene markers were detected in ZY47 and ZY95. Morphological and GISH analysis confirmed that ZY47 and ZY95 possess the rye genome (AABBRR). Molecular marker analysis of three F2 segregating populations (ZY110 × Kronos, ZY117 × Langdon, and ZY1 × Chuanmai 42) confirmed that each contained a single resistance gene; the diagnostic markers for Pm68 co-segregated with Bgt resistance, while the marker genotypes for Pm26 co-segregated with the expected recessive inheritance model. Sequence alignment confirmed the full-length sequence of Pm68 in durum wheat accessions ZY110 and ZY117, supporting that Pm68 has been used in Central Asian wheat breeding. The candidate Pm26 allelic variant in ZY1, and the candidate sources of novel rye-derived powdery mildew resistance in accessions ZY47 and ZY95, may enrich the powdery mildew resistance gene pool for wheat breeding.

title: A nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat gene OsCNL1 contributes to strain-specific resistance to bacterial blight in rice
abstract: Bacterial blight (BB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), remains a major threat to rice production, and continued discovery and functional validation of resistance genes remain important for durable disease management. Here, we functionally characterized OsCNL1 (LOC_Os11g37759), a rice coiled-coil (CC)-type nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) gene associated with BB resistance in the resistant line B5N494. OsCNL1 encodes a 968-amino-acid CC type NLR protein and showed pathogen-responsive expression after PXO99A inoculation. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of OsCNL1 in B5N494 reduced resistance, whereas introduction of a genomic OsCNL1 fragment into susceptible backgrounds and overexpression of the full-length coding sequence enhanced resistance to PXO99A. These reciprocal loss- and gain-of-function assays indicate that OsCNL1 is a genetic component that positively regulates BB resistance against specific Xoo strains. Resistance-spectrum assays further showed that the effect associated with OsCNL1 is strain specific and strongly influenced by host genetic background. No major agronomic penalty was observed in the transgenic materials when compared to wild type under the field conditions. Furthermore, heterologous and in planta assays pointed to a potential physical association between the CC-containing region of OsCNL1 and the non-transcription activator-like effector (non-TALE) XopAE, providing a preliminary framework for future mechanistic studies. Overall, our results suggest that the functionally validated CNL-type NLR OsCNL1 participates in strain-specific BB resistance and has potential in resistance pyramiding strategies for rice BB management.

title: Multi-metal screening of candidate herbaceous plants for bioretention under preference uncertainty using SMAA–PROMETHEE II
venue: Journal of Environmental and Agricultural Studies
abstract: Aqueous-phase concentration reduction, accumulation in harvestable shoots, and root retention in bioretention systems may favor different plant species, whereas fixed criterion weights cannot represent uncertainty in management preferences. In pot experiments with four landscape herbaceous species, this study measured aqueous-phase concentration reduction and organ accumulation of Cd, Cu, Pb, and Zn in Poa annua, Lolium perenne, Axonopus compressus, and Festuca arundinacea. Four criteria were constructed: aqueous-phase concentration reduction, shoot accumulation, scenario-dependent root allocation, and a composite measure of cross-metal performance balance. The species were ranked using SMAA–PROMETHEE II with 100,000 sets of Dirichlet-distributed random weights. The species favored by aqueous-phase concentration reduction differed from those favored by tissue accumulation. Under the harvestable-shoot-accumulation scenario, L. perenne had a first-rank probability of 83.92%. Under the root-retention scenario, the first-rank probabilities of L. perenne and P. annua were 57.47% and 42.53%, respectively. Changes in preference thresholds and the structure of g4, as well as comparisons with equal-weight PROMETHEE II, TOPSIS, and VIKOR rankings, did not change the leading candidate, although probability distributions and lower ranks varied. The framework replaces a single fixed-weight ranking with a probabilistic account of candidate competition across management preferences and provides a transparent, reproducible basis for prioritizing subsequent validation and planting decisions under multi-metal exposure.

title: Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Hormonal, miRNA-Associated, and NLR-Linked Aphid Defense in Lycium barbarum
abstract: Aphid infestation constrains goji berry production, yet its defense architecture remains poorly resolved. We integrated comparative transcriptomics, phytohormone profiling, small RNA sequencing, and genome-wide nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) analysis to dissect aphid defense in Lycium barbarum (cv. Ningqi-10)and susceptible L. chinense. Aphid bioassays confirmed that L. barbarum imposes a significant fitness cost on aphids, reducing survival, longevity, and fecundity. Transcriptomic comparison revealed fewer but more defense-enriched differentially expressed genes in the resistant accession. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a stress-associated turquoise module (288 genes, r = 0.981) receptor-like kinases and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) components, bridging extracellular signals sensing and hormone signaling. Phytohormone profiling showed that salicylic acid (SA) accumulated to 72 h, whereas jasmonic acid (JA) peaked transiently at 24 h, producing an increased SA/JA ratio suggesting a shift to SA-dominated signaling. MiR398a-3p and miR319-3p dynamics coincided with this SA/JA shift, suggesting a possible link to hormone-coordinated regulation and candidate targets for validation. NLR analysis identified 151 candidate genes, including 18 L. barbarum-biased NLRs up-regulation under SA-dominated signaling, implying a link to SA signaling. Collectively, these findings support a multi-layered framework integrating SA signaling, transcriptional reprogramming, and coupled miRNA and NLR responses in aphid defense.

title: A multi‐race blast resistance locus identified and validated in US elite rice via association and biparental mapping
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae (syn. Pyricularia oryzae), remains a major disease in US rice (Oryza sativa L.) production, highlighting the need for additional resistance loci and continued development of blast-resistant rice varieties. We evaluated 258 US elite long-grain breeding lines for resistance to four M. oryzae strains representing blast races IB-1, IB-17, IB-49, and IE1K and conducted a genome-wide association study using 543,136 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Thirteen significant loci were detected, including three multi-race resistance loci. The strongest locus, qBlast4.1, overlapped the Pi63 region and conferred resistance to IB-1, IB-49, and IE1K. A second locus, qBlast12.1, located near the Pita gene cluster, contributed resistance to IB-1 and IB-17. qBlast4.1 and qBlast12.1 explained up to 38% and 56% of phenotypic variation, respectively, and jointly accounted for 74% of the variation for IB-1. Both loci were validated in a recombinant inbred line population. Additional screening with eight M. oryzae strains demonstrated complementary resistance profiles for qBlast4.1 and qBlast12.1. These results show that qBlast4.1 confers resistance to multiple blast races. Together, qBlast4.1 and qBlast12.1 provide valuable targets for marker-assisted breeding. Resistant alleles at both loci were present in only 6.4% of elite breeding lines, highlighting substantial opportunities for resistance allele pyramiding.

title: The H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in trained macrophages induced by early respiratory virus infection drives non-T2 asthma in children
abstract: Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. Conversely, treatment of patient monocytes with an NR1D1 agonist led to a marked decrease in IFN-γ production. In mice, non-T2 asthma was significantly inhibited by either the inhibition of H3K27me3, the activation of NR1D1, or the neutralization of IFN-γ. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. Consequently, SAM, NR1D1, and IFN-γ may serve as potential drug targets for the treatment of non-T2 asthma.

title: Type III effectors of symbiotic Rhizobia include diverse predicted transcriptional and post-transcriptional modulators
abstract: Rhizobia are soil bacteria that establish nitrogen-fixing symbioses with legumes. While many rhizobia use a Type III Secretion System to deliver "Nodulation Outer Protein" (Nop) effectors, some uniquely use these proteins to initiate nodule organogenesis, bypassing classical signalling. The molecular functions of these effectors remain largely unknown due to extreme sequence divergence. Using AlphaFold2-mediated structural proteomics, we identified a modular architecture in rhizobial effectors composed of 22 distinct structural units. We reveal that many Nop effectors are cryptic transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulators, harbouring unrecognised nucleic acid-binding modules and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domains. Crucially, these modules are conserved in specific plant pathogens, such as gall-inducing Pantoea, where our predicted structural units align with experimentally validated DNA-binding domains. Furthermore, we discovered the BPN (B3 and PUA-like nucleic acid binding) domain as a structural mimic of plant B3-domain transcription factors, pointing to a direct mechanism for hijacking legume development. Our findings strongly suggest that rhizobia employ a modular domain-fusion strategy to act as direct genetic modulators, uncovering a conserved mechanism used by both symbionts and pathogens to hijack host developmental programmes.

title: Paired TIR-NLRs of Arabidopsis thaliana have diverse recognition and activation mechanisms
abstract: Recognition of pathogens by immune receptors is essential for immune response activation in plants. The NLR (Nucleotide-binding, Leucine-rich repeat) family of intracellular immune receptors recognise the presence of pathogens from within host plant cells. Some NLRs are exclusively ‘paired,’ and require each other for function. With the pathogen sensing and immune activation function separated between the ‘sensor’ and the ‘executor’ NLR, the paired NLR system is promising target for engineering for broad spectrum disease resistance. Here, we review our current understanding of the diversity, molecular mechanism, and evolution of Arabidopsis paired NLRs with N-terminal TIR (Toll, Interleukin-1 receptor) domains (TIR-NLRs). We conclude with examples of paired TIR-NLRs beyond Arabidopsis and Brassicaceae species.

title: A structure–sequence synergistic learning framework for prioritizing functional peptides from food protein hydrolysates
abstract: Food-derived peptide libraries generated by protein hydrolysis are heterogeneous, making screening costly and difficult to scale across assay endpoints. Existing computational approaches rely on sequence information and often fail to capture conformational determinants or maintain robust performance under limited and partially disjoint data settings. We present a structure-sequence synergistic learning framework for prioritizing functional peptide candidates from food protein hydrolysates. The framework combines a pre-trained protein language model for contextual sequence encoding with a geometry-aware graph neural network for three-dimensional structural representation, and fuses both modalities for task-specific prioritization. Using an LC-MS/MS-derived dataset spanning five screening tasks, 6224 labeled peptide-task instances were constructed through docking-informed surrogate supervision. The proposed model achieved an average balanced accuracy of 0.870, exceeding sequence-only and structure-only baselines with average values of 0.838 and 0.799, respectively. The gain was more evident in data-limited tasks, supporting the complementary value of geometric features beyond linear sequence representations. Sample-level rescue showed that structural information corrected more sequence-only errors than it introduced across all tasks. In external peptide-disjoint evaluations on 1383 unseen sequences from three independently collected datasets, the framework retained measurable ranking ability, with PR-AUC values of 0.717, 0.641, and 0.675. Conformational sensitivity analysis supported stable candidate ranking across low-energy conformers, and preliminary assays provided candidate-level validation for WWF and YYW. Overall, this study provides a structure-sequence computational framework for narrowing LC-MS/MS-derived peptide search spaces before synthesis and activity assays.

title: From conservation scores to language models: a feature engineering perspective on machine learning for genetic variant interpretation
abstract: The interpretation of genetic variants remains central to precision medicine, and machine-learning-based variant effect prediction tools have become indispensable for supporting decision-making processes. In this review we trace the progression from hand-crafted features and traditional machine learning classifiers, through supervised ensembles, to deep-learning architectures and foundation models that learn representations directly from biological sequences. We classify methods for genetic variant effect prediction by underlying machine learning model and variant type handled, from missense to non-coding and structural, as well as across feature categories, describing their biological rationale, adoption rate, and known limitations. We further examine three cross-cutting methodological challenges-feature orthogonality, data circularity, and training data bias-that affect reliability and clinical applicability, providing a critical overview of the current landscape and the challenges that lie ahead.

title: InstructPLM-mu: protein fitness prediction from structure instructions
abstract: Multimodal protein language models (PLMs) deliver strong performance on mutation-effect prediction, but training such models from scratch demands substantial computational resources. In this paper, we propose a fine-tuning framework called InstructPLM-mu and investigate the question: Can a pretrained sequence-only PLM, augmented with structural information during fine-tuning, match the performance of end-to-end trained multimodal models? Surprisingly, our experiments show that fine-tuning ESM2 with structural inputs can reach performance comparable to ESM3. To understand how this is achieved, we systematically compare three different feature-fusion designs and fine-tuning recipes. Our results reveal that both the fusion method and the tuning strategy strongly affect final accuracy, indicating that the fine-tuning process is not trivial. We hope this work offers practical guidance for injecting structure into pretrained PLMs and motivates further research on better fusion mechanisms and fine-tuning protocols.

title: Protein large language model–assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration
abstract: Cross-species integration of single-cell transcriptomes requires establishing gene correspondences to enable comparative analysis of expression profiles across organisms. Current approaches predominantly rely on Ensembl homology tables; although gene-family expansion and contraction can reflect biologically meaningful evolutionary divergence, default many-to-many mappings can overweight expanded gene-family signals during integration and generate mapping-associated microclusters that lack clear cell-type identity, thereby complicating direct cell-type alignment. Although restricting mappings to a one-to-one scheme suppresses such artifacts, it reduces the number of homology gene pairs by ∼8% (about 900 pairs). To address this limitation, we develop a protein large language model (pLLM)-based gene homology mapping strategy that boosts the number of homology gene pairs. By enforcing a one-to-one mapping constraint and integrating pLLM-derived representations with sequence similarity, we construct a fused mapping approach, which achieves top performance in a comprehensive benchmark based on a curated cross-species atlas spanning nine data sets, 11 species, and more than 3.2 million cells. Our method further identifies previously unannotated cell-type marker pairs, facilitating novel cross-species marker discovery. These results establish a robust framework for gene homology mapping in cross-species transcriptome integration, improving both accuracy and biological interpretability.

title: Prognostic biomarkers in non‐muscle‐invasive bladder cancer: biological basis and evidence
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To review prognostic and treatment-response biomarkers for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), with particular attention to biological function, specimen type, assay method, statistical evidence, and possible clinical use. METHODS: We conducted a focused narrative search of PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for English-language human studies published from January 2015 to August 2026, supplemented by earlier pivotal studies and reference-list screening. Priority was given to NMIBC cohorts reporting recurrence, progression, survival, or response to intravesical therapy. We considered cohort specificity, sample size, multivariable analysis, testing in an independent population, and assay standardisation. RESULTS: Tumour-tissue markers such as stromal antigen 2 (STAG2), fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), fibroblast activation protein-α, the urokinase plasminogen activator system, and cadherins are linked to chromosomal stability, growth-factor signalling, stromal remodelling, extracellular-matrix invasion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Urinary RNAs and plasma circulating tumour DNA permit non-invasive sampling, although results depend on specimen handling and assay conditions. Blood-derived inflammatory indices are inexpensive but non-specific. Most evidence comes from retrospective single-cohort studies; reported effects and cut-offs are not always consistent, and few markers materially improve clinicopathological models. CONCLUSIONS: None of the biomarkers reviewed can currently replace guideline-based risk stratification or cystoscopic surveillance. Future studies should define assays and thresholds prospectively, test them in independent cohorts, and show that adding a biomarker improves prediction and patient management at an acceptable cost.

title: Protein language models, human NAMs and evidence fusion for allergenicity and immunotoxicity risk assessment of novel food proteins
abstract: Novel food proteins from precision fermentation, edible insects, cell-cultured systems, microbial biomass and protein engineering are expanding faster than traditional toxicology workflows can evaluate them. Their principal safety question is not classical systemic toxicity alone, but whether sequence novelty, post-translational modification, processing, digestion, food-matrix exposure and immune recognition combine to create IgE-mediated allergenicity, coeliac-relevant peptides or broader immunotoxic concern. This review develops a next-generation risk assessment framework in which protein language models, structure prediction, digestomics, immunopeptidomics, human intestinal and immune new approach methodologies (NAMs), exposure modelling and physiologically based kinetic reasoning are integrated into a transparent weight-of-evidence process. The review is deliberately positioned beyond single-tool allergen prediction: it argues that sequence similarity, AI classification and in vitro digestibility become useful for regulatory decision-making only when anchored to an adverse outcome pathway, human-relevant assays, exposure context, uncertainty analysis and external validation. The central conclusion is that AI-enabled NAMs can transform novel protein assessment from a binary hazard screen into a mechanistically interpretable, exposure-aware and decision-oriented system, but only if datasets, benchmark design, applicability domains and reporting standards are improved. An author-proposed scoring rule and a retrospective EFSA yellow-mealworm case illustrate the workflow.

title: RCSB PDB AI Help Desk: retrieval-augmented generation for protein structure deposition support
abstract: Motivation: Structural biologists have contributed more than 260 000 experimentally determined three-dimensional structures of biological macromolecules to the Protein Data Bank. Incoming depositions are validated and biocurated by approximately 20 expert biocurators at the collaborating data centers worldwide. Biocurators at the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics Protein Data Bank, who process more than 40% of global depositions, face growing difficulty sustaining efficient Help Desk operations, having received roughly 19 000 depositor messages across some 8000 entries in 2025. Results: We developed an artificial intelligence Help Desk assistant built on retrieval-augmented generation. Source documents are converted to Markdown with layout preserved, divided by a two-stage chunking procedure, embedded, and stored in a relational vector database. At query time, maximal marginal relevance retrieval selects diverse supporting passages, a topical guardrail filters out-of-scope questions, and a purpose-built system prompt prevents disclosure of internal curation terminology. Separate language model configurations handle question condensing and answer generation. The service runs in production on a container orchestration platform, providing around-the-clock depositor assistance with streaming, citation-backed responses. Availability and implementation: Freely available at https://rcsb-deposit-help.rcsb.org. Source code: https://github.com/rcsb/rcsb-pdb-helpdesk (archived at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19560785).

title: AI-Based Comparison of UniProt annotations and Literature Across Human Kinases
abstract: Curated protein records and their supporting publications organize biological evidence at different levels of detail. Here, we used AI to independently answer a set of biological questions using either UniProt records or the full texts of the literature cited by those records, and then used AI-based evaluation to compare the resulting answers in terms of information coverage and semantic agreement. Fifty human proteins were selected from ten groups in a kinase sequence collection. Target-identity filtering retained 1,749 protein-publication records representing 1,655 distinct publications. For each protein, an AI language model generated one answer set from UniProt and another from the associated literature. A separate AI-based semantic evaluation compared all 2,500 pairwise combinations of the 50 UniProt-derived and 50 literature-derived answer sets, producing 87,500 question-level comparisons. Literature provided answers to 1,211 of 1,750 protein-question combinations, compared with 1,151 for UniProt. After correction for multiple testing across the 35 questions, literature coverage was significantly higher for autoinhibition and inhibitor type. Mean AI-assigned semantic agreement scores were higher for matched protein pairs (0.692) than for unmatched proteins within the same kinase group (0.384) and for proteins from different kinase groups (0.279). The matching literature-derived answer set ranked first for 49 of the 50 UniProt-derived queries, even after questions about gene symbol and kinase family were excluded. The sole exception was GUCY2C, whose UniProt-derived answer set showed slightly greater agreement with the NPR2 literature-derived answer set than with the GUCY2C literature-derived set. TYR proteins had the greatest overall answer coverage, whereas CK1 and RGC proteins had comparatively limited coverage in UniProt and the literature, respectively. Overall, AI analysis showed that UniProt records and their cited publications contain complementary yet strongly protein-specific biological information. Reporting gaps, question scope, and score aggregation influenced apparent agreement, underscoring that the framework evaluates consistency between AI-derived answers, not their biological accuracy.

title: Decoding ferroptosis via integrated multi‐omics analyses in rice blast
abstract: The rice-Magnaporthe oryzae pathosystem is presented as a host-pathogen ferroptosis model. Multi-omics insights connect ferroptosis to several cellular processes, such as iron homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS)/redox imbalance, and polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipid (PUFA-PL) peroxidation, under multiple regulators in rice and M. oryzae, respectively. Interestingly, ferroptosis drives two opposite biological outcomes: fungal infection-related development and rice immunity.

title: Chemical reactions for the ligand-directed modification of native proteins
abstract: Selective modifications of native proteins provide powerful opportunities to study and manipulate biological systems, yet achieving site-selective functionalization remains challenging due to the surfeit of competing amino acids, often addressed by genetic engineering of target proteins. Ligand-directed protein modification addresses these limitations by exploiting reversible molecular recognition to position reactive groups in proximity to a defined protein site, thereby enabling selective covalent modification of native proteins under physiological conditions. Importantly, ligand-directed protein modification is evolving from a specialized labeling methodology into a versatile platform for the selective manipulation of protein function in native biological environments. In this review, we discuss recent advances in ligand-directed strategies that employ synthetically accessible small molecules and peptides as recognition elements. Current approaches are categorized into (i) ligation reactions, in which the ligand remains attached to the protein, (ii) transfer reactions, which install a functional moiety while releasing the ligand, and (iii) ligand-directed catalysis, where ligand-tethered catalysts promote protein-substrate reactions with catalytic turnover. For each strategy, employed chemical reactions, amino acid selectivities, and applications in chemical biology and biotechnology are described. We further compare the strengths and limitations of these approaches considering the balance between reactivity, selectivity, and biocompatibility.

title: A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity
abstract: Stem cells self-organize into models of early development, but even under carefully controlled conditions, the resulting organoids exhibit substantial "inter-individual" heterogeneity. To explore its origins, we generated monoclonal gastruloids, each derived from a single mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC). Molecular profiling revealed extensive heterogeneity: some gastruloids failed to develop, others were biased toward mesodermal or neural fates, and yet others contained cell types atypical of conventional polyclonal gastruloids. Applying DNA Typewriter, a cell lineage recorder, we identified heritable fate biases arising prior to gastruloid induction and found that more closely related founder mESCs give rise to more phenotypically similar gastruloids. Linking mESC subclones to their descendants' fates revealed cryptic, fate-predictive differences in gene expression and chromatin accessibility, including at imprinted, methylation-sensitive loci linked to developmental potency. Intrinsic, heritable fluctuations in mESC state are therefore an important source of organoid heterogeneity, and DNA Typewriter enables high-resolution lineage trees in stem cell models.

title: Surf2Spot: a surface-informed geometry-aware model for predicting partner-independent binder and nanobody design hotspots
abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and nanobody-antigen interactions (NAIs) play essential roles in cellular function, yet potential hotspot prediction remains challenging. We present Surf2Spot, a deep learning framework that integrates sequence embeddings, structural features, and protein surface properties to predicts surface regions with a high propensity to contain PPI hotspot residues. Unlike complex-prediction approaches that require predefined binding partners, Surf2Spot identifies interaction-prone regions directly from target sequences or predicted monomeric structures, enabling partner-independent hotspot prediction. By jointly modeling structural and physicochemical determinants, Surf2Spot achieves strong hotspot prediction performance on curated PPI and NAI datasets, outperforming existing methods in terms of F1-scores and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Case studies on NbPDS1 and VdPDA1 demonstrate that Surf2Spot can identify putative hotspot residues within functional domains that are enriched in experimentally validated binder designs. For the tested targets, Surf2Spot-guided designs (with RFdiffusion and BindCraft) yielded a four-fold increase in successful design throughput and enhanced binding affinities compared to baseline strategies in a target-dependent manner. These results establish Surf2Spot as a powerful tool for hotspot discovery and rational protein engineering.

title: LIF and let die: Generation, mechanistical and structural characterization of bispecific antibodies triggering leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) receptor activation independent of the cytokine LIF
abstract: Here, we report on the generation and characterization of single-domain antibody (sdAb)-derived bispecifics that mimic the function of LIF by triggering agonism on its heterodimeric receptor composed of the subunits LIF receptor (LIFR) and glycoprotein 130 (gp130). For this, LIFR-targeting sdAbs were identified by yeast surface display (YSD) after camelid immunization. Resulting 14 LIFR-specific paratopes were expressed in a bispecific antibody (bsAb) format all harboring the identical gp130-adressing sdAb. Profiling of bsAbs on Ba/F3 cells expressing human LIFR as well as gp130 revealed LIF-like functionality of one bsAb as characterized by the induction of cell proliferation. Cryo-EM structural analysis revealed that the bsAb targets a distinct LIFR epitope, indicating the formation of a receptor architecture that differs from previously reported LIF signaling complex structures. In addition, the identified sdAb-based bispecific LIF mimetic elicited STAT3 phosphorylation in HeLa as well as TF-1 cells naturally expressing the LIF receptor subunits. Moreover, agonism capabilities were further improved by antibody engineering. Taken together, we demonstrate that cytokine members of the IL-6 family can be mimicked by harnessing sdAbs as building blocks.

title: DyME: An MD-based engine exploiting HTP mutagenesis for protein engineering and recognition mimicry
abstract: Protein recognition mimicry (PRM) is of great interest in the field of molecular bioengineering and rational design, with mutagenesis frequently employed to analyze the effects of altering amino acids involved in molecular recognition. The conformational and energetic effects of such alterations can be investigated in detail with the help of molecular dynamics (MD) methodologies. While existing MD-based computational tools can be used to explore a particular set of mutations at a time, suitable for small-scale studies, high-throughput (HTP) exploration of protein recognition for engineering purposes would greatly benefit from an integrative platform that streamlines preparation, mutagenesis, simulation and post-processing of up to several thousand molecular systems, along with robust tools for comprehensive and straightforward comparative analysis. DyME (Dynamic Mutagenesis Engine) is a distributed platform that enables systematic investigations of protein recognition mimicry by combining HTP mutagenesis, solvated MD simulations and a Toolbox for comparative analysis (TCA), including interfacial water-site mapping. DyME uses 3D structural information of any protein-protein or protein-DNA complex as input. Its automated MD-based mutagenesis engine facilitates systematic investigation of how site-specific alterations affect recognition, enabling the organization of single, double and triple modifications into combinatorial libraries for comprehensive comparative analysis. In DyME, relevant MD trajectory-derived data is scavenged and stored into a central database, providing aggregation capabilities that ease multi-feature analysis across an extensive collection of simulations. An interactive web-GUI and specialized widgets simplify preparation and efficient molecular and numerical comparative exploration. DyME's capabilities are evaluated using available experimental data. Its source code is available at https://github.com/pisabarro-group/DYME.

title: Integrative Approaches in Protein Structure/Function Analysis, Design, and Engineering
abstract: Over the past decade, protein design has drawn considerable attention and emerged as a promising tool for sustainable and efficient biocatalytic processes, driven by breakthroughs in DNA sequencing, gene synthesis, bioinformatics, and artificial intelligence. Enabled by strategies such as directed evolution, structure/function analysis, and (semi-)rational design, engineered enzymes can now accommodate nonnatural substrates, catalyze novel reactions, and operate under harsh conditions including elevated temperatures and organic solvents.This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of major strategies in protein design including directed evolution, rational design, and semi-rational design. Emphasis is placed on recent advances in high-throughput screening technologies, identification of functionally critical residues, and optimization of site-specific mutations. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence and multiscale modeling to enzyme design is discussed, highlighting data-driven decision-making and deep learning-assisted prediction of enzymatic performance. Looking forward, biocatalysis is poised to further expand its applications in valorization of renewable resources, biofuels, and synthetic chemistry. Powered by ongoing advances in AI and computational protein design, the development of enzymes with unprecedented catalytic functions is anticipated to accelerate rapidly.

title: RheoScale 2.0: Revealing the hidden roles of protein positions via substitution patterns
abstract: Abstract A central challenge in molecular biology is understanding how amino acid substitutions modulate various features of protein function and stability. To illuminate the complexities of this relationship, high-throughput (HTP) assays are increasingly used to assess site-saturating mutagenesis libraries. A common downstream analysis is to average the set of twenty outcomes at each amino acid position for comparison with structural and evolutionary features. Average values clearly identify positions that tolerate most substitutions (neutral positions) and positions where most substitutions abolish activity (toggle positions). However, average values conceal the existence of rheostat positions, where different amino acid substitutions sample a wide range of outcomes. To quantitatively identify rheostat positions, we previously developed a histogram-based analysis that we here expand by: (i) incorporating new position classes observed in experimental studies of rheostat positions; (ii) formalizing a hierarchy of class assignments; (iii) refining error-based identification of neutral positions; and (iv) statistically assessing the robustness of class assignments to changes in experimental and computational parameters. RheoScale 2.0 is implemented in Excel and newly implemented in Python for facile integration with existing HTP pipelines; all parameters are customizable. Example analyses are shown for three HTP datasets of the SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease. Results illustrate two aspects that influence interpretation of HTP data: First, position assignments (and substitution outcomes) depend highly on the measured feature. Second, many protein positions play multiple roles in the sequence-structure-function relationship. The recognition of varied position roles will advance understanding of pathogen evolution, protein engineering, and variant interpretation for personalized medicine. Summary RheoScale 2.0 improves how high-throughput mutational data are interpreted by identifying protein positions where amino acid substitutions act like biological dimmer switches. By enabling more nuanced assignment of position behavior, beyond neutral or deleterious outcomes, this analysis framework advances studies of sequence-structure-function relationships and has broad relevance for understanding protein evolution, engineering proteins with desired properties, and interpreting variants linked to human disease. title: Scaffold-Constrained Generative Design Overcomes Failure Modes in Computational Protein Engineering
abstract: Applying unconstrained generative protein models to fixed structural scaffolds can produce systematic design artifacts, including glycine enrichment, grammar violations, and discordant complex predictions. We developed DARPinMPNN, a scaffold-constrained computational framework that restricts production sequence generation to permitted DARPin Greek Grammar residue pools. A state-aware chimeric multiple sequence alignment strategy supported AlphaFold2-Multimer (AF2) screening, followed by complementary AlphaFold 3 (AF3) evaluation. Of 15,000 generated variants targeting mesothelin, VEGF-A, and HER2, 149 library designs and five separately analyzed controls had deposited 25-model AF3 results. Using the unrounded median of 25 corrected target-DARPin Ranking Scores, eight library designs passed the threshold of 0.70, all targeting mesothelin, corresponding to 0.053% of the generated library. The highest-ranked design had median corrected RS 0.794; the G3 positive control passed separately with median corrected RS 0.866. AF3 median chain-pair ipTM was lower than AF2 ipTM for 148 of 149 library designs. These results demonstrate target-dependent computational prioritization and cross-predictor discordance, not experimental binding or false-positive rates. The candidates require biophysical and cellular validation.

title: Engineering plant immune receptors for programmable and broad-spectrum disease resistance
abstract: Plants rely on immune receptors to perceive pathogens and activate defense responses, yet naturally evolved receptors are often constrained by limited recognition spectra, pathogen adaptation, and fitness trade-offs. Recent advances in structural biology, protein engineering, and synthetic biology have enabled the rational redesign of plant immune receptors beyond their evolutionary constraints. Here, we review engineering strategies for two major immune receptor classes, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs) and pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). NLR engineering has expanded effector recognition through modification of recognition domains, integrated decoy redesign, artificial binder incorporation, and conditional activation switches, whereas PRR engineering has broadened pathogen perception through receptor transfer, domain recombination, ligand optimization, and synthetic receptor discovery. Beyond receptor recognition, engineering immune signaling components provides additional opportunities to optimize immune outputs and improve resistance durability. We further discuss how exogenous chemical inputs can provide an external layer for conditional activation of engineered immune receptors, enabling immune responses to be tuned while potentially reducing growth costs associated with constitutive defense. Integrating receptor engineering with chemical control and computational design may ultimately enable broad-spectrum, precisely controlled and agronomically relevant disease resistance.

title: A Ca2+ sensor-transcription factor cascade regulates cell-wall fortification and broad-spectrum disease resistance in rice
abstract: sensor RESISTANCE OF RICE TO DISEASES1 (ROD1) is a key regulator of defense against major pathogens, including those causing blast, sheath blight, and bacterial blight. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying ROD1-mediated immune suppression remain largely elusive. Here, we characterize an immune signaling cascade comprising the B3-domain transcription factor OsVAL2, the DOF transcription factor OsDOF3, as well as their downstream target OsCSE encoding a caffeoyl shikimate esterase. We demonstrate that the OsVAL2-OsDOF3-OsCSE module promotes lignin deposition and cell-wall fortification to confer broad-spectrum disease resistance. ROD1 interacts with and sequesters OsVAL2 in the cytoplasm, thereby preventing its nuclear accumulation and subsequent initiation of this immune program. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal regulatory mechanism that maintains immune homeostasis, highlighting the crucial role of cell-wall remodeling in crop disease resistance.

title: Climate-Altered Plant-Pest Interactions: How Rising Temperatures Reconfigure Disease Resistance, Vulnerability and Immune Resilience
venue: Book Publisher International (a part of SCIENCEDOMAIN International)
abstract: Rising temperatures do not act on plant disease through a single linear pathway. They simultaneously alter host immune competence, pathogen and pest performance, vector activity, phenology, tissue physiology and the environmental conditions that permit infection. This critical narrative review evaluates how warming reconfigures plant resistance and vulnerability across molecular, organismal and ecological scales. Literature published from 1 January 1990 to 30 June 2026 was selected through searches of major open scholarly sources, complemented by citation chaining and reference verification. The strongest mechanistic evidence shows that temperature can destabilise nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor function, weaken salicylic-acid and N-hydroxypipecolic-acid defence programmes, suppress particular pattern-triggered responses and redirect growth-defence allocation. Yet these effects are neither universal nor uniformly deleterious. Moderate warming can favour selected pattern-triggered immune outputs, hypersensitive cell death can be uncoupled from pathogen restriction, antiviral RNA silencing may strengthen at higher temperature, root-zone warming can induce systemic protection, and natural genetic variation can preserve resistance under warm conditions. Antagonists also show heterogeneous thermal responses: bacterial virulence traits, fungal and oomycete infection risk, nematode resistance breakdown, insect metabolic demand and geographic redistribution are all temperature dependent, but their optima frequently differ from those of the host. Consequently, disease outcome is best understood as the overlap of host, antagonist and environment-specific thermal response curves rather than as a generic effect of warming. Major weaknesses in the evidence base include reliance on static growth-chamber temperatures, narrow genotype sampling, inconsistent definitions of heat stress, insufficient control of humidity and other covariates, and overreliance on symptoms or hypersensitive response as proxies for resistance. A translationally useful research agenda should prioritise thermally explicit phenotyping, multi-genotype and multi-pathogen validation, fluctuating temperature regimes, mechanistic separation of host and antagonist effects, and field testing of immune nodes that retain function under warming. The emerging goal is not constitutive defence, but temperature-resilient immunity that remains effective without unacceptable penalties to growth and yield.

title: Msx1 orchestrates retinal progenitor cell homeostasis from mechanical locking to synthetic arrest through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway
abstract: Despite the known association between the muscle segment homeobox 1 (Msx1) gene and neural diseases, its function in maintaining homeostasis in adult retinal progenitor cells (RPCs) unclear. We using an in vitro adult RPC model combined with short hairpin RNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, and tandem mass tag -based proteomics define Msx1 as a homeostatic rheostat that orchestrates cell structural dynamics and metabolic signaling pathways. We demonstrate that Msx1 loss triggers a mechanical locking state, defined by a paradoxical uncoupling of actomyosin dynamics: elevated Myh14 coexists with global attenuation of stability factors (Cnn1, Mad2l1b), causing aberrant punctate aggregation of Rho-GTPases and arresting cell movement, with subsequent metabolic paralysis through suppression PI3K/AKT signaling and induction of G2/M cell cycle arrest. Ultimately, these events converge toward synthetic arrest by the transcriptional translational decoupling of ribosomal protein large subunit hubs. These results indicate a severe blockade of de novo protein synthesis. Our findings indicate that Msx1 knockdown not only inhibit cell cycle progression but also disrupt the homeostatic rheostat, causing RPCs to undergo irreversible fate failure via a cascade of mechanical, metabolic, and synthetic failures. This regulatory model offers new insights into retinal regeneration, suggesting that therapeutic restoration of cytoskeletal and translational homeostasis may be required to re-establish the remodeling competence of retinal progenitor cells in degenerative retinal diseases.

title: Integrating longitudinal seizure, medication, and quality of life data into epilepsy eare: A randomized crossover study of an Epic-integrated dashboard
abstract: Objective Epilepsy treatment decisions require clinicians and patients to synthesize longitudinal seizure diaries, anti-seizure medication (ASM) history, quality of life (QOL), and clinical data, which are often distributed across multiple sources. We evaluated whether an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated Epilepsy Dashboard improved patient/caregiver and clinician short-term outcomes compared with standard clinical practice. Methods We conducted a prospective randomized crossover study in outpatient adult and pediatric epilepsy clinics at the University of California, San Francisco. Physicians were randomized to start with Epilepsy-BRIDGE or standard practice and crossed over after a washout interval. Epilepsy-BRIDGE is a custom Epic EHR-integrated epilepsy dashboard displaying longitudinal SeizureTracker™ diary data with overlaid ASMs, QOL scores, recent lab results/medication levels, and epilepsy history. Post-visit surveys assessed patient/caregiver measures of experience and shared review of information, and clinician-rated measures of functional suitability, efficiency, usability, and AAN epilepsy quality measures. Results Thirty-nine patients/caregivers participated, including 20 Epilepsy-BRIDGE encounters and 19 standard-practice encounters. Fourteen clinicians contributed 38 post-visit surveys, including 17 Epilepsy-BRIDGE and 21 standard practice encounters. Clinicians rated Epilepsy-BRIDGE higher for efficiency, completeness, correctness, and relevance, desire for frequent use, and ease of use, and lower for complexity, inconsistency, and cumbersomeness. The majority of patient/caregiver-reported outcomes, including measures related to satisfaction, health literacy, and self-efficacy, did not differ between study arms after the study visit, with the exception of viewing medical information on the computer screen with the physician, which was more frequent during Epilepsy-BRIDGE encounters (11/15, 73.3% vs 3/12, 25.0%; p = 0.02). Significance An EHR-embedded epilepsy dashboard integrating electronic seizure diaries, QOL measures, ASMs, and imaging/EEG reports improved clinician-rated efficiency and health record usability, and increased shared review of clinical information between patients and clinicians. Additional work is needed to evaluate the long-term impact on patient/caregiver outcomes of long-term exposure to integrated epilepsy dashboards.

title: Nuclear localization controls BED-NLR Xa1–mediated immunity in rice
abstract: Transcription activator-like effectors (TALEs) are major virulence factors of Xanthomonas oryzae, the causal agent of bacterial blight in rice. The BED-domain nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor Xa1 confers resistance by recognizing TALEs, but the mechanisms underlying Xa1 activation remain unclear. Here we show that structurally conserved canonical TALEs differ in their ability to activate Xa1, revealing unexpected specificity in effector recognition. Using transient expression assays, endogenous epitope tagging, and prime editing of the native Xa1 locus, we demonstrate that nuclear localization is essential for Xa1-mediated immunity. We identified three functional nuclear localization signals (NLSs) within the Xa1 N-terminal region. Prime-edited rice lines carrying mutations in these motifs exhibited compromised resistance, with mutation of the first NLS causing the strongest susceptibility phenotype. Disruption of the NLS motifs in either Xa1 or TALEs did not prevent their physical interaction, indicating that effector binding can occur independently of nuclear localization. However, only nuclear-localized Xa1 triggered cytosolic Ca2+ influx, a hallmark of immune activation. Together, our results establish nuclear localization as a prerequisite for Xa1 immune function and reveal a nuclear surveillance mechanism for BED-NLR-mediated immunity in plants.

title: Assessment of genetic variability among monoconidial isolates of Magnaporthe grisea causing pearl millet blast in Haryana, India
abstract: Magnaporthe grisea (syn. Pyricularia oryzae) is the causative agent of Pearl millet blast disease and is among the most destructive fungal pathogens affecting various crops from the family Poaceae worldwide. The pathogen's genetic variability plays a critical role in understanding its adaptability, virulence and resistance to control measures. To assess the genetic variability among Magnaporthe grisea isolates (Mg), 16 M. grisea isolates were obtained from pearl millet blast-infected samples collected from different geographical locations of Haryana. The present study was conducted at the Department of Plant Pathology, Chaudhary Charan Singh Haryana Agricultural University, Hisar, during 2021–2022 and evaluated the correlation between genetic variability and geographic distribution. The genetic variability of M. grisea isolates was assessed by using 9 inter-simple sequence repeat (ISSR) molecular markers. The dendrogram based on Jaccard’s similarity index divided 16 M. grisea isolates into 2 major groups at a similarity coefficient of 0.47. Major cluster “A” comprised 13 isolates, while cluster “B” had only 3 isolates. The cluster analysis showed that the isolate Mg 4 collected from Nuh, Mg 6 collected from Rewari and Mg 16 collected from Mahender Garh districts were most diverse and isolates Mg 10 and Mg 12 collected from Charkhi Dadri and Bhiwani districts had the highest similarity coefficient among all 16 M. grisea isolates. The ISSR-based cluster analysis revealed a correlation between the genetic grouping of M. grisea isolates and their geographical origins.

title: Unsupervised discovery of functional sequence patterns from protein language model with MotifAE
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn sequence patterns at evolutionary scale, but these patterns remain inaccessible within these “black box” models. To discover them, we developed MotifAE, an unsupervised framework based on the sparse autoencoder (SAE) architecture that projects pLM embeddings into an interpretable, sparse latent space. MotifAE introduces an additional smoothness loss to encourage coherent feature activation, which markedly improves the identification of known functional motifs compared to the standard SAE. The sequence patterns captured by MotifAE exhibit rich diversity, align with known functional motifs, and are reflected in the model’s weight space. Beyond short motifs, MotifAE also captures some structural domains, with latent feature activation scores correlating with residue importance for diverse domain functions. By aligning MotifAE features with experimental data, we further identified features associated with domain folding stability. These features enable the prediction of a stability-specific fitness landscape. Overall, MotifAE provides a general framework for systematic sequence pattern discovery and interpretation, with the potential to advance protein function analysis, mutation effect interpretation, and rational protein engineering. Protein language models (pLMs) capture biologically meaningful sequence patterns, but the features learned by these models remain largely opaque. Here the authors present MotifAE, an interpretable sparse autoencoder framework that reveals diverse sequence motifs and structural domains from pLM embeddings, improves recovery of known functional motifs and identifies features linked to domain function and folding stability, enabling stability-specific fitness landscape prediction.

title: pLM-HP: Peptide hormone prediction using pre-trained protein language model representations
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Peptide hormones play key roles in metabolic regulation, growth and development, and the maintenance of homeostasis and are important targets for drug discovery and design. However, traditional experimental methods for screening and identifying peptide hormones are costly and inefficient. Although existing machine learning methods have made some progress, they pay limited attention to class imbalance, and there is still room to improve prediction performance. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to develop an effective deep learning framework for imbalanced peptide hormone prediction and to improve the recognition of hormone peptides as the minority class. METHODS: We developed pLM-HP, a deep learning framework based on a pre-trained protein language model. The framework combines the ESM2 protein language model with a bidirectional long short-term memory network. ESM2 was first used to obtain high-dimensional global contextual embeddings from peptide sequences, and BiLSTM was then applied to model sequential dependencies between residues. Class weights were incorporated into the loss function to reduce bias caused by class imbalance. RESULTS: Compared with traditional feature-based methods, pLM-HP achieved a BACC of 95.61% and an MCC of 0.802 in five-fold cross-validation, and a BACC of 95.64% and an MCC of 0.824 on the independent test set. The model also maintained stable and strong performance under imbalanced data conditions. CONCLUSION: These results indicate that combining protein language models with sequence modeling and class-imbalance learning strategies is an effective way to improve peptide hormone prediction. pLM-HP may provide a useful tool for high-throughput functional peptide screening and prioritization of candidate peptide hormones. The source code of pLM-HP is freely available at https://github.com/aochunyan123/pLM-HP.git.

title: A structure-aware generative AI framework for revealing functional relationships in protein families
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Proteins can be studied through their sequence statistics or structural properties. These represent complementary views that are useful but lack a quantitative framework to tell, family by family, which is most informative and how to combine them. We introduce a framework that builds both views in parallel: amino acid (AA) alignments are translated into parallel alignments over a 3D interaction (3Di) structure-informed alphabet. Variational autoencoders compress each into a two-dimensional map, and direct coupling analysis places a shared coevolutionary energy on both maps, turning them into latent generative landscapes. On these landscapes, we define information-theoretic distance metrics that quantify how sequence changes drive structural and functional variation in protein families. We demonstrate the framework on five families: in malate dehydrogenases, the 3Di landscape identifies the structurally conserved scaffold that this family uses to encode thermal adaptation via sequence variability revealed in the AA landscape. In globins and transient receptor potential melastatin (TRPM), the 3Di landscape recovers known functional subfamilies. In the Flaviviridae E1 and E2 glycoproteins, structure reveals evolutionary relationships invisible at the sequence level. Because many sequences encode the same fold, our framework lets us disentangle family-sequence variability from structural and functional variation. These generative landscapes allow sampling near functional regions, and we show they can help us gain mechanistic insight into the evolutionary forces shaping sequence-structure-function variation and guide the design of new proteins.

title: Computational identification of B- and T-cell epitopes: a unified task taxonomy and review of databases, datasets, predictive pipelines, and gaps
abstract: The immune system leverages B and T cells to recognize specific molecular patterns, known as epitopes, on pathogens and cancer cells to effectively combat infections and diseases. The critical success of immunotherapies in cancer treatment and COVID-19 vaccine development has established precise epitope identification as a central and rapidly growing priority in therapeutic design. Because traditional wet-lab based identification of B- and T-cell epitopes is expensive and timeconsuming, our systematic literature search (2015-2026) identified 148 Artificial Intelligence (AI) based linear B-cell, conformational B-cell, and T-cell epitope prediction models within the stated search scope. However, the true potential of these models remains unclear due to fragmented evaluation practices, with models rarely tested across a comprehensive range of datasets, insufficient comparison with existing predictors, systematic under-utilization of available public databases, and other methodological inconsistencies across five different stages of the predictive pipeline. Moreover, the 7 existing review papers fail to adequately highlight these research gaps or to support the development of robust AI models. This review paper consolidates the computational landscape of B-cell and T-cell epitope recognition and introduces a unified taxonomy that organises the field into twelve prediction tasks: linear and conformational B-cell prediction together with ten T-cell subtasks (T1-T10) that span the antigen-recognition cascade from human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing to vaccine design. It analyses these twelve tasks across five major stages of a shared predictive pipeline. Within this taxonomy, the recognition sub-tasks (T1-T7) apply to the epitopes of any antigen, whereas neoantigen identification (T8) and tumor T-cell antigen (TTCA) classification (T9) are oncology-specific translational applications and multi-epitope vaccine design (T10) spans infectious-disease and cancer targets. It systematically examines 155 studies published from 2015 to 2026 to perform comprehensive categorization of 43 dedicated epitope/immunology databases, 144 benchmark datasets, 272 representation learning approaches, 148 classifiers, 54 evaluation and optimization approaches, and 148 predictive models accessibility status across all twelve prediction tasks. Additionally, it highlights persistent challenges across each stage of the predictive pipeline and offers key directions for improvement. This comprehensive analysis provides actionable recommendations for developing more robust, generalizable epitope predictors, and it ultimately accelerates the translation of computational predictions into effective immunotherapies against diverse diseases.

title: Critical review of artificial intelligence in synthetic biology: DBTL cycle applications, challenges, and design rules for microbial strain engineering
venue: World Journal of Microbiology and Biotechnology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the field of synthetic biology research. This approach has the potential to make the design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycle more predictable by improving design prioritization, experimental planning, and data analysis. This review aims to analyze the application of artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and language models, across synthetic biology, specifically neural networks for genetic circuit design, protein engineering, metabolic pathway optimization, and multi-omics data analysis. The main focus is to identify how AI tools are applied across the DBTL cycle, from design to final data analysis, and to assess their validation and evidence levels. The reviewed studies indicate that, in specific applications, AI-based methods can reveal patterns and relationships that may be difficult to identify using conventional approaches, while deep learning (DL) and language models can reveal patterns and relationships that may be difficult to identify using conventional approaches. These studies also indicate that AI methods can improve prediction performance and reduce redundant experiments in specific applications. Furthermore, AI can support high-throughput technologies and has potential for genome-scale design. However, important limitations remain, including uncertainty in model behavior, limited data validation and transparency, difficulties in data analysis and interpretation, uncertainty in model predictions, and safety and ethical concerns. Therefore, the safe and widespread adoption of AI technologies in the healthcare, energy, and environmental biotechnology sectors requires the development of stronger regulatory and ethical standards.
